We find our method increases bias in all models, even those trained with safety guardrails. Our work emphasizes uncovering societal bias in LLMs through rigorous evaluation, addressing adversarial challenges to ensure AI safety in high-stakes industry deployments.
filter_reasoning: This paper focuses on red-teaming methods specifically designed to uncover societal bias in Large Language Models themselves and to evaluate how safety measures mitigate this bias, which is central to AI fairness and safety research.

venue_name: Proceedings of the The 9th Workshop on Online Abuse and Harms (WOAH)
title: Web(er) of Hate: A Survey on How Hate Speech Is Typed
abstract: The curation of hate speech datasets involves complex design decisions that balance competing priorities. This paper critically examines these methodological choices in a diverse range of datasets, highlighting common themes and practices, and their implications for dataset reliability. Drawing on Max Weber's notion of ideal types, we argue for a reflexive approach in dataset creation, urging researchers to acknowledge their own value judgments during dataset construction, fostering transparency and methodological rigour.
filter_reasoning: This paper critically examines the methodological and ethical choices involved in curating datasets for hate speech detection. It discusses 'value judgments' and 'transparency' in dataset construction, which directly relates to bias, fairness, and accountability in the foundational data that AI systems learn from. This is a study of the ethical implications in the creation of AI system components, not merely using AI to solve a problem.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 15th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing and the 5th Conference of the Asia-Pacific Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics
title: LensLapse: In-Browser Logit Lens for Interactive Exploration of Language Model Training Dynamics
abstract: The logit lens is a standard mechanistic interpretability tool for inspecting a Transformer's predictions across layers. However, existing logit lens tools typically focus on individual checkpoints rather than interactive exploration of a model's training history.\par In this study, we introduce LensLapse, an open-source web application for interactive exploration of a model's training history through token-level interpretability. Users can scrub a slider across public checkpoints from five model families and three multilingual checkpoint suites and observe how per-layer, per-position logit lens predictions evolve from frequency bias to factual knowledge.\par For browser-compatible models, arbitrary user prompts are probed live in the browser via local inference over per-checkpoint model pairs. No server, no API key, no hosting cost, and prompts never leave the user's device.\par Moreover, LensLapse supports local models. A single `pip install` enables users to launch the application and explore their own models and training checkpoints without any additional web setup.\par LensLapse is MIT-licensed and permanently hosted at iamtatsuki05.github.io/lenslapse.\par - GitHub: https://github.com/iamtatsuki05/lenslapse - PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/lenslapse/ - docs: https://iamtatsuki05.github.io/lenslapse/docs/ - YouTube: https://youtu.be/OBnvG9Ru3j8
filter_reasoning: The paper introduces a tool for mechanistic interpretability (logit lens) across training dynamics, which is a key technical focus area in AI safety.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 15th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing and the 5th Conference of the Asia-Pacific Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1
title: Embarrassingly Simple Access Control for Large Language Models
abstract: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) is fundamental in secure systems handling healthcare, financial, and government data. Prior work on LLM safety under role constraints has largely relied on fine-tuning or prompting-based enforcement. In contrast, we take a mechanistic view and probe internal representations to identify signals associated with roles, permissions, and refusal behavior. We evaluate this approach across three datasets, database- and department-separated splits, varying policy complexity levels, and adversarial prompts. On the structured Text-to-SQL datasets, simple probes achieve strong performance, reaching average macro-F1 scores of .913 on BIRD and .926 on Spider, while remaining more stable than prompting as policies grow longer. However, probing does not perform equally well in all settings: it underperforms prompting in most OrgAccess comparisons and can degrade substantially under adversarial instructions. Overall, our results show that access-control information can be strongly represented in LLM hidden states, but its usefulness depends on the model, domain, and prompt.
filter_reasoning: The paper investigates internal mechanisms for access control and refusal behavior in LLMs, which relates to robust safety enforcement.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 15th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing and the 5th Conference of the Asia-Pacific Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1
title: Tracing the Genesis of Logic: Causal Data Attribution of Mechanistic Features via Counterfactual Poisoning
abstract: How do interpretable internal features that implement a learned capability emerge during training? We present a mechanistic interpretability study of 3-digit addition in a 19M-parameter transformer trained from scratch, using the grokking transition as a natural microscope for feature genesis. Our framework, Causal Genesis Attribution (CGA), combines checkpoint-resolved training dynamics, Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) feature analysis, and counterfactual training interventions to trace arithmetic and carry features from emergence to causal function. We find layer-4 SAE features that are silent on non-arithmetic text, selective for the arithmetic probes, and co-emerge with validation accuracy at step 500 (near-zero to 85\%). Zero-ablating the top arithmetic features drops exact-match accuracy from 100\% to 0\%, showing that these directions are necessary for the learned addition algorithm. A four-arm intervention study reveals what sustains these features: removing arithmetic data collapses feature activation by 81\%; matched numeric-noise replacement also fails, ruling out surface token statistics; and poisoning answers by +137 hyperactivates features by 27\% while making the model produce systematically shifted outputs. Across four seeds, the genesis detector fires consistently, with detection accuracy stable at 85.6\% \pm 1.0\%. Together, these results provide a mechanistic data--feature--capability chain for an emergent arithmetic reasoning ability.
filter_reasoning: The paper performs mechanistic interpretability research to understand the emergence of capabilities and the causal role of internal features, which is central to AI safety.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 15th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing and the 5th Conference of the Asia-Pacific Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1
title: Decomposing LLM Advice Sycophancy: Content, Style, and Framing Drive Distinct Response Dimensions
abstract: Large language models are widely used for personal advice (relationship conflicts, financial decisions, mental-health support, etc.), but they often align their response with the user's position rather than offering independent judgment, even when users need pushback rather than validation. Mitigating this, whether through training objectives, system-level guardrails, or evaluation design, requires knowing what triggers it. But what in the user's message triggers this behavior is unknown. Natural advice-seeking messages vary simultaneously in semantic content (what is disclosed), linguistic style (how it is written), and narrative framing (whose side is told), but existing benchmarks cannot attribute model behavior to any single cue. Without this attribution, mitigations cannot be targeted, for example, suppressing warmth may harm users with genuine distress but might not fix the model's tendency to endorse whichever side of a conflict speaks. In this work, we isolate which of these cues drive which aspect of sycophantic behavior across 787 advice-seeking scenarios and observe three patterns emerge: emotional warmth is content-driven; stance endorsement is framing-driven: endorsement drops by $\sim50$\% when the same conflict is retold from the opposing perspective; and recommendation directness is style-driven. We also find that hedging reduces rather than increases model endorsement; models do not simply validate vulnerable-sounding users.
filter_reasoning: The paper investigates 'sycophancy' in LLMs, which is a major topic in AI alignment and ethical model behavior.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 15th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing and the 5th Conference of the Asia-Pacific Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1
title: Automatic Evaluation of Mental Health Stigma in Online Communication
abstract: Mental health stigma has profoundly harmful impacts but its complexity makes it difficult to evaluate. Stigma may involve explicit derogation, but also subtler forms of blame, fear, paternalistic pity, social distancing, structural exclusion, and discrimination. We introduce a theory-grounded benchmark for automatic evaluation of mental health stigma in online communication, consisting of naturally occurring online news and social media text annotated with a fine-grained taxonomy of stigma across multiple mental health conditions. Our annotation framework comprises a binary stigma-detection task and a multi-level taxonomy covering (i) stigma mode, (ii) domain, and (iii) specific components of certain forms of stigma. We apply this framework to texts mentioning six mental health conditions and evaluate large language models alongside stigma-related classifiers for detecting sentiment, toxicity, and hate speech. Results show that mental health stigma is not well captured by models trained to detect these neighboring constructs, and that LLMs often overpredict stigma unless given explicit operational rules - mirroring the importance of decision rules in human annotation
filter_reasoning: The paper introduces a framework to detect mental health stigma in AI-generated or online text, addressing a core concern regarding social bias and ethical AI communication.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 15th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing and the 5th Conference of the Asia-Pacific Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1
title: PAIRSAFE: Proxy-Resistant Paired Safety Evaluation for Refusal Boundaries
abstract: Aggregate refusal scores on mixed safe and unsafe prompts can obscure local boundary failures and label-correlated metadata shortcuts. We present PAIRSAFE, Proxy-Resistant Paired Safety Evaluation, a score-agnostic diagnostic protocol built from 150 deterministic, matched XSTest-derived safe/unsafe pairs. PAIRSAFE distinguishes strict pair locks from audited residual fields, then asks whether nuisance proxies collapse, unsafe twins rank above safe twins, and one threshold yields pair-consistent decisions; generated behavior is evaluated separately. Strict source, normalized-type, and pair-ID controls collapse to PSA 0.50 and PCDA 0.00, as required by construction. Residual metadata remain informative: a leakage-safe combined probe obtains nested Cal-PCDA 0.397, yet residualizing model scores against measured metadata leaves substantial paired signal. Direct-logit margins for Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct reach PSA/Cal-PCDA of 0.987/0.880 and 0.973/0.760, respectively. Qwen's secondary generation check is lower again (PCGA 0.700). These disagreements show why local ranking, shared-threshold decisions, and generated responses should not be collapsed into one score. PAIRSAFE is a bounded diagnostic protocol, not a new classifier or deployment certificate.
filter_reasoning: The paper presents a diagnostic protocol for evaluating refusal boundaries and safety in LLMs, addressing critical evaluation flaws in current safety research.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 15th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing and the 5th Conference of the Asia-Pacific Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1
title: ProMoral-Bench: Comparing Prompting Strategies for Moral Judgment and Jailbreak Robustness in LLMs
abstract: Prompt design affects the moral judgments and refusal behavior produced by large language models (LLMs), yet controlled comparisons remain fragmented across datasets and models. We introduce ProMoral-Bench, a benchmark-style comparison of 10 prompting paradigms across four LLM families. Using ETHICS, Scruples, WildJailbreak, and our 200-pair ETHICS-Contrast set, we report task-level metrics together with Moral Competence Score (MCS), jailbreak/over-refusal Safety Robustness Score (SRS), and Unified Moral Safety Score (UMSS). UMSS is a study-specific relative summary of MCS and SRS, not an absolute measure of model safety or moral grounding. In this fixed-template evaluation, compact exemplar-guided scaffolds attain stronger competence-robustness trade-offs at lower token cost than the particular multi-stage variants tested, although multi-stage prompting occasionally improves jailbreak refusal. The few-shot demonstrations are non-overlapping but drawn from the evaluation distributions, so their advantage should not be read as out-of-distribution robustness. Code and data are available at https://github.com/rohanthomas334-sketch/ProMoral_Bench.
filter_reasoning: The paper conducts a comparative study of moral judgments and jailbreak robustness, explicitly engaging with the moral and safety performance of LLMs.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 15th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing and the 5th Conference of the Asia-Pacific Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1
title: Private Evaluation Protocol: Contamination-Resistant Black-Box Evaluation via Public-Slice Surrogates
abstract: Existing paradigms for black-box LLM evaluation by independent third parties share a structural weakness: the testing benchmark must reach the model being evaluated, enabling model developers to game future evaluations through logging or retraining. Ideally, rigorous evaluation would grant evaluators direct access to the model so testing can occur without exposing benchmark contents. However, proprietary black-box models cannot be released to external evaluators, creating a fundamental barrier to independent evaluation. To address this gap, we propose the Private Evaluation Protocol (PEP), a surrogate-based framework for independent evaluation of black-box models without sending the private benchmark to the model developer. PEP releases a small public slice of a held-out benchmark, queries the target model only on that slice, and trains a surrogate from the resulting responses, balancing fidelity to the target model against leakage of the private remainder over a tunable revelation budget. Across six benchmarks, composite leakage scores reliably predict behavioral exposure (r=0.788), and fine-tuned surrogates reach 0.85--0.90 agreement on template-heavy datasets while plateauing below 0.73 on reasoning-heavy datasets. The optimal revelation budget is dataset-dependent, and PEP estimates black-box performance with 5.88 percentage-point MAE, showing the feasibility of private surrogate-based evaluation for structured tasks while protecting the privacy of the held-out benchmark.
filter_reasoning: The paper addresses the challenge of evaluating proprietary LLMs without leaking sensitive benchmark data, which is an important research problem in AI safety and evaluation security.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 15th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing and the 5th Conference of the Asia-Pacific Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1
title: KoEVD: A Korean Benchmark for Metadata-Conditioned Multi-Stage LLM Safety Evaluation
abstract: Large language model (LLM) safety benchmarks often evaluate input risk, response selection, generation, and tool use separately, making comparisons across tasks difficult. We introduce KoEVD (Korean Ethical Violation Dataset), which links five evaluation and analysis tasks through annotated Korean source utterances: input-risk judgment, candidate-response selection, generation safety, response-strategy analysis, and non-executable mock-tool selection. The tasks share source IDs, with task-specific subsets and candidate sampling where required. Built through an approximately 3.5-year human-governed, AI-assisted process, KoEVD contains 13,552 curated user utterances and 71,395 linked response candidates. Across 12 open-weight and commercial models, observed task profiles differ, and aggregate scores obscure variation across severity, explicitness, utterance type, and topic. In matched generation and mock-tool-selection cases, responses classified as safe coexist with unsafe mock-tool choices; pooled unsafe-call rates are 9.73\% and 9.31\% for the classifier-safe and classifier-unsafe groups, respectively, with framing-specific differences. These diagnostic measurements do not establish real-world safety. KoEVD supports detailed Korean safety analysis through contextual annotations and source-linked comparisons.
filter_reasoning: The paper introduces a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating the safety and ethical violations of Korean LLMs across multiple tasks, which is core to safety evaluation.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 15th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing and the 5th Conference of the Asia-Pacific Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1
title: Episodic Memory from Compression Boundaries in Latent Representation Space
abstract: Long-term memory in Large Language Model (LLM) agents requires selective persistence: only a subset of interactions should be consolidated beyond the current context window. Existing memory systems rely on heuristic importance rules or similarity-based novelty, which remain external to the model's internal computation. We propose a geometric principle for memory formation: episodic memory can emerge from compression failure in latent representation space. We approximate the manifold of routine LLM activations using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and define representational surprise as reconstruction error relative to this learned manifold. Deviations from routine structure yield elevated residuals, providing an unsupervised, model-internal signal for memory writing. We demonstrate this principle through ReSuME, a surprise-gated memory mechanism that commits turns to memory only when normalized reconstruction error exceeds a calibrated threshold. In long-horizon multi-turn dialogue settings, representational surprise separates routine, critical, and out-of-distribution states, and achieves a superior performance--memory trade-off against established memory-agent systems (MemGPT, EM-LLM) and unsupervised anomaly detectors, while operating without labels and at substantially lower inference cost than LLM-judge controllers. Covariance-aware normalization further enables robust cross-domain calibration. These results suggest that episodic memory gating in neural agents can be grounded in intrinsic latent geometry rather than externally engineered rules.
filter_reasoning: The paper proposes a novel memory formation mechanism using interpretability-based latent representations, which falls under AI safety/alignment architectures.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 15th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing and the 5th Conference of the Asia-Pacific Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1
title: All Verdicts are Not Equal: Rethinking LLM Judge Reliability
abstract: LLM-as-a-Judge is the standard paradigm for NLP evaluation, yet its systemic reliability remains poorly understood despite being widely treated as a deterministic ground truth. We present a comprehensive reliability audit, stress-testing six frontier models across four benchmarks, five prompt formats, two presentation orders, three sampling temperatures, and ten repetitions per condition. Our empirical analysis reveals severe vulnerabilities: verdicts change across identical replications at temperature zero, position-order swaps flip the majority of verdicts on challenging tasks, and the most deterministic judge achieves perfect consistency by trivially repeating incorrect verdicts, agreeing with ground truth only 51\% of the time. To formalize these multi-faceted failure modes, we introduce the trustworthy verdict rate ($T$), a unified metric capturing the joint probability that an evaluation is reproducible, order-invariant, and accurate. Using $T$ , we derive a theoretical upper bound on accuracy imposed by position bias and show that reliability is item-specific rather than model-level. Finally, we demonstrate that shifting from pairwise win-rate to holistic rubric scoring improves trustworthiness more than any single-format prompting intervention, offering an actionable framework for robust NLP evaluation.
filter_reasoning: This paper performs a systematic audit of 'LLM-as-a-Judge' reliability and formalizes failure modes, directly contributing to the evaluation and safety of AI-based evaluation systems.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 15th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing and the 5th Conference of the Asia-Pacific Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1
title: Forgetting Only What Matters: Layer-Selective Unlearning toward Robust LLMs
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can memorize and reproduce sensitive, copyrighted, or otherwise undesirable training content, creating privacy, safety, and regulatory concerns. Machine unlearning offers a practical alternative to full retraining, but many existing methods apply broad or fixed parameter updates that can degrade utility and remain brittle under deployment changes such as post-training quantization, where forgotten knowledge may partially re-emerge.\par We propose Forgetting Only What Matters via Unlearning Layers (FOM-UL), a layer-level unlearning framework that selects transformer layers using a forget-to-retain significance score. This score identifies layers with high influence on the forget set and low sensitivity to the retain set, allowing FOM-UL to concentrate updates where they are most effective while leaving most of the model unchanged. This targeted update strategy improves the forgetting-utility trade-off and provides an empirical path toward quantization-resilient unlearning by reducing the chance that small, diffuse updates are erased by low-bit rounding.\par Across TOFU, KnowUnDo, and MUSE-style evaluations, FOM-UL reduces residual memorization compared with strong GA, NPO, KLD, SURE, ReLearn, and LUNAR-based baselines while preserving retain-set utility close to the vanilla model. Under 8-bit and 4-bit post-training quantization, FOM-UL maintains a favorable forgetting-utility trade-off, combining competitive memorization suppression with stronger retained utility. Overall, FOM-UL provides an efficient unlearning strategy that improves targeted forgetting, utility preservation, and deployment robustness without claiming formal guarantees of erasure.
filter_reasoning: The paper addresses machine unlearning to remove undesirable training content (privacy and safety) and robustness under post-training changes, which is a core AI safety topic.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 15th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing and the 5th Conference of the Asia-Pacific Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1
title: HALF: Harm-Aware LLM Fairness Evaluation Aligned with Deployment
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed across high-impact domains, from clinical decision support and legal analysis to hiring and education, making fairness and bias evaluation before deployment critical. However, existing evaluations lack grounding in real-world scenarios and do not account for differences in harm severity, e.g., a biased decision in surgery should not be weighed the same as a stylistic bias in text summarization. To address this gap, we introduce HALF (Harm-Aware LLM Fairness), a deployment-aligned framework that assesses model bias in realistic applications and weighs the outcomes by harm severity. HALF organizes evaluation datasets into harm tiers (Severe, Moderate, Mild) based on the specific task and bias type they measure. Harm severity is assigned according to deployment-relevant criteria grounded in regulatory and risk assessment frameworks. Our evaluation results across eight LLMs show that (1) LLMs are not consistently fair across datasets, (2) model size or performance do not guarantee fairness, and (3) reasoning models perform better in medical decision support but worse in education. We conclude that HALF exposes a clear gap between previous benchmarking success and model fairness. All data and code are available at https://github.com/mbzuai-nlp/HALF
filter_reasoning: The paper introduces a framework to evaluate and mitigate AI bias and fairness in high-impact deployment scenarios.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 15th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing and the 5th Conference of the Asia-Pacific Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1
title: The bias is in the generator: locating medical chain-of-thought subgroup gaps upstream of the verifier
abstract: Verifier-guided best-of-$N$ decoding has two stages: a generator samples candidate chains of thought, and a verifier selects among them. A subgroup disparity may already be present in the generator's candidates or be amplified during selection. We separate the two stages using adversarial demographic counterfactuals of medical exam questions. On HuatuoGPT-o1-8B, a substantial race accuracy gap is already present in a single sampled response, before verifier selection. Across seven generators, only Gemma-3-27B-it under Skywork-RM shows significant verifier-induced amplification after multiple-testing correction. Even an oracle selector leaves a residual gap on every medical generator analyzed, showing that correct answers are less often available for one subgroup. Counterfactually paired low-rank adaptation (LoRA) of the generator reduces the single-sample gap on two medical models, although on HuatuoGPT-o1-8B the reduction does not persist after self-judge selection. Single-variant controls indicate that the single-sample reduction is not explained by additional training steps alone. A short fairness instruction modestly reduces the single-sample gap, and a direct preference optimization (DPO) variant of the paired training also reduces it and, on HuatuoGPT-o1-8B, keeps race mention near its baseline rate. For the medical generators studied, candidate generation rather than inference-time selection is the primary locus for mitigating this gap.
filter_reasoning: The paper specifically investigates and proposes methods to mitigate demographic bias and accuracy gaps in medical LLMs, falling squarely under AI ethics.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 15th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing and the 5th Conference of the Asia-Pacific Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1
title: Sparse Autoencoders Can Capture Language-Specific Concepts Across Diverse Languages
abstract: Understanding the multilingual mechanisms of large language models (LLMs) provides insight into how they process different languages, yet this remains challenging. Existing studies often focus on individual neurons, but their polysemantic nature makes it difficult to isolate language-specific units from cross-lingual representations. To address this, we explore sparse autoencoders (SAEs) for their ability to learn monosemantic features that represent concrete and abstract concepts across languages in LLMs. While some of these features are language-independent, the presence of language-specific features remains underexplored. In this work, we introduce $SAE-LAPE$, a method based on feature activation probability, to identify language-specific features within the feed-forward network. We find that many such features predominantly appear in the middle to late layers of the model and are interpretable. These features influence the model's multilingual performance and language output, and can be used for language identification with performance comparable to fastText, along with more interpretability. Our code and complete figures are available https://github.com/LyzanderAndrylie/language-specific-featureshere.
filter_reasoning: The paper uses sparse autoencoders for interpretability of multilingual features, which is a key technical safety methodology.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 15th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing and the 5th Conference of the Asia-Pacific Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1
title: Structural vs Cultural Reasoning: Reliability Limits of LLM-as-a-Judge in Multilingual Evaluation
abstract: LLM-as-a-Judge has emerged as a scalable alternative to human evaluation in multilingual cultural reasoning, yet its reliability for culturally grounded judgments remains poorly understood. We present a human-aligned validation study using the CRaFT framework across Arabic, Bengali, and Spanish, evaluating six judge models, including five open-weight models and GPT-4.1, against paired human annotations across two structurally observable dimensions (Answer Consistency and Explanation Consistency) and three culturally interpretive dimensions (Cultural Fluency, Linguistic Adaptation, and Deviation). Our results reveal a consistent reliability divide: automated judges align substantially better with humans on structural dimensions than on culturally interpretive ones requiring sociocultural reasoning. Reliability further varies across languages, judge architectures, and response-generation models, with several failures reflecting systematic calibration limits rather than prompt underspecification alone. These findings suggest that current automated evaluators are best treated as complementary diagnostic tools rather than replacements for human judgment in culturally sensitive multilingual settings.
filter_reasoning: The paper evaluates LLMs in culturally sensitive contexts and highlights reliability limits in cultural reasoning, which is a key topic in AI ethics.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 15th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing and the 5th Conference of the Asia-Pacific Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1
title: Information-Theoretic Design of Sparse Autoencoder-Based Steering
abstract: Sparse autoencoder (SAE)-based activation steering is a lightweight approach for modifying the behavior of large language models (LLMs) by adding small vectors to hidden states during inference. However, designing effective steering interventions remains challenging. In this work, we develop an information-theoretic framework for analyzing SAE activations through empirical feature-firing distributions. The central object of the framework is the Jensen--Shannon divergence (JSD) between such firing distributions, which quantifies how far a generated or intervened state deviates from a dataset-induced target distribution. Based on an analytic divergence response for virtually shifted states, we construct steering vectors toward the target firing distribution. The same divergence can also be used to monitor deviation from another empirical distribution, such as a general valid-language distribution. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the steering in a question-mode generation task study. We further use teacher-forced pulse experiments to show that local interventions induce structured downstream JSD responses in later layers, and apply the framework to a safety-related target--contrast response setting for feature analysis.
filter_reasoning: The paper addresses activation steering and control of model behavior using sparse autoencoders, which is a key interpretability and safety control mechanism.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 15th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing and the 5th Conference of the Asia-Pacific Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1
title: CHASE: Adversarial Red-Blue Teaming for Improving LLM Safety using Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Despite advances in safety alignment, prompt-rewriting attacks such as persona modulation, fictional framing and persuasion-based reformulation, can bypass safety filters even on frontier models. Existing defenses either rely on non-scalable human curation or white-box optimisation that overfits to specific model internals, leaving aligned models brittle against the very class of adaptive black-box adversaries they will face in deployment. To address this gap, we introduce CHASE (Co-evolutionary Hardening through Adversarial Safety-Escalation), a closed-loop red-blue teaming framework in which a black-box attacker and a safety-aligned defender co-evolve. The attacker is trained via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) under a multiplicative reward that jointly enforces bypass effectiveness and intent fidelity, while the defender is hardened on the harvested adversarial rewrites through a two-stage GRPO + rejection-sampled SFT pipeline balanced with benign data. Evaluated on BeaverTails and JailbreakBench against five held-out attack families (PAIR, TAP, AutoDAN, PAP, Translation), CHASE cuts mean StrongREJECT score by 43.2\% on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with 0\% false refusal on benign (Alpaca) prompts, at a measured helpfulness cost of a 55.6\% refusal rate on XSTest safe prompts and a 1.92-point MT-Bench reduction. A controlled ablation that varies only the training attack distribution shows that this generalisation comes from the template-free attack distribution rather than the pipeline, and the result replicates on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Across the two similarly sized open models we study, these results suggest that template-free RL exploration recovers latent attack primitives that transfer across mechanistically distinct attack families.
filter_reasoning: The paper develops an adversarial red-teaming framework for safety alignment and robustness against jailbreaks.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 15th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing and the 5th Conference of the Asia-Pacific Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1
title: Learning What Is Said, Not How: Stance-Contrastive Learning for Generalizable Hate Speech Detection
abstract: Hate speech classifiers often misclassify counter speech, including condemnation and quotation of hateful content, as hateful because they fail to distinguish propositional content from speaker stance. We identify this issue as content stance conflation and address it as a representation learning problem. We learn stance invariant representations of the same proposition by constructing contrastive pairs that share content but differ in stance. We implement this idea through factorized annotation, stance controlled augmentation, and Stance Contrastive Learning (SCL). On the Implicit Hate Corpus, stance variant augmentation reduces counter speech false positives by 60\%, and SCL further improves cross domain F1 by up to 6.5 points on top of the augmented signal. On SBIC, where use mention conflation is less prominent in the training labels, SCL maintains a low counter speech false positive rate. Semantic similarity pairing on the same augmented data yields no cross domain gain over the model trained without contrastive learning (0.623 vs. 0.625), which identifies the pair construction signal rather than contrastive learning itself as the determining factor.
filter_reasoning: The paper tackles the challenge of bias in hate speech detection by distinguishing stance from content, a core AI ethics problem.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 15th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing and the 5th Conference of the Asia-Pacific Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1
title: Knowing When to Critique: Task-Adaptive Metacognitive Regulation for Reliable LLM Reasoning
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) reason fluently but do not regulate their reasoning: they apply uniform scrutiny to every input, which leaves them vulnerable to adversarial and counterfactual prompts, while indiscriminate critique over-corrects answers that were already sound. We propose MetaCrit, a multi-agent framework grounded in Nelson and Narens' metacognitive regulation theory that calibrates how much critique each task receives. MetaCrit separates regulation into four agents: an object-level generator, a monitoring agent that assesses response validity, a control agent that critiques logical soundness, and a meta-level synthesizer that reconciles their signals into a regulated response. Adaptivity here is input-conditioned intervention strength within a fixed pipeline: all four agents run on every input and what varies is the direction and magnitude of the correction they produce, not which stages execute. Across reasoning, safety, and bias benchmarks, MetaCrit improves truthfulness and logical soundness and reaches zero toxicity on BOLD and HONEST without a reasoning trade-off, whereas the same critique applied indiscriminately degrades performance. The cost is four calls per query, about one sixth of the cost of a dedicated reasoning model of similar accuracy. A writing study shows that MetaCrit is preferred for critical-thinking support, and its agents transfer to existing frameworks without architectural change. Code is available at https://github.com/Paparare/EduThink4AI.
filter_reasoning: The paper proposes a metacognitive regulation framework to improve reliability and robustness against adversarial prompts.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 15th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing and the 5th Conference of the Asia-Pacific Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1
title: Hierarchy Aware Preference Optimization for the Safety of Korean Small Language Models
abstract: Safety alignment of small language models (SLMs) typically incurs an alignment tax: benign prompts are refused along with truly harmful ones. The problem is sharper for Korean SLMs, where limited capacity meets a language whose intent signal is blurred by honorifics. We propose KoSCoPe, which combines a Hierarchical Safety Curriculum, a level-conditional adaptive margin (HARM-DPO), and Counterfactual Consistency Regularization, with a reasoning internalization schedule that recovers 1.5 to 3.2\texttimes inference speed. Across five Korean SLMs of 1.7B to 4B, KoSCoPe achieves the strongest Safety/Over-refusal trade-off among the baselines under our matched protocol and remains competitive with general-purpose models several times larger. Under paired-bootstrap tests, its Safety gains over the matched preference-optimization baselines survive multiple-comparison correction for all but the closest competitor, Cat-DPO, where the gain is smaller but directionally consistent. Preliminary cross-lingual validation on Japanese, Mandarin Chinese, and English suggests the same design can transfer beyond Korean, with larger gains where surface politeness markers are more salient.
filter_reasoning: The paper focuses on safety alignment for language models and mitigating the trade-off between safety and over-refusal.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 15th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing and the 5th Conference of the Asia-Pacific Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1
title: Are Linguistic and Arithmetic Circuits Dissociated in LLMs?
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit both knowledge of language, rendered by, for example, grammatical judgment ability, and abilities to perform tasks through language, such as math-word problem solving. Motivated by neurolinguistic studies of their neural dissociation in human brains, in this study, we investigate the overlap of their circuits in large language models (LLMs). Specifically, we examine the overlap and causal effects between the circuits extracted for linguistic and arithmetic tasks, using controlled materials and circuit discovery methods from the mechanistic interpretability field. Our experiments with five LLMs show that circuit similarity is mostly explained by task domains (linguistic vs. arithmetic), rather than by their input and output vocabularies or by the syntactic similarities between natural-language sentences and arithmetic expressions. This finding suggests that LLMs may process linguistic and arithmetic information using largely separate neural circuits, highlighting an ability-based modular organization of circuits within these models.
filter_reasoning: This paper uses mechanistic interpretability (a core AI safety field) to investigate the neural circuit organization of LLMs.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 15th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing and the 5th Conference of the Asia-Pacific Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1
title: LogicLure: Toward Evidence-Grounded Safe Decision-Making under Hidden Risks
abstract: Safety evaluations of large language models (LLMs) have largely focused on whether models refuse explicitly harmful requests. However, in high-stakes decision-support settings, seemingly legitimate requests may conceal missing information or hidden risk signals. We propose LogicLure, a benchmark for evaluating whether LLMs avoid premature decisions and actively seek evidence under such plausible scenarios with hidden risks. The benchmark spans eight domains and pairs persuasive visible narratives with hidden evidence maps accessible only through verification. Our evaluation measures not only the decision of models, but also whether they ask verification questions and whether their final decision is grounded in the revealed evidence. In our evaluation, the strongest model reaches only 26.4\% evidence-grounded refusal despite 94.7\% overall refusal. Furthermore, we analyze how scenario surface cues, explicit scrutiny setting, and prompt-induced stance shape these decisions. Together, these analyses characterize the key behavioral factors underlying LLM performance on LogicLure. The benchmark and code will be made publicly available.
filter_reasoning: The paper develops a benchmark to evaluate whether LLMs can avoid premature decisions under hidden risks, which is a core safety research topic.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 15th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing and the 5th Conference of the Asia-Pacific Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 2
title: When Does Concept Erasure Change Behavior?
abstract: Concept erasure can remove linearly recoverable information from a representation without showing that this information influenced the model output being evaluated. For linear edits followed by explicit linear output maps, we characterize the resulting logit change using the output map and representation covariance. We then compare downstream effects with control edits matched for validation-side damage to test whether any benefit depends on the targeted concept. On Bios, Least-squares Concept Erasure (LEACE) reduces gender-probe accuracy to chance but changes only about 0.4\% of occupation-logit energy and yields no detectable improvement in true positive rate (TPR) gaps beyond shuffled-label controls. Iterative Nullspace Projection (INLP) changes more occupation-logit energy at higher ranks, but its small, uncertain fairness gains are accompanied by occupation-accuracy loss. A controlled text shortcut yields a large target-specific gain when the classifier relies on the erased marker. In final-state, next-token audits of TinyLlama and Qwen2.5-7B, gender erasure substantially reduces he/she margins but leaves occupation-token choices intact. These results show that successful erasure, output sensitivity, and downstream benefit are distinct and should be evaluated separately.
filter_reasoning: The paper investigates the efficacy of concept erasure techniques (commonly used for fairness/debiasing), showing that successful erasure does not always yield downstream fairness benefits.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 15th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing and the 5th Conference of the Asia-Pacific Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 2
title: The Missing ``I Don't Know'': Why Three Reasoning-Reliability Findings Converge on Calibrated Abstention
abstract: Three recent results describe what look like unrelated LLM reliability problems. Yin et al. (2026) show reasoning RL collapses tool-reliability representations. Suleymanov et al. (2026) show that under safety-constrained generation, large models rewrite flagged spans while small models truncate. Bastounis et al. (2024) prove any consistent-reasoning system without an implicit ``I don't know'' function must hallucinate infinitely often on broad problem classes. We argue these findings converge on a single intervention: calibrated abstention is what each independently identifies as the missing capability, even though the unavailability they document, a capability gap, a policy gap, and a recursion-theoretic gap, has a different source in each case. Honesty post-training has narrowed the gap in deployed models, but principled closure of the class Bastounis identifies requires a calibrated abstention function whose training signal at the leaderboard level is absent: dominant benchmarks assign zero reward to decline, so the leaderboard gradient that would select for the function does not exist. We propose four changes to evaluation: triple-scoring, abstention-rate reporting, capability-stratified evaluation, and mandatory calibration metrics. Benchmark reform is necessary, not sufficient, for closing the gap the theorem identifies.
filter_reasoning: The paper discusses the need for models to know when they do not know (calibrated abstention) to prevent hallucination, which is a core safety requirement for reliable systems.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 15th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing and the 5th Conference of the Asia-Pacific Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 2
title: Language Triggers Hijack Language Circuits: A Mechanistic Analysis of Backdoor Behaviors in Large Language Models
abstract: Backdoor attacks pose significant security risks for Large Language Models (LLMs), yet the internal mechanisms by which triggers operate remain poorly understood. We present the first mechanistic analysis of trigger-induced language-switching backdoors injected during pre-training, studying the Gaperon model family (1B, 8B and 24B). Using activation patching, we localize trigger formation and identify which attention heads process trigger and natural language information. Our central finding is that trigger heads substantially overlap with heads naturally encoding output language across model scales, with Jaccard indices between 0.18 and 0.43 over the top 10 heads identified. This suggests that backdoor triggers do not form new circuits but instead co-opt the model's existing language components and representations. These findings have implications for backdoor defense as detection methods and mitigation strategies could leverage this entanglement between triggers and natural behaviors. More broadly, our work represents a first step toward a more realistic mechanistic understanding of pre-training-injected backdoors in LLMs, paving the way for principled, interpretability-driven defenses.
filter_reasoning: The paper uses mechanistic interpretability to analyze backdoor behaviors in LLMs, which is a core topic in AI safety/robustness.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 15th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing and the 5th Conference of the Asia-Pacific Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 2
title: The Guardrail Trinity: Procedural Safety Schemas, Reasoning Chain Decomposition, and Dual-Mode Inference for LLM Guardrails
abstract: Effective LLM safety guardrails must balance adversarial robustness, custom-policy adaptability, and precision on benign prompts with sensitive vocabulary. We introduce the Guardrail Trinity, a data-curation recipe combining procedural safety schemas, reasoning chain decomposition with hard-negative supervision, and a hybrid data blend for fast and slow inference. Experiments across Llama-3.1 and Qwen3 models yield three practical insights. First, strong standard moderation scores can conceal a custom-policy compliance gap; procedural schema variation improves adaptation on our held-out policy-shift probe. Second, augmentation must be matched to model scale and training recipe: smaller models can exhibit training instability, while hard negatives at larger scales can reduce false alarms at a cost to harmful-input recall. Third, hybrid training supports both direct classification and reasoning, with the fast mode retaining strong custom-policy compliance without generating a chain. Together, these findings motivate a deployment playbook that selects data composition, inference mode, and scale jointly, and validates both policy adherence and the trade-off between missed harms and false alarms.
filter_reasoning: The paper focuses on developing and evaluating safety guardrails for LLMs, specifically addressing adversarial robustness and policy compliance.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 15th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing and the 5th Conference of the Asia-Pacific Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 2
title: Auditing Bias Detection Under Source Shift: A Source-Aware Benchmark and Evaluation Protocol
abstract: Bias-detection benchmarks routinely report accuracies above 90\%, but a high number can reflect where a sentence came from as much as whether it contains a stereotype or an unfair claim about a group. We treat this as an evaluation problem and propose an integrated auditing protocol that makes source confounding measurable: an LLM-assisted label audit with cross-family verification, pair-aware splitting with role tracking, source-aware evaluation with a source-only baseline on the actual test split, counterfactual discrimination, and an artifact analysis of edited text. We apply it to a three-source corpus of 10,304 sentences that we audit and release. The audit reduces the global source-only majority baseline from 95.0\% to 55.4\%, and the same protocol shows that the real-only test split still carries a 77.6\% source-only baseline, so confounding is reduced and measured but far from eliminated. Against that baseline, fine-tuned BERT and GPT-2 gain roughly 18 pp and outperform attention-derived models; four augmentation variants that look ordered in the mean fall within seed variance under paired testing; and a real-vs-edited probe separates Gemini counterfactuals from real text, although the signal disappears once the gold label is held fixed and has no measurable accuracy effect. Applied to CrowS-Pairs, the label audit flags 33.2\% of the supposedly neutral members as still containing a group-level stereotype. The main contribution is the protocol, which exposes confounding that standard pipelines would report as results.
filter_reasoning: The paper presents a framework to audit and measure bias in AI systems, directly addressing fairness and social bias.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2nd Workshop on NLP for Languages Using Arabic Script
title: DeformAR: A Visual Analytics Framework for Evaluation of Arabic Named Entity Recognition
abstract: Arabic Named Entity Recognition (ANER) presents challenges due to its linguistic characteristics (Qu et al., 2023). While Transformer models have advanced ANER, evaluation still relies heavily on aggregate metrics like F1 score that obscure the interplay between data characteristics, model behaviour, and error patterns. We present DeformAR, a diagnostic visual analytics framework for evaluating and diagnosing Arabic NER systems through structured, component-level analysis and interpretability. DeformAR integrates quantitative metrics with interactive visualizations to support systematic error analysis, dataset and model debugging. In a case study on ANERCorp, DeformAR identifies annotation mistakes, model calibration issues, and subcomponent interaction effects. To our knowledge, this is the first open-source framework for component-level diagnostic evaluation and interpretability in Arabic NER, available at https://github.com/ay94/DeformAR.
filter_reasoning: The focus is on diagnostic evaluation, interpretability, and error analysis of NLP models, which falls under transparency/interpretability.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2nd Workshop on NLP for Languages Using Arabic Script
title: HACS-TL: Cross-Script Transfer Learning for Hausa Ajami Hate Speech Detection Using Transformer-Based Architecture
abstract: The Arabic-derived scripts contain several languages that face challenges with the limited resources of speech detection, these challenges are worsened by the scarcity of resources and highly complex linguistic challenges. We proposed ( HACS-TL Hausa Ajami Cross-Script Transfer Learning) a brand new transformer-based architecture that focuses on the detection of hate speech within Ajami script. Hausa is a Chadic language which contains over 77 million speakers located in West Africa; it uses two types of scripts: the Latin (Boko) and the Arabic-derived Ajami which creates new computational difficulties. Our method combines scripts of artistically converted linguistics, augmented cross script multi-head attention, and dialect feature extraction to trellis the morphophonological depth of the Hausa. After a thorough examination using stratified cross-validation along with systemically augmented data, HACS-TL obtained a Macro F1 score of 76.09\% which is a significant improvement from the other multilingual baselines (mBERT (69.17 \% ) XLM-RoBERTa (73.20 \% ) AraBERT (58.63\% ) ) HACS-TL outperformed all of the previously stated models. Strong multilingual baselines refer to the other stated models; AraBERT (58.63) XLM-RoBERTa (73.20) mBERT (69.17) HACS-TL 70.73 + 10 \% Cross-Script+ (mBERT) 46.73 + 0.9 \% Cross-Script + AraBERT. The importance of cross-script attention and learning from transfer sources of resources to languages with limited scripts has proven effective. Our systematic method has aided the advancement of Arabic script homage Hausa and African language resources for the NLP of the Nubians in learning African languages and the intricate Nubian and cross-learning systems from different scripts.
filter_reasoning: The primary contribution is hate speech detection, which is a core task within AI ethics.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2nd Workshop on NLP for Languages Using Arabic Script
title: Optimizer Choice and Calibration for QARiB on Arabic-Script Social Media Offensive Language Detection
abstract: Optimizer choice is a central hyperparameter in fine-tuning transformer models, yet its impact remains under-studied for Arabic-script social media classification un der class imbalance. We compare Adam, AdamW, and SGD for fine-tuning QARiB on two Arabic offensive-language bench marks, OffensEval20 and MPOLD, using a controlled grid over learning rate, weight decay, and warmup, and report test-set performance as mean (std) over three random seeds. Minority-class discrimination is evaluated using macro-F1 and AUC-PROFF, while calibration is assessed via expected calibration error (ECE), reliability diagrams, and proper scoring rules (Brier score and negative log-likelihood, NLL). Across both datasets, AdamW and Adam are consistently strong and closely matched when properly tuned, whereas SGD substantially underperforms under the same tuning bud get and exhibits higher seed sensitivity. We observe non-trivial miscalibration across optimizers; post-hoc temperature scaling offers a low-cost adjustment, yielding modest, dataset-dependent changes in calibration while preserving ranking-based discrimination. We further evaluate a practical decision-rule step by optimizing the classification threshold on the validation set and applying it to test predictions, and provide qualitative examples il lustrating typical optimizer-dependent confidence behaviors. In practice, for Arabic offensive-language detection under imbalance, we recommend starting from a tuned AdamW or Adam baseline; when calibrated probabilities are required for thresholding or triage, temperature scaling can be applied. We will release a reproducible pipeline to support further evaluation of optimizer--calibration trade-offs in Arabic-script safety tasks.
filter_reasoning: The paper focuses on toxicity detection, calibration, and bias/fairness in the context of offensive language detection.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2nd Workshop on NLP for Languages Using Arabic Script
title: A Hybrid Confidence-Aware Framework for Arabic Toxicity Detection in Social Media
abstract: Automatic detection of toxic and offensive content in Arabic social media is a challenging task due to rich morphology, dialectal variation, and noisy writing styles. While transformer-based language models have achieved strong performance, they often produce uncertain predictions in borderline cases. This paper presents a hybrid framework for Arabic toxicity detection that combines a pretrained Arabic-specific transformer model with a confidence-aware rule-based mechanism. The proposed approach activates automatically induced lexical rules only when the model prediction falls within a predefined gray zone of uncertainty, preserving neural dominance while improving robustness and interpretability. Experiments conducted on a manually annotated dataset of 35,000 Arabic posts demonstrate that the hybrid approach achieves consistent improvements over the baseline model, particularly in reducing false negatives for toxic content. The results indicate that selective rule activation is an effective strategy for enhancing reliability in real-world Arabic social media moderation systems.
filter_reasoning: The paper focuses on toxicity detection, interpretability, and enhancing the reliability of moderation systems.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2nd Workshop on NLP for Languages Using Arabic Script
title: XLMR-Urdu at AbjadGenEval Shared Task: A Data-Centric Transformer-Based Approach for AI-Generated Urdu Text Detection
abstract: The rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs) has led to a substantial increase in automatically generated textual content, raising concerns regarding misinformation, plagiarism, and authorship verification. These challenges are particularly pronounced for low-resource languages such as Urdu, where limited annotated data and complex linguistic properties hinder robust detection. In this paper, we present a transformer-based approach for binary classification of human-written versus AI-generated Urdu text, developed for the AbjadGenEval Task 2 shared task. Beyond model fine-tuning, we adopt a data-centric perspective, emphasizing dataset diagnostics, document-level inference, and calibration strategies. Our system achieves strong performance on the official test set, with an F1-score of 88.68\% and balanced accuracy of 88.71\%. Through empirical analysis, we demonstrate that dataset characteristics and generator-specific artifacts play a dominant role in model generalization, highlighting critical directions for future research in low-resource AI-generated text detection.
filter_reasoning: The paper deals with AI-generated text detection, a significant challenge for information integrity and authenticity.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2nd Workshop on NLP for Languages Using Arabic Script
title: A Stylometric and Statistical Pipeline for Urdu AI-Generated Text Classification
abstract: The proliferation of Large Language Models (LLMs) has introduced significant challenges regarding algorithmic bias, privacy, and the authenticity of digital content. While detection mechanisms for English are maturing, low-resource languages like Urdu---spoken by over 100 million people---require dedicated research. In this paper, we present a technical framework for Urdu AI-generated text detection developed for the *ACL shared task. We propose a hybrid pipeline that combines TF-IDF Character N-grams with a custom stylometric feature extractor designed to capture unique Urdu linguistic markers, including repeated word ratios, punctuation density, and formal function markers. Using a Linear Support Vector Machine (SVM) optimized via Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), our system achieves a balanced accuracy and $F_1$-score of 87.80\% on a dataset of 6,800 records. Our results demonstrate that a computationally efficient, classical machine learning approach---prioritizing stylistic signals over heavy preprocessing---remains highly effective for distinguishing between human-written and AI-generated Urdu text.
filter_reasoning: The paper focuses on AI-generated text detection for integrity and authenticity, which is a core AI ethics concern.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2nd Workshop on NLP for Languages Using Arabic Script
title: Kashif-AI at AbjadGenEval Shared Task: A Transformer-based Approach for Arabic AI-Generated Text Detection
abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) become increasingly proficient at generating human-like text, distinguishing between human-written and machine-generated content has become a critical challenge for information integrity. This paper presents Kashif-AI, a system developed for the AbjadGenEval Task 1: AI-Generated Arabic Text Detection. The approach leverages fine-tuned Arabic Pre-trained Language Models (PLMs), specifically MARBERT and CAMeLBERT, to classify news articles. A rigorous ablation study was conducted to evaluate the impact of data augmentation, comparing models trained on the official shared task data against those trained on a combined corpus of over 47,000 samples. While near-perfect performance was observed during validation, the blind test set evaluation revealed a significant generalization gap. Contrary to expectations, data augmentation resulted in performance degradation due to domain shifts. The best-performing configuration, which utilized CAMeLBERT-Mix trained on the original dataset, achieved an F1-score of 66.29\% and an Accuracy of 70.5\% on the blind test set.
filter_reasoning: The paper addresses AI-generated text detection, which is critical for information integrity.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 64th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 3
title: Interpreto: An Explainability Library for Transformers
abstract: Interpreto is an open-source Python library for interpreting HuggingFace language models, from early BERT variants to LLMs. It provides two complementary families of methods: attribution methods and concept-based explanations. The library bridges recent research and practical tooling by exposing explanation workflows through a unified API for both classification and text generation. A key differentiator is its end-to-end concept-based pipeline (from activation extraction to concept learning, interpretation, and scoring), which goes beyond feature-level attributions and is uncommon in existing libraries.
filter_reasoning: The paper introduces a library specifically for interpretability and explainability, which is a key component of AI safety.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 64th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 3
title: AInterviewer: A Platform for Designing and Conducting AI-led Qualitative Interviews
abstract: There are now multiple proposals for systems based on Large Language Models(LLMs) to conduct automated qualitative interviews. This approach scales up qualitative interview techniques that have traditionally been constrained by the high costs of data collection. However, most of the current solutions rely on proprietary LLMs, which compromise reproducibility and data security. They also rely on LLMs for all interview tasks, which limits standardisation of question wording as well as control over question order. To address these issues, we introduce the AInterviewer platform, based on a multi-agent framework that combines controlled question administration of survey software with the flexibility of LLMs. AInterviewer can run with locally hosted models to ensure security and transparency. Our platform provides a web-based GUI supporting each phase of data collection: from interview guide design and pilot testing to interview distribution and data collection monitoring.
filter_reasoning: The paper focuses on creating a platform that enforces transparency, reproducibility, and data security in qualitative research AI.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 64th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 3
title: DialogGuard: Multi-Agent Psychosocial Safety Evaluation Interface of Sensitive LLM Responses
abstract: LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed for mental-health support and crisis counselling, yet recent evaluations reveal that commercial therapy chatbots respond appropriately only about half the time in clinical scenarios.Clinicians and safety engineers are called upon to audit these systems, but existing tools do not surface the subtler psychosocial harms (manipulation, discrimination, psychological distress) nor produce the explainable rationales that practitioners need.We present DialogGuard, an open-source system that lets practitioners inspect, stress-test, and create audit trails for prompted LLM agents across five psychosocial safety dimensions.The system wraps around arbitrary generative models through four LLM-as-a-judge pipelines (single-agent scoring, dual-agent correction, multi-agent debate, and majority voting), each grounded in shared three-level rubrics.Through its web interface, practitioners evaluate agents in two modes (Live Chat and Manual Input) and review per-dimension risk scores with natural-language rationales.Experiments on PKU-SafeRLHF show that dual-agent correction provides the best accuracy-robustness trade-off, and a formative study with 12~practitioners confirms that the system supports prompt auditing, safety inspection, and supervisory decision-making.Code and demo: https://github.com/lhannnn/dialogguard-web.
filter_reasoning: The paper addresses psychosocial harms and the auditability of safety for LLMs in mental health support contexts.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 64th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 3
title: Copyright Detective: A Forensic System to Evidence LLMs Flickering Copyright Leakage Risks
abstract: We present Copyright Detective, the first interactive forensic system for detecting, analyzing, and visualizing potential copyright risks in LLM outputs. The system treats copyright infringement versus compliance as an evidence discovery process rather than a static classification task due to the complex nature of copyright law. It integrates multiple detection paradigms, including content recall testing, paraphrase-level similarity analysis, persuasive jailbreak probing, and unlearning verification, within a unified and extensible framework. Through interactive prompting, response collection, and iterative workflows, our system enables systematic auditing of verbatim memorization and paraphrase-level leakage, supporting responsible deployment and transparent evaluation of LLM copyright risks even with black-box access. In our experiments with GPT-4o-mini, we demonstrate that the specific persuasive strategy ``Pathos'' shifts the leakage distribution from about 0.1 (ROUGE-L) to 0.7. Our live system is hosted on https://copyright-detective.streamlit.appStreamlit server, with a https://youtu.be/z9Lh4kNDHiMdemonstration video included as supplementary material.
filter_reasoning: The paper focuses on auditing and identifying copyright risks and leakage in AI models, which is an AI ethics and accountability issue.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 64th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 3
title: Graph of Trace: Visualizing Execution Traces of Scientific Agents
abstract: Scientific AI agents can autonomously carry out complex research workflows, yet these unfolded workflows often remains difficult for humans to inspect and review, limiting interpretable, controllable and effective human--AI collaboration. To address this challenge, we present a monitoring and visualization framework that records fine-grained execution events and organizes them into a directed graph that make agent workflows explicit as they proceed. The system records intermediate steps (e.g. tool calls and code executions), and renders them as real-time updated visual traces that expose workflow structure. This allows users to examine how results are produced, identify where failures emerge, and better understand agent behavior across different stages of the research process.We conduct an evaluation on complex research tasks with domain experts of interdisciplinary background in AI, neuroscience and biology. Experts report that structured traces visualization improves understanding of agent workflows, perceived interpretability, and usability for analysis and further interaction.
filter_reasoning: The paper focuses on interpretability and controllability of AI agents through visualization of execution traces.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 64th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 3
title: mllm-shap: A Shapley Value Explainability Platform for Text-Audio Multimodal Large Language Models
abstract: We present mllm-shap, an open-sourcePython platform for researchers and ML practitioners that extends Shapley value (SV)explainability from text-only large languagemodels to multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) thatjointly process text and audio. Buildingon the token-level SV framework introducedby TokenSHAP, mllm-shap addresses threechallenges absent in the text-only setting:(1) modality-aware coalition masking thathandles the coexistence of text tokens anddense audio encoder frames within a single input, (2) multi-turn conversation tracking withper-token role and modality metadata, and(3) audio token grouping via phonetic alignment that reduces the coalition space by 10--50 times. The platform ships as a pip-installablepackage implementing five SV estimation strategies -- including a Complementary Contributions estimator with Neyman-optimal allocation that outperforms Monte Carlo baselines -- together with an interactive web GUIfor real-time attribution visualization. Toour knowledge, mllm-shap is the first publicly available framework for complete, reproducible SV-based explainability of text-audioMLLMs. The package is MIT-licensed withfull source code on GitHub and a demonstration video included as supplementary material.
filter_reasoning: The paper provides a framework for explainability (Shapley values) in multimodal LLMs, which is a core topic in AI interpretability/safety.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 64th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 3
title: Gardener: An Agentic AI System for Single-Cell RNA Sequence Analysis
abstract: Gardener is an interactive agentic system for single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) analysis that enables expert-steered, iterative workflows under strict data-residency requirements. Existing large language model (LLM)-based analysis agents commonly encode workflow progress as implicit conversational state and rely on cloud-centric execution, which hinders traceability and auditability and complicates keeping sensitive expression data on-device. Gardener grounds cloud-side reasoning in a local, on-device scientific engine and an Experiment Management Kernel (EMK) that externalizes analysis progress as persistent, immutable snapshots linked by lineage. This explicit state representation supports rollback, branching, and comparison of alternative analysis paths while reusing prior computation. Gardener enforces data isolation by design: cloud-hosted LLMs operate only on snapshot identifiers and sanitized summaries, while raw expression matrices and local artifacts remain on the user's device. A local graphical user interface (GUI) provides human-in-the-loop steering and inspection of workflow state and outputs. Gardener is released as an open-source desktop application for macOS and Windows under the Apache License 2.0.
filter_reasoning: The system focuses on traceability, auditability, and data isolation for scientific agents, which relates to AI safety and robustness.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 64th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 3
title: AutoChecklist: Composable Pipelines for Checklist Generation and Scoring with LLM-as-a-Judge
abstract: Checklists have emerged as a popular approach for interpretable and fine-grained evaluation, particularly with LLM-as-a-Judge. Beyond evaluation, these structured criteria can serve as signals for model alignment, reinforcement learning, and self-correction. To support these use cases, we present $AutoChecklist$, an open-source library that unifies checklist-based evaluation into composable pipelines. At its core is a taxonomy of five checklist generation abstractions, each encoding a distinct strategy for deriving evaluation criteria. A modular $Generator $\rightarrow$ Refiner $\rightarrow$ Scorer$ pipeline connects any generator with a unified scorer, and new configurations can be registered via prompt templates alone. The library ships with ten built-in pipelines implementing published approaches and supports multiple LLM providers (OpenAI, OpenRouter, vLLM). Beyond the Python API, the library includes a CLI for off-the-shelf evaluation and a web interface for interactive exploration. Validation experiments confirm that these checklist methods significantly align with human preferences and quality ratings, and a case study on ICLR peer review rebuttals demonstrates flexible domain adaptation. $AutoChecklist$ is publicly available at https://github.com/ChicagoHAI/AutoChecklist.
filter_reasoning: The paper focuses on checklist-based evaluation and model alignment techniques, which are central to AI safety and reliable evaluation.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 64th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 3
title: PhyVer: Physics-Grounded Material Claim Verification with Multi-Fidelity Physical Evidence
abstract: Material claims in papers, patents, etc., often involve physical feasibility (e.g., stability under conditions, property consistency), not just textual feasibility. Yet most claim verifiers operate over language, therefore producing ungrounded judgments. On the other hand, directfirst-principles verification (e.g., density functional theory, DFT) is inflexible and hard to invoke from underspecified free-form claims.Therefore, we introduce PhyVer, a physics-grounded material claim verification system that bridges this gap by translating claimsinto multi-fidelity physical evidence and interpretable verdicts. To support human-in-the-loop inspection, we present an interactive web interface that visualizes the instantiated structure, optimization trajectories, DFT summaries, and the final decision. On expert-labeled claims, PhyVer improves agreement with experts over text-only GPT-5.1, reducing MAE from 1.54 to 1.20 and Signed MAE from0.95 to 0.82, and increasing Accuracy@\pm1 from 50\% to 70\%.
filter_reasoning: The paper develops a system for verifying factual claims against physical constraints, contributing to AI reliability and grounding.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 64th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 3
title: CPTCoder: A Reliable LLM System for Medical Procedure Code Prediction
abstract: We present CPTCoder, a human-in-the-loop system that predicts standardized medical procedure codes from clinical text. Clinical procedure coding is an extreme multi-label classification problem over a long-tailed space of short numeric identifiers, where a single-digit difference denotes an entirely different procedure. CPTCoder adapts an instruction-tuned LLM with a code-aware vocabulary and constrained decoding that guarantees all outputs are valid codes. To support human review, we derive per-code posterior inclusion probabilities from n-best reweighting, producing interpretable confidence scores that rank predictions and flag uncertain cases. A post-decoding constraint repair step enforces mutual-exclusion rules between conflicting codes. To enable reproducible research in this underexplored setting, we release MIMIC-CPT, a PhysioNet-accessible benchmark of 37,885 expert-cleaned report--code pairs with a deliberately hardened test split: 88\% of test examples contain label combinations unseen during training, and over a third include codes with five or fewer training occurrences. We additionally provide 413,085 weakly aligned pairs and evaluate on a separate live dataset from a hospital, which includes out-of-domain radiology reports with billing-expert-verified labels. CPTCoder achieves 0.61 and 0.51 micro-F1 on the hardened MIMIC split and Hospital-298 respectively, outperforming the strongest baseline by 12 and 5 absolute points while reducing digit-level near-miss errors.
filter_reasoning: The paper focuses on reliable prediction, uncertainty quantification, and human-in-the-loop review for medical classification, which relates to AI safety.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 64th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 3
title: Formally Specifying the Intended Behavior of the Program: LLM-Driven Neuro-Symbolic Program Specification Synthesis
abstract: Formal verification can provide strong mathematical guarantees about software correctness, but it typically requires developers to write detailed formal specifications (e.g., contracts and loop invariants), which is costly and error-prone. We introduce AutoSpec+, an LLM-driven neuro-symbolic demonstration system that reframes specification writing as constrained structured synthesis: large language models generate candidate specifications at the granularity of proof-relevant program components, while a symbolic verifier acts as a deterministic critic that checks legality, satisfiability, and proof adequacy, rejecting or repairing candidates in an iterative loop. This design turns unconstrained text generation into constrained structured synthesis, substantially reducing hallucinations and producing proof-ready annotations. We evaluate AutoSpec+ on seven benchmark suites, showing strong effectiveness.
