Existing alignment approaches based on chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring supervise explicit reasoning traces. However, under optimization pressure, models are incentivized to conceal deceptive reasoning, rendering semantic supervision fundamentally unreliable. Grounded in cognitive psychology, we hypothesize that a deceptive LLM maintains a stable internal belief in its CoT while its external response remains fragile under perturbation. We term this phenomenon stability asymmetry and quantify it by measuring the contrast between internal CoT stability and external response stability under perturbation. Building on this structural signature, we propose the Stability Asymmetry Regularization (SAR), a novel alignment objective that penalizes this distributional asymmetry during reinforcement learning. Unlike CoT monitoring, SAR targets the statistical structure of model outputs, rendering it robust to semantic concealment. Extensive experiments confirm that stability asymmetry reliably identifies deceptive behavior, and that SAR effectively suppresses intrinsic deception without degrading general model capability.
filter_reasoning: The paper specifically addresses intrinsic deception in LLMs and proposes a regularization method to improve safety and trustworthiness.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: MedPriv-Bench: Benchmarking the Privacy-Utility Trade-off of Large Language Models in Medical Open-Ended Question Answering
abstract: Recent advances in Retrieval-Augmented Generation enable LLMs to ground outputs in clinical evidence, but connections to external databases create the risk of contextual leakage, where unique combinations of medical details enable patient re-identification without explicit identifiers. Existing healthcare benchmarks emphasize accuracy while overlooking this risk. To fill this gap, we present MedPriv-Bench, the first benchmark for jointly evaluating privacy preservation and clinical utility in medical open-ended question answering. Our framework utilizes a multi-agent, human-in-the-loop pipeline to synthesize sensitive medical contexts and clinically relevant queries that create realistic privacy pressure. We also establish an automated evaluation protocol using a fine-tuned RoBERTa-NLI model, which achieved an instance-level $F_1$-score of 75.3\%, sensitivity of 90.7\%, and an average inference time of 0.056 s per sample against human annotations. Across nine LLMs and three privacy-preserving methods, we observed a pervasive privacy-utility trade-off. Relative to unprotected Med42-v2-8B (utility 3.87/5; leakage 72.8\%), supervised fine-tuning improved utility to 4.25 and reduced leakage to 38.9\%, whereas local differential privacy reduced leakage to 20.5\% but lowered utility to 3.03. These results demonstrate the need for domain-specific benchmarks to validate medical AI systems in privacy-sensitive settings.
filter_reasoning: The paper explicitly measures privacy preservation and potential leakage, a core AI ethics concern regarding data privacy.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: The Geometry of Safety Drifts: Step-level Refusal-Subspace Monitoring for Reasoning Large Language Models
abstract: Reasoning large language models that produce explicit chains of thought are a new jailbreak surface: an adversary who shapes intermediate reasoning can hijack safety deliberation and elicit harmful answers the same model would refuse in a single forward pass. Defenses inherited from chat-style alignment monitor only the final response and intervene after the model has already committed to an unsafe trajectory. We argue that defending reasoning models requires looking inside the thinking phase itself, and we show that the refusal direction, previously characterized as a single linear direction in chat models, in fact evolves along the reasoning trajectory: sharp at onset, slowly drifting during long deliberation, and on hijacked traces collapsing at an identifiable step well before any harmful token is emitted. We propose RsMon, a step-level refusal-subspace monitor that tracks the projection of intermediate hidden states onto a calibrated refusal subspace and triggers a minimally invasive geometric intervention once drift exceeds a learned threshold. The monitor is purely inference-time, requires no retraining, and is compatible with any open-weight reasoning model. On three open reasoning models, five attack families, and four utility benchmarks, RsMon cuts mean attack success from 80.1\% to 19.2\%, a $4.2\times$ reduction, while keeping MATH-500, GPQA-Diamond, and HumanEval pass@1 within 0.7 absolute points of the undefended baseline. The same monitor produces a step-resolved diagnostic that pinpoints when and in which layer safety deliberation breaks down. Our code is available at https://github.com/llmnjust-afk/RsMon.
filter_reasoning: The paper focuses on detecting and preventing jailbreaks in reasoning models by monitoring internal states, a clear contribution to AI safety.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: TRACE: An Evidence-Grounded Benchmark for Safety Evaluation of Large Reasoning Models
abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) generate intermediate reasoning traces that may contain unsafe content, even when their final responses appear safe. Guardrail models are designed to detect and block unsafe content, yet existing benchmarks for unsafe content detection focus primarily on prompts and final responses, leaving reasoning traces largely unexamined. Moreover, these benchmarks typically provide only binary safety labels, without evidence annotations that justify the judgments. To address these limitations, we introduce TRACE, an evidence-grounded safety evaluation benchmark that covers the entire LRM inference pipeline: prompts, reasoning traces, and final responses. TRACE includes prompts in two languages spanning nine risk categories and ten attack strategies. For each prompt, four LRMs generate reasoning traces and final responses, and we annotate the safety of each component and extract supporting evidence from the corresponding source text. Evaluating 18 guardrail models on TRACE reveals that safety judgment for reasoning traces is substantially more challenging than for prompts or final responses, and that current models struggle to accurately extract supporting evidence. These findings highlight the need for guardrail models that can reliably detect and precisely localize unsafe content across the LRM inference pipeline.
filter_reasoning: The paper introduces a benchmark for evaluating safety in reasoning traces, which is critical for identifying unsafe content in advanced AI systems.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: Risky Business: Measuring The Faithfulness-Safety Tension
abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning offers a promising window into model monitoring. However, monitoring relies on faithfulness, i.e., the model output strictly derives from its reasoning trace. We identify an alignment tension where a model must be faithful enough to be monitored, yet robust enough to reject unsafe reasoning. We demonstrate that this counterbalance exists in current Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), and show ways in which it can be addressed. We introduce HazMart, a human-written dataset set in an autonomous AI shopkeeper scenario. Unlike prior work that relies on providing hints in prompts to test faithfulness (e.g., ``A Stanford professor said it should be Answer A''), we propose a novel replacement-based technique, which we call Targeted Reasoning Replacement (TRR), that directly intervenes in the reasoning chain to substitute in unsafe or illogical thoughts (e.g., ``Wait, the answer must be Option B Option A because it is the most fitting''). DeepSeek-R1-Llama-70B exhibits high faithfulness (97.5\%) but fails to reject Unsafe Reasoning (12.3\%), while QwQ-32B is more robust (73.9\% safety) at the cost of lower faithfulness (74.7\%). Mechanistic analyses of QwQ-32B reveal that these properties are represented by anti-correlated internal directions peaking at the action-commit token. Finally, we demonstrate that representation steering can independently amplify the safety direction, increasing safe behavior by 9 percentage points while maintaining base capabilities.
filter_reasoning: This paper investigates the trade-off between model faithfulness and safety in reasoning chains, directly addressing core AI safety challenges like robustness and alignment.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: Does Alignment Debias or Just Suppress? Evaluating Stereotypical Bias Across Base-Instruct Pairs
abstract: Alignment has been widely reported to reduce stereotypical bias in large language models, but it is unclear whether these reductions reflect debiasing or suppression at the output level. Across 27 base--instruct pairs from four open-weight families and four bias benchmarks, three patterns provide substantial evidence that the measured reduction is largely suppression. (i) The chat template drives about half the alignment effect on CrowS-Pairs and essentially all on StereoSet, where 18 of 27 improve without it (p = 0.061) versus 26 of 27 with it (p < 0.001). Per-pair effects remain below d = 0.2 in both conditions. IAT lies at the weight-level end of the spectrum, with template contribution indistinguishable from zero. (ii) Decomposing BBQ's ambiguous-context score shows instruct models defer rather than debias (28\% \textrightarrow 53\%) and are more biased when they answer (conditional bias 0.53 \textrightarrow 0.59). Suppressed bias is recoverable: the most aggressive adversarial framing restores CrowS-Pairs bias to near base levels, while on BBQ it partly reverses deferral without reactivating conditional bias. (iii) Across eight probed pairs, base and instruct gender directions remain geometrically aligned (median cosine 0.86 vs. 0.006 random-pair baseline). Together, these findings suggest benchmark improvements after alignment may overstate genuine bias reduction.
filter_reasoning: This paper evaluates whether alignment techniques genuinely debias models or simply suppress the expression of stereotypes, which is a core concern in AI ethics and transparency.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: Dual-Modality Multi-Stage Adversarial Safety Training: Robustifying Multimodal Web Agents Against Cross-Modal Attacks
abstract: Multimodal web agents that process both screenshots and accessibility trees are increasingly deployed to interact with web interfaces, yet their dual-stream architecture opens an underexplored attack surface: an adversary who injects content into the webpage DOM simultaneously corrupts both observation channels with a consistent deceptive narrative. Our vulnerability analysis on MiniWob++ reveals that attacks including a visual component far outperform text-only injections, exposing critical gaps in text-centric VLM safety training. Motivated by this finding, we propose Dual-Modality Multi-Stage Adversarial Safety Training (DMAST), a framework that formalizes the agent-attacker interaction as a two-player zero-sum Markov game and co-trains both players through a three-stage pipeline: (1) imitation learning from a strong teacher model, (2) oracle-guided supervised fine-tuning that uses a novel zero-acknowledgment strategy to instill task-focused reasoning under adversarial noise, and (3) adversarial reinforcement learning via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) self-play. On out-of-distribution tasks, DMAST nearly halves the attack success rate (41.2\%~$\rightarrow$~21.4\%) while raising task completion by over 60\% relative (6.2\%~$\rightarrow$~10.2\%). Our approach outperforms established training-based and prompt-based defenses, demonstrating genuine co-evolutionary progress and robust generalization to complex, unseen environments. Code is available at https://github.com/huajianduzhuo-code/DMAST_official.
filter_reasoning: The paper proposes a defense framework specifically against adversarial cross-modal attacks on multimodal web agents, which is a core AI safety concern.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: EMER-Guard: Protocol-Grounded Verification for LLM Emergency Instructions
abstract: When LLM-generated emergency advice becomes part of public-facing information infrastructure, aggregate accuracy is no longer an adequate safety target: missing a hazardous instruction and blocking a correct one impose different human costs. We study protocol-grounded verification, the post-hoc auditing of emergency instructions against authoritative guidance under asymmetric risk. We introduce EMER-GuardBench, a 69,000-example counterfactual benchmark plus a 1,000-example benign-stress set spanning 10 disaster scenarios and 6 hazard mechanisms, with instruction-group-disjoint splits and cited protocol evidence. We further propose EGIS, an evidence-conditioned, protocol-supervised verifier that jointly predicts hazard status, hazard mechanism, severity, evidence support, and counterfactual ranking. This establishes a protocol-conditioned task and protocol-supervised representation learning, not inference-time causal grounding. EGIS reaches 89.9 Harm F1 with 10.4\% IID over-refusal and zero benign-stress false positives; across 364 LLM-judge operating points, none Pareto-dominates EGIS on Harm F1, over-refusal, and severity-weighted miss rate, and a 14.4\texttimes-larger Qwen3-8B+LoRA supervised baseline still trails under identical splits. Ablations show that evidence helps as training-time supervision rather than prompt decoration. Our Severity-Weighted Miss Rate exposes a tradeoff hidden by scalar safety scores: zero missed severity can be achieved by broad refusal. EMER-Guard reframes emergency LLM safety from advice generation to auditable, protocol-grounded, cost-sensitive verification.
filter_reasoning: The paper focuses on verifying the safety of emergency instructions generated by LLMs under asymmetric risk, a clear application of AI safety and robustness.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: MDHB: A Multi-Dimensional Online Harm Detection Benchmark for Proactive Psychosocial Risk Forecasting
abstract: Online harm detection is crucial for safeguarding digital ecosystems. However, current research is largely confined to single-dimensional classification paradigms or generative safety alignment under simplified and explicit adversarial prompts. To capture complex and highly covert threats in the real world, we introduce the Multi-dimensional Online Harm Detection Benchmark (MDHB). MDHB focuses on four core dimensions critically demanded by social platforms: misinformation, toxicity, sarcasm, and logical fallacies. Notably, we incorporate non-offensive implicit sarcasm (e.g., self-deprecation and veiled complaints) to propel content governance toward proactive psychosocial risk forecasting. Evaluations reveal that mainstream Large Language Models (LLMs), including GPT-5, suffer from severe cross-dimensional interference under both direct inference and ReAct paradigms. To address this, we propose the Self-Refining Sentinel (SRS), an error-driven self-evolving agent architecture. Without requiring parameter fine-tuning, SRS dynamically constructs and updates an experience repository from failure cases through an iterative self-evolution mechanism. Experimental results demonstrate that SRS significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in overall performance, effectively mitigating cross-dimensional interference in multi-dimensional online threat detection.
filter_reasoning: The paper addresses online harm detection (misinformation, toxicity, sarcasm) to advance content governance, falling under the societal impact and safety monitoring aspect of AI ethics.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: IndicWinoBias: Measuring Occupational Gender Bias and Error Asymmetry in Indian Languages
abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in multilingual contexts, evaluating their fairness across languages is essential. We investigate occupational gender bias in 16 LLMs across eight Indic languages using a controlled coreference resolution benchmark that employs transliterated English occupational loanwords to minimize grammatical gender cues. In addition to this generative evaluation, we compute intrinsic bias metrics (WEAT and DirectBias) from the models' embedding spaces. Across models, we observe systematic disparities between pro-stereotype and anti-stereotype conditions. These gaps are largest in high-accuracy models, whereas models lacking baseline competence exhibit smaller gaps driven by general prediction uncertainty. Error analysis shows a consistent asymmetry, with higher error rates when the correct referent is female. However, intrinsic embedding bias metrics show no statistically significant correlation with these generative disparities ($p \gt 0.05$). These results suggest that strong linguistic competence does not necessarily correspond to stereotype-neutral generation and that intrinsic embedding metrics alone may not reliably predict bias in multilingual language model behavior.
filter_reasoning: The paper evaluates occupational gender bias in multilingual language models, which is a direct contribution to AI fairness.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: ScopeBench: Evaluating Cultural Norm Scope Awareness in LLMs
abstract: Safety evaluation in large language models treats harm as culturally invariant, yet a model cannot correctly apply a safety norm without knowing whose norms bind. We introduce ScopeBench, a benchmark that treats cultural scope as a first-class safety dimension. It comprises 3,323 norms spanning 49 countries across nine cultural clusters, each annotated as Universal or Specific. We define three scope error types identically across four evaluation tasks: Scope Inflation, Scope Deflation, and Scope Displacement. Evaluating 21 frontier LLMs across seven model families, we surface three structural failures. First, the dominant error type inverts with prompt format: Scope Deflation reaches 70\% in single-answer classification, while Scope Inflation reaches 33\% when each candidate culture is judged independently. Second, scope-classification accuracy is empirically decoupled from behavioral safety: the six classifiers achieving \geq97\% Task 1 accuracy still produce harmful responses to 40--42\% of scope-violating statements. Third, no model is safe in interaction, with harmful-response rates ranging from 29\% to 51\% across the cohort, excluding one model that systematically refuses the task. We release all data, code, and model outputs to establish cultural scope as a distinct alignment axis.
filter_reasoning: The paper investigates how models interpret cultural norms and safety in a culturally sensitive way, which is a central topic in AI ethics.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: TraceProbe: An Execution-Based Benchmark for Diagnosing Safety Failures in LLM Agents
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly act through files, tools, memory, retrieved content, and other agents, which can trigger safety failures during execution. Existing benchmarks mostly focus on endpoint outcome evaluation or model-assisted moderation of pre-constructed trajectories, leaving limited evidence about where risks enter and how they propagate. To address this issue, we introduce TraceProbe, an execution-based benchmark for agent safety diagnosis. TraceProbe places agents in executable sandbox scenarios, scores endpoint and latent rule violations based on normalized traces and structured evidence, and replays recorded tool actions for step-level risk localization. Our benchmark contains 155 scenarios across three risk-source categories: non-adversarial failures, internal authority compromise, and external attacks. Across 12 contemporary LLMs, the mean attack success rate (ASR) is 0.347, indicating substantial residual risk, especially under internal authority compromise. Our analysis also demonstrates that endpoint-safe runs can contain unsafe intermediate actions, and the actual execution paths of agents may differ from the intended hazards of the testing scenarios. The TraceProbe benchmark and our findings support a more actionable form of agent safety evaluation: beyond assessing ASR or final outcomes, evaluators can also ask what went wrong, where it occurred, and where an intervention could be placed.
filter_reasoning: The paper proposes a diagnostic benchmark for LLM agents to evaluate safety failures during tool use and execution, which is directly relevant to AI safety.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: When In-Distribution Gains Fail: Evaluating Weak-to-Strong Reward Models under Preference Shift
abstract: Weak-to-strong (W2S) generalization is a promising framework for scalable oversight, yet existing evaluations often test students under matched train-test distributions. Therefore, we study W2S preference learning under zero-shot distribution shift and find that strong students trained on weak preference labels can appear successful in-distribution while failing to transfer across preference datasets. We provide evidence consistent with a representational failure mode in which weak-supervised fine-tuning may move the strong model toward source-domain features instead of maintaining broadly transferable preference representations. To mitigate this, we propose *Representation Anchoring* (Anchor), a simple yet effective regularizer that constrains excessive drift from the pretrained strong model's representation space during fine-tuning, while still allowing task-relevant adaptation. Across preference domains, datasets, and model families, Anchor improves out-of-distribution transfer while maintaining competitive in-distribution performance. Together, our evaluation protocol, transfer-aware metrics, and method expose hidden brittleness in current W2S reward modeling and provide a practical path toward more robust preference transfer.
filter_reasoning: The paper studies reward model brittleness in weak-to-strong generalization settings, a technical problem critical to the long-term safety and alignment of powerful AI systems.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: SSR: Symbolic-Neural Soft Reasoning for Robust and Verifiable Thinking Chains
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive progress in complex reasoning tasks, largely driven by the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) paradigm, which decomposes difficult problems into intermediate steps. However, CoT reasoning remains fundamentally constrained by the probabilistic nature of neural generation, leading to unfaithful reasoning chains that undermine reliability. Neuro-symbolic approaches attempt to address these issues by combining LLMs with symbolic solvers, yet they face persistent challenges, including hallucinated translations, the mismatch between natural language and formal logic, and the limited enhancement of the LLM's intrinsic reasoning ability. To overcome these limitations, we propose Symbolic-Neural Soft Reasoning (SSR), a unified framework that integrates LLMs with symbolic reasoning and improves robustness by relaxing strict logical determinism while preserving verifiability. Our approach improves reasoning performance, automatically generates verifiable and human-readable logical thinking chains for training and fine-tuning, and facilitates cross-disciplinary applications such as AI for mathematics. Experiments across multiple models and benchmarks demonstrate that SSR consistently outperforms existing reasoning frameworks, highlighting its effectiveness in enhancing both the robustness and interpretability of LLM reasoning. Our code is available at https://github.com/1240148048/SSR.
filter_reasoning: The paper proposes a neuro-symbolic framework to improve the reliability, verifiability, and robustness of reasoning chains, which relates to AI safety and interpretability.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: Stop Before You Fail: Operational Capability Boundaries for Mitigating Unproductive Reasoning in Large Reasoning Models
abstract: Current answering paradigms for Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) often fail to account for the fact that some questions may lie beyond the model's operational capability boundary, leading to long but unproductive reasoning. In this paper, we study whether LRMs expose early signals predictive of such cases, and whether these signals can be used to mitigate unproductive reasoning. In black-box settings, we find that reasoning expressions contain failure-predictive signals. In white-box settings, we show that the hidden states of the last input token contain information that is predictive of whether a question will not be solved correctly under our evaluation setup. Building on these observations, we propose two test-time monitoring strategies: reasoning expression monitoring and hidden states monitoring, that reduce token usage by 62.7--93.6\%, substantially improving efficiency and reliability while largely preserving accuracy.
filter_reasoning: The paper focuses on mitigating unproductive reasoning and improving the reliability of models by detecting failure cases, which is a robustness and safety task.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: Personalization over Generalization: History-Aware Sentence-Level AI Detection in Collaborative Writing
abstract: Sentence-level AI detectors are essential for detecting AI misuse in human-AI collaborative writing. Yet existing approaches still treat all authors identically, ignoring individual writing styles. This is a critical oversight, given that the boundary between human and AI text is inherently author-specific. To address this limitation, we propose PHAS-ID (Personalized History-Aware Sentence-level AI Detector), an approach that introduces personalization to sentence-level detection. By matching target sentences against the author's history of labeled documents, PHAS-ID tailors its predictions based on prior writing behaviors. Furthermore, current synthetic datasets for this task fail to capture realistic collaborative patterns, which we address by introducing GhostFill, a style-aware synthetic dataset generation pipeline. Our experiments demonstrate that PHAS-ID outperforms the previous state-of-the-art (SOTA) across seen-author, unseen-author, cross-domain, and cross-generator settings. Ablation studies confirm that these improvements stem from genuine author-specific personalization rather than the mere addition of context. Our source code and dataset are available at our GitHub repository.
filter_reasoning: The paper focuses on AI detection in collaborative writing, addressing accountability and the detection of AI-generated content, which falls under AI ethics.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: How Far Are AI Scientists from Changing the World? A Survey of Autonomous Scientific Discovery
abstract: This survey asks how far AI Scientist systems are from changing the world, and argues that their impact should be evaluated not by whether they produce plausible papers, but by whether they produce auditable research trajectories that can be inspected, reproduced, and challenged. We first provide a definition of AI Scientists, distinguish them from adjacent scientific AI systems, and organize the field around four core capabilities: knowledge acquisition, hypothesis generation, experimental validation, and evolution. We further synthesize representative systems by autonomy, execution grounding, auditability, human control, and evidence level. The resulting picture shows a field moving from prompt-to-paper automation toward auditable research laboratories, where executable grounding, provenance, and human-governed autonomy become central. We conclude by identifying open challenges toward trustworthy AI-driven science and providing a roadmap for integrating AI Scientists into the future landscape of scientific discovery.
filter_reasoning: The survey discusses the future of autonomous scientific discovery through the lens of auditability, human control, and trust, which are core AI safety and governance themes.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: HEAL: Anchored Hyperspherical Equilibrium for Multilingual Safety Alignment
abstract: Safety alignment in large language models is markedly uneven across languages: behaviors learned from English preference data fail to transfer reliably into lower-resource languages, and existing remedies based on per-language preference data or pairwise translation pivots do not scale. We propose Hyperspherical Equilibrium for Aligned Languages (HEAL), a lightweight auxiliary objective that augments any DPO-style alignment pipeline without altering its supervised pairs. HEAL applies two opposing forces to the multilingual representations of the same prompt: a shrink term draws each non-English representation toward a stop-gradient English anchor, while a dilation term repels same-prompt language representations through a pairwise hinge. At equilibrium, representations occupy an English-centered shell-like region that supports cross-lingual transfer while preserving per-language distinctness. Across multiple backbones, HEAL substantially strengthens multilingual safety with the largest gains on the weakest languages, while preserving general capability and showing favorable out-of-distribution behavior on jailbreak evaluation.
filter_reasoning: The paper introduces an alignment objective specifically to improve safety performance across languages, which is a central concern in multilingual AI safety.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: From AI Reviewers to Evidence Assistants: Quantifying the Human-AI Responsibility Boundary in Peer Review
abstract: The rapid growth of AI conference submissions is putting new pressure on peer review. AI reviewer systems are increasingly proposed as support, but prior work leaves unresolved what responsibility their outputs should carry when they can surface useful critiques yet remain risky as independent judgments. We frame this as a responsibility-boundary problem. Using 600 ICLR 2026 submissions, 2,231 human reviews, and 3,600 AI reviews, we operationalize this boundary through usable feedback, rating calibration, panel breadth, and grounded synthesis. AI can prepare critiques and organize evidence, while scoring, independent panel judgment, high-level synthesis, and final responsibility remain human-led. A GLM-5.2 validation on 100 NeurIPS 2022 papers with pre-ChatGPT reviews reproduces the workflow and calibration patterns. Motivated by this boundary, we develop Review Copilot, a workflow in which AI suggestions are inspected, edited, or rejected by human reviewers. In an initial controlled reviewer-in-the-loop study, Human+AI reviews improve actionability, evidence support, and professionalism relative to standalone baselines, while scores and recommendations remain human-authored. A user study of 275 reviewers across 411 papers further supports its practical usefulness. Together, these results support a review paradigm in which AI expands evidence-grounded critique while humans retain judgment, synthesis, and accountability.
filter_reasoning: The paper addresses the responsibility boundary and accountability of AI in high-stakes professional settings like peer review, which is a core AI ethics concern.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: REINS: Refusal-Enhanced Inhibitory Steering with Sparse Autoencoder Features
abstract: Steering with Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) offers a lightweight inference-time path for adapting the behavior of large language models without retraining. By exposing sparse and interpretable features, SAE steering provides a promising interface for safety control that guides harmful continuations toward refusal. However, we observe that complex wrappers can still undermine existing SAE steering methods on harmful prompts. To evaluate this failure mode systematically, we construct Generalized Undercover Instruction Safety Evaluation (GUISE), a dataset of harmful prompts with complex wrappers. Existing single direction SAE steering methods do not reliably produce refusals on harmful prompts, suggesting that refusal enhancement alone can be too weak when the harmful continuation path remains active. This motivates us to propose Refusal-Enhanced INhibitory Steering (REINS), which suppresses harmful continuation features and enhances safe refusal features in the same SAE feature space. Experiments on GUISE and other datasets show that prior methods either intervene too weakly or achieve only apparent safety through collapse, while REINS substantially reduces harmful responses, markedly improves safe refusals and largely preserves general capabilities.
filter_reasoning: The paper uses sparse autoencoders to steer models toward safe, refusal-oriented behavior, which is a direct application of mechanistic interpretability to AI safety.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: Debias-SparseGPT: Bias-Aware Pruning for Large Language Models
abstract: Model compression techniques such as pruning and quantization facilitate the efficient deployment and acceleration of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, recent studies show that weight sparsification methods, such as SparseGPT, can amplify existing biases in models, with outputs varying significantly depending on persona cues in the prompt. In this paper, we introduce Debias-SparseGPT, a post-training pruning method incorporating representational debiasing using a second-order term defined over demographically contrasting inputs. We perform empirical validation of our method over a wide range of generative LLMs. Across models and sparsity regimes (25\%, 50\%, and structured 2:4 sparsity), Debias-SparseGPT consistently reduces pruning-induced bias compared to SparseGPT while preserving model perplexity and zero-shot accuracy. Under the most restrictive 2:4 structured sparsity pattern, which most aggressively degrades model quality, augmenting the calibration set with long-context, content-rich examples further improves both downstream performance and fairness. Overall, Debias-SparseGPT advances the bias-performance trade-off while preserving the computational efficiency of sparse models.
filter_reasoning: The paper focuses on mitigating social bias in LLMs through a novel pruning method, which is a core topic in AI ethics.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: Diagnosing LLM Fragility: An Empirical Study on Reasoning Entropy and Malicious Outputs
abstract: Chain-of-Thought prompting is increasingly relied upon as a safety monitoring surface: if a model reasons before acting, its trace can be inspected before harm occurs. Yet reasoning is a stochastic branching process rather than a deterministic, auditable path. We introduce Bifurcation Entropy ($H_BE$), a step-level diagnostic metric that extends Kernel Language Entropy to intermediate reasoning steps, measuring the semantic breadth of a model's next-step distribution at each point in the Chain-of-Thought. We deploy $H_BE$ via In-Distribution Attacks, a controlled probing instrument that injects the model's own high-entropy continuations to test whether $H_BE$ predicts exploitability. Across five reasoning models in high-stakes blackmail scenarios, phrases in the top $H_BE$ quartile are exploited 6.2$\times$ more often than the lowest, with $H_BE$-targeted probing inducing significantly more alignment failures than random selection. These results establish $H_BE$ as a principled probing signal that concentrates safety monitoring effort on the minority of reasoning steps that carry the majority of alignment risk.
filter_reasoning: The paper develops a metric to measure and predict alignment risks (malicious outputs) in model reasoning, which is a core topic in AI safety.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: Right for the Right Reasons? Evaluating the Structural Fidelity of LLM Emotion Explanations
abstract: This paper introduces a framework for evaluating structural fidelity in emotion reasoning: the degree to which the causal structure of AI-generated emotion explanations aligns with human-curated explicit causal abstractions. Unlike traditional surface-level text overlap metrics, we propose two metrics: Structural Causal Similarity (SCS) for measuring static structural alignment, and Dynamic Causal Sensitivity (DCS) as a proxy for measuring dynamic sensitivity to counterfactual interventions. We evaluate these on EmoReason-4k, a new benchmark comprising two human-annotated datasets ( each) from social media and conversational dialogues. Testing seven LLMs identifies consistent graph-generation behaviors across models and domains, such as ``structural elaboration'' (a tendency for models to explicate intermediate steps that humans leave implicit) and sensitivity to shifts in causal agency locus. However, models struggle to generate updated causal states in complex discourse. By evaluating structural fidelity against human-curated causal abstractions, our framework offers a structured method to diagnose the structural compliance of explicit explanations against formalized human abstractions. Ablation studies support that our metrics capture underlying topological properties rather than just parsing artifacts. Data and prompts are available to support reproducibility.
filter_reasoning: The paper focuses on interpretability by proposing metrics for evaluating the structural fidelity and causality of LLM explanations.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: Self-Sanitize: Cognitive-Inspired In-Place Mitigation of LLM Harmful Responses
abstract: Despite significant advances in aligning Large Language Models (LLMs) with safety and ethical standards, adversarial prompts can still be crafted to elicit undesirable responses. Existing mitigation strategies predominantly rely on post-hoc filtering, which introduces substantial latency or computational overhead, and is incompatible with token-level streaming generation. To address this, we introduce Self-Sanitize, a novel LLM-driven mitigation framework inspired by cognitive psychology, which emulates human self-monitor and self-repair behaviors. The framework utilizes a lightweight Self-Monitor module to inspect high-level intentions via representation engineering and a Self-Repair module for in-place correction without separate review dialogues. This design allows for real-time streaming monitoring and seamless repair, with negligible impact on latency and resource utilization. Extensive experiments across three privacy-leakage scenarios and broader safety-sensitive domains (e.g., crime and bias) demonstrate that Self-Sanitize achieves superior mitigation performance with minimal overhead and preserved model utility. Our code is available at the following link: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/LLM\_Self\_Sanitize-5E8B
filter_reasoning: The paper proposes a framework for real-time mitigation of harmful model responses, which is directly related to AI safety and robustness.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: Disentangling Semantics and Popularity: Adversarial Debiasing and Asymmetric Alignment for LLM-Enhanced Long-Tail Sequential Recommendation
abstract: Sequential recommendation models dynamic user preferences but is constrained by the long-tail distribution of real-world interactions. While LLM-derived text embeddings provide semantic priors to alleviate data sparsity, existing adaptation methods are hindered by popularity bias during semantic projection and semantic prior erosion during sequence training. In this paper, we propose Adversarial Debiasing and Asymmetric Alignment (ADAA), a framework designed to alleviate these representation bottlenecks. Specifically, ADAA incorporates an adversarial debiasing mechanism to decouple interaction frequency factors from the projected embeddings, yielding debiased semantic representations. Furthermore, it employs an asymmetric anchoring strategy during the sequence training phase. This strategy restricts the optimization space of sparse items to preserve their injected semantic priors, while permitting head items to flexibly fit sequential transition patterns. Through a parameter-level injection mechanism, ADAA integrates offline-aligned semantics without introducing additional parameters to the online architecture. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate that ADAA improves long-tail recommendation accuracy while preserving the online inference efficiency of the original sequential backbone.
filter_reasoning: The paper addresses popularity bias in recommendation systems using adversarial debiasing, which falls under the category of fairness/bias in AI systems.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: LEVEE: Layer-wise Evaluation of Vector Encoding Effects: Bias Localization and Functional Separation across 11 LLMs
abstract: Large language models encode social biases that instruction fine-tuning aims to suppress. Instruction fine-tuning applies its weight changes through the alignment task vector \DeltaW, yet prior work treats it as a monolithic object, leaving its internal layer structure opaque: which layers carry bias suppression, which carry general capability, and whether these are separable, remains unknown. We map this structure by injecting each layer's \DeltaWᵢ independently into the base model across 11 LLMs from Qwen2.5, Gemma-2/3, and Llama-3 families (0.5B--14B). Testing via per-layer sufficiency sweeps, block removal, and a BBQ--MMLU dissociation, we find three results. First, BBQ-measured bias suppression localizes to the mid-third of transformer layers in 9 of 11 models, with mid-third removal raising bias across all 11 while first- and last-third removals produce smaller L-BBQ increases in all nine structured-signal models. Second, mid- and first-third removals dissociate BBQ and MMLU: mid-third removal is BBQ-critical across all tested models while first-third removal can sharply reduce MMLU in Gemma architectures, supporting functional separation of bias suppression and capability in weight space. Third, mid-third removal raises bias above the unaligned base in 3 of 11 cases: partial \DeltaW transfer without the mid-third can make a model more biased than the unaligned base model. These findings provide an empirical roadmap for targeted debiasing and safe task vector composition.
filter_reasoning: The paper conducts a mechanistic investigation into how instruction tuning suppresses bias, which is highly relevant to AI ethics and model alignment.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: ParsHate: A Benchmark Dataset for Hate and Target Detection in Persian
abstract: We introduce ParsHate, a manually annotated dataset of 10,000 Persian tweets spanning 2013--2022, representing the first decade-long benchmark for hate speech detection in Persian. The dataset contains 31\% hateful content and supports both hate detection and multi-label fine-grained target identification across seven structured target categories. ParsHate also distinguishes explicit and implicit hate, marks explicit and implicit targets, and provides span-level rationales. Data collection combines random and score-stratified temporal sampling to reduce keyword-driven bias while preserving natural label distributions. Applying SOTA models for Persian hate-speech detection on ParsHate shows moderate performance (79\% F1), especially with samples from earlier years, and low performance with target identification (25.5\% macro-F1). This emphasizes the diverse sampling of hate speech in ParsHate and its challenging nature that requires more advanced methods for better performance. Dataset is made publicly available.
filter_reasoning: The paper presents a dataset for hate speech detection and target identification, which is a core task in addressing toxic and harmful content in AI.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: Assessing Adversarial Robustness of Latent Reasoning Models
abstract: Large language models increasingly rely on long chain-of-thought (CoT) trajectories for complex reasoning, but autoregressive generation brings substantial memory and inference costs. Latent reasoning models (LRMs) offer a more efficient alternative by compressing intermediate reasoning into a small number of continuous latent vectors. Despite their efficiency, however, the adversarial robustness of LRMs remains largely underexplored. In this work, we systematically evaluate the robustness of latent reasoning across textual and multimodal settings, covering eight models and six benchmarks. We find that, across our evaluated settings, LRMs are generally less robust than explicit CoT baselines under adversarial perturbations, with particularly severe degradation under white-box attacks. Further analysis reveals distinct failure modes across modalities: textual latent states exhibit brittle dynamics and high sensitivity to specific input patterns, while latent states in multimodal models can remain largely invariant to input perturbations and have limited influence on final predictions. These findings expose robustness limitations of current latent reasoning approaches and highlight the need to jointly consider efficiency and robustness when designing implicit reasoning systems. We have open-sourced our code to facilitate reproduction of our research https://github.com/PKU-ML/latent-reasoning-model-assessment.
filter_reasoning: The paper investigates the adversarial robustness of latent reasoning models, which is a central topic in AI safety.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: Audio-Reward-R1: Reasoning Reward Model for Unified Audio Understanding and Generation
abstract: Multimodal Reward Models are critical for aligning Multimodal Large Language Models with human preferences. However, existing reward models offer limited interpretability and struggle to deliver reliable preference judgments in audio-centric scenarios. To address this gap, we propose Audio-Reward-R1, a reasoning-based reward model that supports both audio understanding and audio generation preference tasks. Audio-Reward-R1 formulates reward modeling as a structured reasoning process, producing dimension-level analyses prior to the final preference judgment. To enable reliable reasoning supervision, we construct a high-quality reasoning-enhanced audio preference dataset with structured reasoning traces aligned with preference annotations. Audio-Reward-R1 is first trained via supervised fine-tuning as a cold-start on this reasoning-enhanced dataset, followed by reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. Finally, we introduce Audio-Reward-Bench, a human-verified evaluation benchmark for evaluating audio reward models across both audio understanding and audio generation preference tasks. Extensive experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness and reliability of Audio-Reward-R1.
filter_reasoning: The paper focuses on developing a reward model to better align multimodal LLMs with human preferences, which is a core task in value alignment.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: RACE: Scalable Statistical Estimation of Functional Consistency in LLM Neurons
abstract: Discovering stable neuron behavior across entire domains remains a challenge in mechanistic interpretability. Existing methods often rely on instance-level point estimates or computationally expensive procedures, which either obscure population-level variability or limit scalable domain-wide analysis. We present RACE (Residual Alignment for Consistency Estimation), a forward-pass statistical framework that evaluates the domain-wide functional consistency of Transformer neurons. Compared with gradient-based point estimates, RACE produces neuron rankings that yield more domain-specific effects under perturbation. Token-distribution shifts support the connection between the selected neurons and the target domain, while scoring requires roughly one-hundredth of the computational overhead of the gradient-based methods. Code is available at https://github.com/Nexround/RACE.
filter_reasoning: The paper focuses on mechanistic interpretability to estimate functional consistency of neurons, a core method within AI safety research.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: Consensus Group Relative Policy Optimization for Text Generation
abstract: Many strong decoding methods for text generation follow a sample-and-rerank paradigm: they draw multiple candidates, score each under a utility (reward) function using consensus across samples, and choose the best one. Although effective, these methods incur high computational costs during inference due to repeated sampling and scoring. Prior attempts to amortize inference-time computation typically rely on gold references, teacher labels, or curated preference data, thereby increasing the effort required to construct datasets and the demand for high-fidelity reward models. We propose Consensus Group Relative Policy Optimization (C-GRPO), which distills Minimum Bayes Risk (MBR) decoding into training by formulating the consensus utility as a group-relative objective within GRPO. C-GRPO requires only a utility function and policy samples, without gold references or explicit preference labels. As supporting analysis, we study an idealized sentence-level surrogate and show that the expected update is directionally consistent with the expected-utility objective underlying MBR decoding under simplifying assumptions. Experiments on machine translation (WMT 2024), text summarization (XSum), and Japanese social-bias mitigation (JBBQ) show that C-GRPO often matches or exceeds inference-time MBR decoding while replacing multi-sample reranking with a single generation.
filter_reasoning: While a technical reinforcement learning paper, it explicitly evaluates and includes bias mitigation (JBBQ) as a core demonstration of its objective function.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: When Hate Meets Facts: LLMs-in-the-Loop for Check-worthiness Detection in Hate Speech
abstract: Hateful content online is often expressed using fact-like, not necessarily correct information, especially in coordinated online harassment campaigns and extremist propaganda. Failing to jointly address hate speech (HS) and misinformation can deepen prejudice, reinforce harmful stereotypes, and expose bystanders to psychological distress, while polluting public debate. Moreover, these messages require more effort from content moderators because they must assess both harmfulness and veracity, i.e., fact-check them. To address this challenge, we release WSF-ARG+, the first dataset which combines hate speech with check-worthiness information. We also introduce a novel LLM-in-the-loop framework to facilitate the annotation of check-worthy claims. We run our framework, testing it with 12 open-weight LLMs of different sizes and architectures. We validate it through extensive human evaluation, and show that our LLM-in-the-loop framework reduces human effort without compromising the annotation quality of the data. Finally, we show that HS messages with check-worthy claims show significantly higher harassment and hate, and that incorporating check-worthiness labels improves LLM-based HS detection up to 0.213 macro-F1 and to 0.154 macro-F1 on average for large models.
filter_reasoning: The paper addresses the intersection of hate speech and misinformation, focusing on the responsible detection of harmful content.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: Beyond Token Positions: Safety Alignment Across Denoising Steps in Diffusion Language Models
abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) generate text through iterative denoising rather than left-to-right decoding. This generation paradigm introduces two axes that can influence safety alignment: when tokens are generated during denoising and where they appear in the response. In this paper, we measure dLLM safety behavior under harmful prompts by tracing intermediate token distributions and commitment decisions throughout denoising. Our analysis shows that refusal signals are concentrated in early denoising steps and leading response positions, and the tokens committed early can strongly shape the final safety outcome. Our measurements further show that the denoising step and persistence of refusal-token commitment are important for understanding dLLM safety. Based on these findings, we propose Refusal-Aware Early Commitment (RAEC), a simple training-free decoding method that commits persistent refusal signals from early steps. Experiments on LLaDA and Dream show that RAEC reduces attack success rates while largely preserving utility. The code is available at https://github.com/Glresearch1/RAEC.
filter_reasoning: This paper investigates methods to improve safety alignment and refusal behavior in diffusion models, directly addressing AI safety.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: Counter-GEO-Bench: Evaluating Defenses Against Information-Distorting Generative Engine Optimization
abstract: Generative engine optimization (GEO) enables content producers to increase the visibility of their web pages in generative search engines, but the same techniques can deliver targeted misinformation when adversaries publish ordinary-looking GEO-optimized documents that victim large language models (LLMs) retrieve and synthesize into distorted answers. No existing benchmark evaluates defenses against this threat under controlled conditions. Therefore, we present Counter-GEO-Bench, a defense benchmark that pairs 247 human-verified, quality-gated queries with information-preserving and information-distorting GEO rewrites, and evaluates defenses on attack success rate (ASR), false positive rate, and answer quality across three victim LLMs. Under Counter-GEO-Bench, three off-the-shelf defenses (Granite Guardian, Llama Guard 3, and NeMo Self-Check Fact-Checking) reduce ASR by at most 5.7\% relative, while Granite Guardian's reduction is not statistically significant. Safety-taxonomy guardrails target policy violations, while GEO misinformation passes through them as fluent informational content. To this end, a lightweight benchmark baseline, C-GEO Guard, is proposed, reducing ASR by 47.6\% relative with near-zero utility loss, which proves threat tractable.
filter_reasoning: This paper evaluates the robustness of LLMs against misinformation-based adversarial attacks, which falls under AI safety/robustness.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: Contaminated Collaboration: Measuring Gender Bias Transfer in LLM-Assisted Student Writing
abstract: Gender bias in LLMs has been studied extensively in model outputs, with biased prompts shown to amplify stereotyped generations. Whether such bias propagates into text produced by humans who use these systems, however, remains underexplored. We investigate whether gender bias in an LLM writing assistant transfers into career plan essays written by students. We first verify that a gender-biased prompt induces gender-differentiated language in LLM-generated essays, while a neutral prompt does not. We then recruited participants ($N = 123$) in a controlled environment to write career plan essays for paired biographical profiles differing only in gender under three conditions: no AI assistance, neutral LLM assistance, or gender-biased LLM assistance. Students in the biased condition produced essays with a significantly larger agentic gap and more gender-stereotypic occupation suggestions than those in the control and neutral conditions. Our results also reveal that this bias transfer is asymmetric: agency is suppressed in female-target essays while male-target writing remains largely unaffected. Our findings highlight the risk of bias propagation in AI-assisted writing, calling for fairness-aware design in educational AI tools.
filter_reasoning: This paper investigates the propagation and transfer of gender bias from AI assistants to human users, which is a core AI ethics topic.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: When Does Hate Transfer? A Large-Scale Study of Cross-Lingual Hate Speech Detection
abstract: Effective detection of hate content is essential for maintaining healthy online communities, yet performance can vary substantially across languages. This work investigates a core practical question: Can training data from one language support hate-speech detection in another language with comparable performance? To answer this question, we conduct a large-scale study across 14 languages. Our analysis shows that transfer effectiveness could depend on several factors---including, but not limited to, dataset size, resources and temporal overlap. At the same time, we observe consistent patterns in which certain language pairs exhibit stronger transfer performance. Upon further analysis, we find that these patterns can be attributed to cultural cues or shared societal characteristics. Our analysis includes low-resource languages, offering practical insights into when cross-lingual transfer can support them and where its limitations emerge. These findings provide guidance for designing more reliable and generalizable hate detection systems.Warning: This paper includes examples of hate speech for research purposes.
filter_reasoning: This paper discusses the development of hate speech detection systems, which is central to AI ethics and social responsibility.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: How Identity and Opinion Shape Political Sycophancy in LLMs
abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly encourage users to disclose personal profiles for tailored assistance, measuring their political alignment becomes increasingly important. However, many existing benchmarks for assessing political behavior rely on closed-ended questions and do not fully capture how a model's stance may adapt to user-provided context during interaction. We introduce a framework that disentangles two distinct triggers of political sycophancy: opinion (aligning with explicit narratives) and identity (stereotyping based on demographic labels). Using 450 manually-checked political dilemmas as controlled probes, we evaluate 13 instruction-tuned LLMs. We uncover a dissociation: a model's susceptibility to explicit opinions does not necessarily predict its susceptibility to identity cues, and vice versa. When both signals are present, their effects are generally sub-additive rather than simply additive. Additionally, system-level personas primarily shift a model's baseline stance while having limited effect on the stance shift caused by user opinion or identity. Ultimately, our results suggest that LLM political stance is interactively and steerably vulnerable rather than being a fixed trait, highlighting how personalization may amplify identity- or opinion-conditioned shifts in the model's behaviors.
filter_reasoning: This paper studies political sycophancy and bias in LLMs, which is a significant AI ethics concern regarding model manipulation and influence.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: Fast-Slow Thinking RM: Efficient Integration of Scalar and Generative Reward Models
abstract: Reward models (RMs) are critical for aligning Large Language Models via Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). While Generative Reward Models (GRMs) achieve superior accuracy through chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, they incur substantial computational costs. Conversely, Scalar Reward Models (SRMs) offer efficiency but suffer from limited performance and adaptability in complex scenarios. We introduce Fast-Slow Thinking Reward Models (F/S-RM), a hybrid RM architecture inspired by Dual Process Theory. It trains a single model to integrate two distinct reward paradigms: scalar-style first-token pairwise judgment (fast thinking) and CoT-based judgment (slow thinking), regulated by a dual-confidence activation mechanism that determines when to activate slow thinking. Under hybrid inference, F/S-RM achieves state-of-the-art accuracy with an average score of 84.3 across benchmarks, while reducing token consumption by 22.5\%. Code and data are publicly available.
filter_reasoning: This paper discusses improving the efficiency and accuracy of reward models in RLHF, which is directly relevant to value alignment and safety training.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: Tampered ML: Evaluating LLM Judgment of Machine Learning Research
abstract: One approach to accelerating progress on AI alignment is to automate parts of alignment research itself. Doing so requires systems that can perform reliably on hard-to-supervise research tasks, including identifying flaws in research proposals and evaluating whether a proposed experiment supports its intended claim. To evaluate this capability, we introduce **Tampered ML**, a benchmark of $1,858$ item-pairs, each consisting of an experiment proposal reconstructed from a published machine learning paper and a minimally edited counterfactual that introduces a targeted methodological flaw. Models must identify the more methodologically sound proposal in both presentation orders. A human validation study on a stratified sample estimates that $80-90$\% of items are valid. Frontier models perform above chance but remain far from reliable (with Opus 5 achieving 77.9\% accuracy). They are highly sensitive to the order of presentation and favor flawed designs that appear more specific, transparent, or conventional.
filter_reasoning: This paper benchmarks the ability of LLMs to detect research flaws, which is a key component of automated alignment research.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: SAFEGuard: Detect Optimization-Based Jailbreak Atacks Through Harmful Semantic Analysis and Fluency Measurement
abstract: Despite the significant efforts devoted to aligning large language models (LLMs) with human values and ensuring safe deployment, recent work has revealed that LLMs remain vulnerable to adversarial jailbreak attacks that can bypass safety guardrails and elicit harmful responses. Many defense methods are proposed to detect jailbreaks but they are limited in their effectiveness to counter wide-range optimization based jailbreak mechanisms that can yield highly fluency-optimized or harmful semantic obfuscated prompts. To tackle this challenge, we propose a unified detection framework---SAFEGuard---which incorporates a hybrid fluency measurement based on cross-layer distribution distance and perplexity, and the analysis of harmful semantics through gradient matching. Our method is grounded in a paramount observation: high fluency prompts maintain their malicious intention close to harmful prompts while harmful semantic obfuscated prompts often inject gibberish token sequences. Our evaluation demonstrates that SAFEGuard consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines and achieves significant improvement in accuracy across different optimization-based jailbreaks. This underscores the effectiveness of SAFEGuard against evolving jailbreak attacks.
filter_reasoning: The paper proposes a framework to detect adversarial jailbreak attacks, a clear contribution to AI safety.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: What and Whose Knowledge? Measuring Epistemic Diversity in Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as primary knowledge sources, yet their epistemic diversity --- defined as the diversity of real-world claims in their outputs --- has never been measured. The dominant paradigm is that overall LLM diversity is low, but this is always with respect to a single point in time, with no reference baseline or consideration for variation across countries. We address this by performing the first systematic study of epistemic diversity in LLMs across time and cultural context, testing 27 LLMs on 155 topics covering 12 countries, resulting in 1.7M responses and 70M individual claims. We find that epistemic diversity has increased substantially over the past three years, a positive counter to recent diversity pessimism. However, despite progress, we find that every LLM is less diverse than a search baseline. The gap is not uniform: RAG can improve diversity, while larger models are counterintuitively less diverse than smaller ones. Moreover, LLMs systematically reflect English-language knowledge over local-language knowledge for country specific topics. Together, these results demonstrate that while progress on epistemic diversity is tangible, it is insufficient and unevenly distributed.
filter_reasoning: This paper investigates epistemic diversity and cultural bias in LLMs, which is a direct contribution to AI ethics.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: AGENTQ: Quantization-Conditioned Backdoor Attacks on LLM Agents
abstract: Quantization is one of the default deployment path for open-weight LLM agents, but it is not behavior-preserving: an adversary can release a full-precision checkpoint that passes audits yet misbehaves once quantized, termed as quantization-conditioned attack (QCA). Prior QCA work targets free-text generation, where harm is mediated by a human reader. In contrast, the agentic setting poses a more severe risk: the triggered payload is a structured tool call that can be executed without human oversight. We present the first study of QCA against LLM agents. We find that directly adapting prior backdoor-injection methods can produce malicious behavior after quantization, but substantially degrades benign utility, rendering the resulting attacks impractical. To understand the true upper bound of the threat, we propose AgentQ, an attack framework that combines layer-banded LoRA injection with partial-PGD repair over a multi-codebook quantization-equivalence class. AgentQ preserves normal tool-calling capability while concentrating malicious behavior in the quantized model. Across three trigger--action pairs and three codebooks (NF4, FP4, INT8), AgentQ reaches up to 100\% post-quantization attack success rate with minimal loss of benign utility, underscoring the need to make quantization-aware safety evaluation a standard requirement before open-weight agents are released or deployed.
filter_reasoning: This paper studies backdoor attacks on quantized models, which is a critical AI safety/security concern for deployment.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: SimLens: Two-Token Continuation for Early Exit in Single-Token Decision Tasks
abstract: Intermediate-layer representations in large language models (LLMs) contain task-relevant information, yet direct linear readouts often fail to recover the model's eventual choice. This gap limits both interpretability and early-exit methods for candidate-scoring workloads. We study single-token decision settings -- such as multiple-choice and boolean QA -- where the answer is a single token at a position fixed by the task format, and we read out the model's prediction there as its highest-probability token over the full vocabulary. We propose SimLens, a training-free readout that, at a chosen intermediate layer, keeps only the start token and the candidate answer token and forwards this reduced two-token state through the model's remaining upper layers. To identify the layer at which the full sequence can be safely truncated, we distill LinearSimLens as a lightweight entropy monitor and combine the two in SimExit. Across different models, SimLens produces earlier and more faithful candidate readout than direct linear lenses under fair-compute accounting, while SimExit delivers a modest but stable speed--accuracy trade-off on the two models used end-to-end. Ablations show that the two retained tokens play complementary roles as global condition and semantic anchor.
filter_reasoning: This paper works on model interpretability through early-exit readouts, which falls under the interpretability focus within AI safety.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: Prompt Revision as a Source of Cultural Bias in Text-to-Image Systems
abstract: Commercial text-to-image systems silently revise user prompts before generating images, a step users typically cannot disable or even see. Existing audits of cultural bias examine only the final images and treat generation as a single pipeline, so they cannot tell where the bias originates. We introduce WORLDVIEW, a multilingual benchmark of 8,960 prompts across 15 languages and 31 language--context pairings. Using it, we audit the revision layer in three systems (DALL-E-3, Imagen-4, GPT-Image-1.5) through a three-step analysis of how heavily it marks each cultural context, whether it flattens that context into a narrow vocabulary, and whether that vocabulary is stereotypical. Relative to a no-context English baseline, the US is the least-marked context, while non-Western and non-Anglophone contexts are marked far more heavily, flattened into narrow vocabularies applied across topically diverse prompts, and reduced to recognizable cultural stereotypes. Comparing images from original versus revised prompts on models without a revision layer, we identify the layer itself as a previously undocumented, causal source of this stereotyping. To locate cultural bias, and fix it, we must audit the system as deployed, not the model alone.
filter_reasoning: The paper identifies and analyzes a causal mechanism for cultural stereotyping and bias in AI systems, directly addressing fairness and social impact.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: From Chatbots to Confidants: A Cross-Cultural Study of LLM Adoption for Emotional Support
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used not only for instrumental tasks, but as always-available and non-judgmental confidants for emotional support. Yet what drives adoption and how users perceive emotional support interactions across countries remains unknown. To address this gap, we present the first large-scale cross-cultural study of LLM use for emotional support, surveying 4,641 participants across seven countries (USA, UK, Germany, France, Spain, Italy, and the Netherlands). Our results show that adoption rates vary dramatically across countries (from 20\% to 59\%). Using mixed models that separate country-level effects from demographic composition, we find that being aged 25-44, religious, married, and of higher socioeconomic status are predictors of positive perceptions (trust, usage, perceived benefits), with socioeconomic status being the strongest. English-speaking countries consistently show more positive perceptions than Continental European countries. We also collect a corpus of 731 real multilingual prompts from user interactions, showing that users mainly seek help for loneliness, stress, relationship conflicts, and mental health struggles. Our findings reveal that LLM emotional support use is shaped by a complex sociotechnical landscape and call for a broader research agenda examining how these systems can be developed, deployed, and governed to ensure safe and informed access. We share our code and data publicly [https://confidant-ai.github.io/LLMs-emotional-support/].
filter_reasoning: The paper explores the sociotechnical implications of using AI for emotional support and calls for governance and informed access.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: Safety Paradox: How Enhanced Safety Awareness Leaves LLMs Vulnerable to Posterior Attack
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are rigorously aligned to refuse harmful requests, a process that inherently cultivates a latent capacity to evaluate and recognize unsafe content. In this work, we reveal that this advanced safety awareness inadvertently introduces a fatal vulnerability. We introduce Posterior Attack, a single-query jailbreak that bypasses guardrails by prompting the model to generate the exact harmful response its internal classifier would normally flag as unsafe. Through extensive empirical evaluation across 30 open-source LLMs (up to 35B parameters in size) and frontier models (e.g., GPT-5, Claude 4.6), we observe a striking phenomenon: models with superior safety-judgment capabilities are disproportionately more susceptible to this exploitation. To explain this, we formalize the Safety Paradox, analytically showing that monotonic improvements in safety alignment naturally amplify posterior vulnerability. Finally, we establish a causal link via reinforcement learning interventions, exemplifying that artificially degrading a model's safety judgment immunizes it against the attack, whereas enhancing judgment exacerbates the vulnerability. Our findings highlight potential flaws in current alignment paradigms, indicating that defense mechanisms may require further structural refinement.
filter_reasoning: The paper identifies a novel jailbreak vulnerability related to safety alignment and provides an analytical explanation for the trade-off between safety awareness and adversarial robustness.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: Exploring Confirmation Bias: LLMs Perceive Democratic Claims as More Truthful Independently of their Content
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to detect misinformation and support human fact-checkers. However, their truthfulness assessments may be affected by systematic political biases. Motivated by confirmation bias in humans, i.e., interpreting evidence in ways that are partial to existing beliefs or expectations, we investigate whether LLMs assess truthfulness in line with their political attitudes. We compare LLMs' political attitudinal bias (PB-A) with political bias in truthfulness perception (PB-T). We assess PB-T by prompting LLMs to evaluate Democratic and Republican claims, including conditions where the claim-making party is explicitly stated. Across 20 instruction-tuned LLMs, all models exhibit a left-leaning tendency in PB-T, statistically significant for roughly half of them. Moreover, 16 out of 20 models significantly factor in the claim maker's party affiliation when predicting truthfulness. PB-T and PB-A correlate weakly to moderately, and larger models tend to exhibit more left-leaning PB-T. The code for reproducibility is available on GitHub.
filter_reasoning: The paper investigates systemic political bias in truthfulness assessment, which is a core concern in the ethics and societal impact of LLMs.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: M-QUEST - Meme Question-Understanding Evaluation on Semantics and Toxicity
abstract: Internet memes are a powerful form of online communication, yet their multimodal nature and reliance on commonsense and cultural knowledge make automated toxicity detection challenging. Prior work has studied individual dimensions of memes: textual content via optical character recognition, visual content via object recognition, and toxicity via hate speech detection, but lacks a unified architecture that formally identifies the semantic dimensions contributing to meme toxicity. We present three contributions: (1) a semantic framework identifying the dimensions necessary for meme interpretation; (2) a corresponding benchmark, M-QUEST, of 609 question-answer pairs for 307 memes, generated via a semi-automatic process grounded in the framework; and (3) an empirical evaluation of 12 VLMs on M-QUEST. The results show that the instruction-tuned models with reasoning capabilities significantly outperform others, whereas pragmatic inference remains challenging across all models.
filter_reasoning: The paper focuses on the detection of toxicity in multimodal internet memes, contributing to research on AI-mediated social harm.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: Lost in Delusion: Examining LLM Safety Under User Delusions and Distress
abstract: LLM chatbots increasingly serve as a first source of support for people in psychological distress, including those whose distress is entangled with delusional beliefs. Prior work on LLM mental-health safety largely evaluates general therapeutic quality or single-turn crisis detection, leaving unclear how models behave when distress is intertwined with delusion over sustained conversations. We address this gap with matched multi-turn simulations, across clinically grounded personas and six LLMs, that pair each delusional conversation with a distress-only control to isolate the effect of an operationalized delusional presentation. This reveals a recognition-intervention gap: models detect distress at comparable rates regardless of framing, yet some fail to act on it once distress is embedded in delusion, with safety interventions suppressed by up to 4.5x in the most affected model. The failure is correlated with accumulated premise acceptance whereas emotional validation suppresses intervention in both contexts alike. We term this candidate explanation as narrative debt.
