Worse, the intuitive fix of prompting models to assess user distress backfires under delusional framing; only delusion-aware prompting with explicit response guidance narrows the gap, and even this depends on a delusion classifier that is itself unreliable on the most vulnerable models. Safe deployment therefore requires treating delusional framing as a distinct risk signal that overrides conversational accommodation.
filter_reasoning: The paper addresses the failure of safety interventions when AI is confronted with specific user scenarios (delusion), touching on the reliability and robustness of safety mechanisms.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking
abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) ``think'' by generating structured chain-of-thought (CoT) before producing a final answer, yet they still lack the ability to reason critically about safety alignment and are easily biased when a flawed premise is injected into their thought process. We propose RECAP (Robust Safety Alignment via Counter-Aligned Prefilling), a principled reinforcement learning (RL) method for post-training that explicitly teaches models to override flawed reasoning trajectories and reroute to safe and helpful responses. RECAP trains on a mixture of synthetically generated counter-aligned CoT prefills and standard prompts, integrates seamlessly into standard reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) pipelines without additional RL optimization steps or architectural modifications, and substantially improves safety and jailbreak robustness, reduces overrefusal, and preserves core reasoning capability --- all while maintaining inference token budget. Extensive analysis shows that RECAP-trained models engage in self-reflection more frequently and remain robust under adaptive attacks, preserving safety even after repeated attempts to override their reasoning. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/poloclub/recap.
filter_reasoning: The paper proposes a specific reinforcement learning intervention (RECAP) to improve safety alignment and robustness against jailbreak attacks.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: Mitigating Hallucination in Vision-Language Models through Barrier-Regulated Adaptive Closed-form Steering
abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) often hallucinate objects that are not present in the input image, largely because visual grounding weakens as decoding progresses. Existing inference-time mitigation methods modify logits or hidden states throughout generation, but they suffer from three key limitations: they lack an explicit grounding objective, intervene even when the model is already well-grounded, and use fixed correction strengths that do not adapt to the severity of grounding failure. We propose BRACS (Barrier-Regulated Adaptive Closed-form Steering), a training-free steering framework that addresses these issues through barrier-regulated adaptive closed-form steering. BRACS monitors the model's own attention to measure visual grounding and applies corrections to the hidden states only when grounding deteriorates. The corrective update is computed analytically in closed form, requiring no training of auxiliary networks or model retraining. Experiments on LLaVA-1.5-7B and Qwen-VL-Chat show that BRACS consistently outperforms prior methods on hallucination benchmarks, reducing CHAIR$_s$ by 9.4 points and improving POPE F1 by 2.7 points, while matching or improving performance on four general multimodal benchmarks. BRACS also remains efficient, operating at 80\% of greedy decoding throughput and achieving $1.3\times$ higher speed on average than the baselines.
filter_reasoning: The paper presents a method to mitigate hallucinations in vision-language models, which falls under the robustness and reliability scope of AI safety.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: From Value Conditioning to Behavioral Shift: Lightweight Value Alignment of LLMs
abstract: Large language models exhibit value-related preferences in their outputs, yet steering such behavior often requires large training datasets or paired preference annotations. In this work, we investigate a lightweight alternative: can fine-tuning on value survey responses induce measurable shifts in value-conditioned model outputs and downstream behavior? We first estimate baseline value profiles for several open-source LLMs by asking them to rate value-related descriptions organized around the ten Schwartz values. We then fine-tune models on survey-style supervision that selectively changes the target value ratings while keeping non-target values close to their baseline responses. We evaluate the resulting shifts in two settings. First, we measure whether the intervention changes responses on held-out survey questions. Second, we test whether these survey-induced shifts transfer to out-of-domain behavioral proxies, including a contextual moral-judgment benchmark constructed from Reddit AITA posts and a text-based interactive decision-making benchmark. Our results show that survey-based supervision can change held-out survey responses and produce downstream shifts in model response distributions on proxy behavioral evaluations. However, this transfer is strongly model- and value-dependent, and is shaped by how value descriptions are framed in the supervision data. These findings suggest that value surveys can serve not only as diagnostic tools, but also as lightweight supervision for studying behavioral value conditioning in LLMs.
filter_reasoning: The paper explores value alignment and the behavioral impact of conditioning models on specific human value surveys, which is central to AI ethics and alignment.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: Detecting AI Impostors: How Do Middle Schoolers Identify LLM Agents in a Live Collaborative Setting?
abstract: LLMs can imitate how people write, which raises concerns about impersonation, trust, and detection in social settings. These concerns are especially important for adolescents, who use generative AI frequently but may struggle to recognize it. We introduce DoppelBot, a cooperative social deduction game designed to study how young people detect and respond to AI impersonation. Through studies with middle schoolers, we investigate whether a DoppelBot prompts reflection on privacy and impersonation, how repeated exposure affects AI-detection accuracy as agents become more personalized, and which strategies students use to identify AI doppelg\"angers. We find that students' detection accuracy improves over time, driven by a shift from relying on linguistic cues to leveraging shared social and contextual signals. Students also demonstrated an understanding of AI limitations such as embodiment and reflected on broader issues such as data privacy. To support future research, we release an anonymized dataset of game transcripts and voting~behavior.[<https://github.com/danschumac1/Detecting\_AI\_Impostors>]
filter_reasoning: The study examines human-AI interaction regarding trust, privacy, and the societal impact of AI impersonation, directly relevant to the ethical deployment of AI.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: Trustworthy Medical LLMs via Bayesian Belief Updating
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) show strong potential in medical QA, but still suffer from hallucinations in multi-step clinical reasoning. Existing methods fail to assess confidence at intermediate steps or reliably integrate external knowledge, leading to propagated errors and misleading conclusions. Inspired by Bayesian inference logic in clinical diagnosis, we propose BELIEF, a Bayesian Evidence Leveraged InfErence Framework that enables LLMs to perform reliable medical reasoning through dynamic belief assessment and knowledge-augmented disambiguation. First, the Bayesian Belief Updating Module (BBUM) treats diagnostic hypotheses as prior probabilities and calculates posterior probabilities based on observed clinical evidence, preventing early-stage error propagation with statistical rigor. Second, the Dynamic Evidence Retrieval Module (DERM) autonomously queries external medical databases to resolve ambiguity when the posterior belief exhibits high entropy. Experiments across 7 datasets and 2 LLM backbones show that BELIEF significantly improves diagnostic accuracy, enhances interpretability, and mitigates hallucinations through explicit probabilistic updates.
filter_reasoning: The paper introduces a framework to mitigate hallucinations and improve reasoning reliability in high-stakes medical contexts, aligning with AI safety goals for robustness.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: Who is the Agent to Blame? Localizing Faithfulness and Citation Mistakes in Agentic Deep Research
abstract: Deep research (DR) systems produce long-form cited reports by orchestrating multiple agents that search and synthesize information from the web. Citations are the primary mechanism for evaluating the faithfulness of these reports, yet current DR systems exhibit poor citation recall. Moreover, improving citation recall is challenging because DR systems are complex multi-agent architectures where information passes through agents like a telephone game, and both content and citations can get corrupted along the way. We propose an evaluation method that pinpoints which agent introduced each error by locally testing agent invocations for faithfulness and verifiability relative to their own inputs. Furthermore, we propose a four-type taxonomy to categorize the discovered errors: hallucination, uncited input reliance, uncited output, or insufficient citations. Applying our method to three top-ranked open-source DR systems, we obtain actionable diagnostics. Almost every agent makes a lot of mistakes with the exception being those that summarize a single document. We find that the dominant error type varies systematically across agents, where the orchestrator mistakes are mostly citation-related. We find that 84.7\% of final-report errors in AI-Q originate at the orchestrator, roughly 31\% of them hallucinations and the rest citation mistakes. Guided by these insights, we demonstrate that two simple interventions raise citation recall by 5\% without degrading output quality.
filter_reasoning: The paper provides diagnostics for faithfulness and hallucination in multi-agent research systems, which is critical for the safety and reliability of complex AI systems.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: DR$^3$-Eval: Towards Realistic and Reproducible Deep Research Evaluation
abstract: Deep Research Agents (DRAs) aim to solve complex, long-horizon research tasks involving planning, retrieval, multimodal understanding, and report generation, yet their evaluation remains challenging due to dynamic web environments and ambiguous task definitions. We propose **DR$^3$-Eval**, a realistic and reproducible benchmark for evaluating deep research agents on multimodal, multi-file report generation. DR$^3$-Eval is constructed from authentic user-provided materials and paired with a per-task static research sandbox corpus that simulates open-web complexity while remaining fully verifiable, containing supportive documents, distractors, and noise. Moreover, we introduce a multi-dimensional evaluation framework measuring Information Recall, Factual Accuracy, Citation Coverage, Instruction Following, and Depth Quality, and validate its alignment with human judgments. Experiments with our developed multi-agent system DR$^3$-Agent based on multiple state-of-the-art language models demonstrate that DR$^3$-Eval is highly challenging and reveals critical failure modes in retrieval robustness and hallucination control.
filter_reasoning: The paper introduces a benchmark to evaluate hallucination control and retrieval robustness in deep research agents, which are key AI safety metrics.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: How Do People Challenge Racial Stereotypes Online? Counter-Story Detection Across Reddit Communities
abstract: Counter-storytelling is a powerful mechanism people use to challenge dominant narratives. Unlike other forms of counterspeech that have been widely studied in computational social science, counter-storytelling has largely been overlooked. Counter-stories are difficult to detect automatically; they are relational (defined with respect to expressions of racial stereotypes) and structurally diverse (drawing on stories that describe lived experiences, witnessed events, exemplars, and hypotheticals). We introduce a first framework for detecting and characterizing counter-storytelling against racial stereotypes at scale. This includes (1) a three-dimensional taxonomy grounded in narratology and Critical Race Theory and (2) a multi-stage pipeline that identifies relational pairs of stereotypes and counter-stories in noisy Reddit discourse. Using this pipeline, we annotate 25,549 Reddit posts across 615 communities and identify 1,312 counter-stories. Our analysis shows that speaker identity and post context shape how counter-stories are told. For example, in-group writers favor first-person testimony, often adopting the role of self-reflective insiders. Our work shows how computational methods can scale qualitative approaches to identify and characterize counter-storytelling as a contextual narrative practice, with implications for content moderation, narratology, and racial discourse analysis.
filter_reasoning: The paper investigates the detection and characterization of counter-storytelling against racial stereotypes, contributing to the understanding of social discourse and bias in AI contexts.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: OrgAccess: A Benchmark for Role-Based Access Control in Organization Scale LLMs
abstract: Conversational language models are increasingly deployed as central knowledge repositories and ``conversational operating systems'' in enterprise environments, where they must comply with role-based access control (RBAC) and organizational hierarchies. However, evaluating models on natural language permission compliance is difficult due to the highly proprietary nature of real-world corporate policies, and existing benchmarks do not capture the semantic nuance of overlapping or conflicting rules within free-text queries. To address this gap, we introduce **OrgAccess**, a benchmark designed to evaluate LLMs on their capacity to adhere to complex organizational hierarchies under natural language constraints. Grounded in NIST cybersecurity frameworks and validated via a multi-round expert Delphi process, OrgAccess defines 40 standard permission types across three difficulty tiers (70,000 total instances), simulating scenarios with up to five concurrent, potentially conflicting permissions. Through extensive evaluations of 16 frontier and open-source models, we systematically assess their classification accuracy and diagnostic failure modes on permission-aware query routing. Our findings reveal a pronounced performance decline: as rule complexity increases, even flagship models fail to resolve combinatorial constraint interactions, frequently yielding over-conservative ``False Partial'' predictions due to safety-tuning hedging. Specifically, the strongest evaluated model achieves an $F_1$-score of only 0.27 on our hardest split. This demonstrates that current instruction-following and safety alignment paradigms do not inherently translate to robust, multi-constraint rule compliance. More broadly, OrgAccess establishes a formal, reproducible testing framework to diagnose these constraint-adherence deficits and support the systematic integration of conversational agents into highly regulated, multi-user collaborative environments. The dataset is available on the https://anonymous-hf.up.railway.app/a/tj0x0lgg2cmu/anonymous project page.
filter_reasoning: The paper investigates role-based access control and constraint compliance in LLMs, which is a critical safety issue for the secure and restricted operation of AI agents.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: Risk-Adjusted Harm Scoring for Automated Red Teaming of LLMs in Financial Services
abstract: Existing LLM safety evaluations rely on binary attack-success rates and domain-agnostic taxonomies, leaving regulated Banking, Financial Services, and Insurance (BFSI) deployments exposed to failures elicited through legally or professionally plausible framing. We introduce RAHS (Risk-Adjusted Harm Score), a risk-sensitive metric jointly capturing disclosure severity, disclaimer mitigation, and inter-judge agreement, and FinRedTeamBench, a 989-prompt benchmark spanning seven BFSI risk areas and 34 sub-categories mapped to regulatory frameworks. Evaluation uses an ensemble of three heterogeneous LLM judges, validated against human experts, and an adaptive multi-turn red-teaming pipeline. On nine open-weight models, RAHS preserves separation under near-ceiling ASR, ranking is stable under hyperparameter sweeps, and multi-turn pressure drives not only more jailbreaks but more operationally severe disclosures, exposing failure modes that single-turn, domain-agnostic evaluations cannot reveal.
filter_reasoning: This paper introduces a metric and benchmark specifically for LLM red-teaming and safety evaluation in a regulated sector, falling squarely under AI safety and robustness.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: Unmasking Superficial Honesty: Mechanistic Head-Driven Activation Steering for Sycophancy-Free Medical VLMs
abstract: Medical Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are vulnerable to misleading clinical prompts and may follow incorrect user assertions instead of image evidence, a behavior commonly referred to as sycophancy. Existing mitigation methods mainly rely on prompt-level constraints to encourage neutral responses. However, through fine-grained integrated gradient analysis, we observe a phenomenon, although prompting strategies can correct the final prediction, the internal multimodal representations remain biased toward text tokens, while visual tokens continue to receive limited attention in late fusion layers. To address this issue, we propose HD-AS (Head-Driven Activation Steering), a training-free inference-time intervention framework. HD-AS identifies sycophancy-related attention heads through activation drift analysis under different prompting conditions. During inference, a lightweight isotropic damping operation is applied through a forward pre-hook on the target projection layers, reducing the dominance of text features in the hidden space and restoring the contribution of visual representations. Experiments on two public medical Visual Question Answering (VQA) datasets show that HD-AS consistently reduces the flip rate while maintaining diagnostic accuracy.
filter_reasoning: The paper addresses sycophancy in medical models, which is a key alignment and robustness issue, and proposes an intervention to restore factual integrity.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: No One Model Catches Every Harm: Benchmarking Content Moderation Across Safety Scenarios
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in real-world applications, yet remain vulnerable to harms ranging from adversarial jailbreaks to implicit hate. Specialized moderators and general-purpose LLMs are both used as safety layers, but there is little systematic guidance on which model to choose for which harm. We present the most comprehensive evaluation of LLM safety to date, testing 53 models on 11 datasets organized into four challenge categories, under both prompt-only (Q) and prompt-with-response (QA) settings. Large frontier models that lead on one category fall behind smaller specialized models on others, and real-world conversational safety remains unsolved across model families. These findings challenge the assumption that scale alone ensures safety and offer practitioners a structured basis for model selection.
filter_reasoning: The paper conducts a systematic evaluation of LLM content moderation and safety across various scenarios, directly contributing to the field of AI safety assessment.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: HSRM: Hidden-State Reward Models for Test-Time Verification
abstract: Large language models can often generate plausible mathematical reasoning traces, but reliably identifying the correct solution among multiple candidates remains a key challenge. Existing test-time reasoning pipelines typically rely on text-based verifiers that re-read each generated solution, making verification an expensive component of inference. Prior work has shown, however, that LLMs often encode correctness-related signals in their internal representations, including awareness of when their own answers are likely to be wrong. Building on this observation, we introduce HSRM, a lightweight hidden-state reward model that verifies candidate solutions by directly reading the generator's internal representations rather than re-processing its text. HSRM extracts hidden states from a frozen generator at reasoning-step boundaries and uses a small Transformer encoder to rank candidates. It is trained from self-generated trajectories with outcome labels, requiring neither human-written process supervision nor a large pretrained verifier. Across four mathematical reasoning benchmarks, HSRM matches or outperforms a 55M-parameter text-only energy verifier in 15 of 16 generator--dataset settings while using only about 2M parameters, providing an efficient alternative to text-only verification by reusing representations already computed during generation.
filter_reasoning: This paper proposes a hidden-state reward model for test-time verification, contributing to the safety and reliability of reasoning chains, which aligns with AI safety research.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: Conformal Certification of Reasoning Trace Prefixes
abstract: Language model reasoning traces are rarely all-or-nothing; they frequently contain valid intermediate steps before a critical error occurs. Existing uncertainty quantification methods typically certify final answers or entire responses, failing to provide statistical guarantees for the proportion of a sequential trace that can be safely retained. To address this, we introduce CROP (Conformal Reasoning Output Prefixes), a verifier-agnostic calibration procedure for clean-prefix certification. Given any step-level risk proxy, CROP selects a calibrated threshold and returns the longest contiguous prefix whose step risk proxies remain below it, routing the uncertified suffix for downstream review or repair. Assuming exchangeability, CROP rigorously controls the marginal probability that the returned prefix contains an annotated error. Across six process-labeled reasoning datasets, we demonstrate that standard step-level metrics such as AUROC do not fully capture prefix utility, suggesting verifiers should instead be evaluated by certified prefix length. Furthermore, CROP balances over- and under-withholding and improves downstream repair accuracy by preserving valid intermediate reasoning while discarding misleading suffixes. Ultimately, this work positions prefix certification as a rigorous, practical bridge between process supervision, abstention, and repair.
filter_reasoning: The paper develops a method for conformal certification of reasoning traces to improve reliability and safety in sequential output generation.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: The Consistency Illusion: How Multi-Agent Debate Hides Reasoning Misalignment
abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems for medical question answering treat consensus as a reliability signal: if multiple agents agree on an answer, it is presumed trustworthy. However, answer-level consensus does not entail reasoning-level alignment. We introduce CARA (Cross-Agent Reasoning Alignment), a family of automated metrics that measure whether agents who agree on an answer also agree on the reasoning. Applying CARA to a standard debate system on two medical QA benchmarks (MedQA-USMLE and MedThink-Bench), we identify the consistency illusion: a failure mode where debate reduces detectable contradictions between agents while simultaneously decreasing the semantic similarity of their reasoning chains; agents appear to agree more but reason less consistently. To improve this misalignment, we propose the Grounded Debate Protocol (GDP), a prompt-level intervention that requires agents to commit to named medical facts and take explicit stances on other agents' claims. GDP produces large, consistent alignment improvements (Cohen's d = +1.43 to +1.99) across two datasets and two backbone models, without adding LLM calls or modifying system architecture. Our results motivate cross-agent reasoning alignment as a quantity to audit alongside accuracy in safety-critical domains.
filter_reasoning: The paper addresses 'reasoning misalignment' in multi-agent systems, focusing on reliability and auditing in safety-critical domains.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: Where to Steer: Input-Dependent Layer Selection for Steering Improves LLM Alignment
abstract: Steering vectors have emerged as a lightweight and effective approach for aligning large language models (LLMs) at inference time, enabling modulation of model behaviors by shifting intermediate representations toward a target behavior. Many existing steering methods apply interventions at globally fixed locations in an LLM, effectively treating the optimal intervention location as input-invariant. However, representations relevant to a target behavior can be encoded at different LLM layers depending on the input. Theoretically, we show that different inputs may require steering at different layers to achieve alignment with a given behavior. Empirically, we observe that the most effective layer for steering varies substantially between inputs. Motivated by these observations, we introduce Where to Steer (W2S), a general framework that adaptively selects intervention layers conditioned on the inputs by learning a mapping from input representations to steering layers. Across multiple LLMs and alignment behaviors, W2S consistently outperforms fixed-layer baselines in both in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings. Our findings suggest that input-dependent layer selection is a key design dimension complementary to methods for steering vector extraction.
filter_reasoning: The paper advances steering vector methods for inference-time alignment, which is a core technical component of AI alignment and safety.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: SCAR: Shapley Credit Assignment for More Efficient RLHF
abstract: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) often suffers from sparse reward signals, making credit assignment to tokens challenging. We propose Shapley Credit Assignment Rewards (SCAR), a method that uses Shapley values from cooperative game theory to distribute sequence-level rewards across tokens or text spans according to their marginal contributions. SCAR provides dense rewards without requiring auxiliary critique models or fine-grained human annotations, while offering a principled game-theoretic foundation for credit assignment. We show theoretically that SCAR preserves the original optimal policy, and empirically demonstrate across sentiment control, summarization, and instruction tuning tasks that it converges faster and achieves higher final rewards than standard RLHF and attention-based dense reward baselines. To improve scalability on long sequences, we further introduce an Owen value--inspired adaptive text segmentation strategy. Our findings suggest that SCAR provides a more effective and theoretically sound method for credit assignment in RLHF, leading to more efficient alignment of LLMs.
filter_reasoning: The paper proposes a new method for credit assignment in RLHF, which is the primary technical method for aligning LLMs with human intent.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: Measuring the Depth of LLM Unlearning via Activation Patching
abstract: Large language model (LLM) unlearning has emerged as a crucial post-hoc mechanism for privacy protection and AI safety, yet auditing whether target knowledge is truly erased remains challenging. Existing output-level metrics fail to detect when this knowledge remains recoverable from internal representations. Recent white-box studies reveal such residual knowledge but often rely on auxiliary training or dataset-specific adaptations, leaving no generalizable metric. We close this gap with the Unlearning Depth Score (UDS), a metric that quantifies the mechanistic depth of unlearning via activation patching. UDS first identifies layers that encode the target knowledge using a retain model baseline, then measures how much of it is erased in the unlearned model on a 0-1 scale. In a meta-evaluation across 20 metrics on 150 unlearned models spanning 8 methods, UDS achieves the highest faithfulness and robustness, confirming our causal approach as the most reliable for unlearning evaluation. Case studies further show that UDS uncovers residual knowledge obscured from observational metrics by representational shifts, with erasure depth varying across prompt types. We provide guidelines for integrating UDS into existing benchmarking frameworks and streamlining the evaluation pipeline.
filter_reasoning: The paper addresses mechanistic interpretability and reliable evaluation of unlearning, which is a key technical challenge in AI safety and privacy.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: Same Answer, Different Representations: Hidden instability in VLMs
abstract: The robustness of Vision Language Models (VLMs) is commonly assessed through output-level invariance, implicitly assuming that stable predictions reflect stable multimodal processing. In this work, we argue that this assumption is insufficient. We introduce a representation-aware and frequency-aware evaluation framework that measures internal embedding drift, spectral sensitivity, and structural smoothness (spatial consistency of vision tokens), alongside standard label-based metrics. Applying this framework to modern VLMs across the SEEDBench, MMMU, and POPE datasets reveals three distinct failure modes. First, models frequently preserve predicted answers while undergoing substantial internal representation drift; for perturbations such as text overlays, this drift approaches the magnitude of inter-image variability, indicating that representations move to regions typically occupied by unrelated inputs despite unchanged outputs. Second, robustness does not improve with scale; larger models achieve higher accuracy but exhibit equal or greater sensitivity, consistent with sharper yet more fragile decision boundaries. Third, we find that perturbations affect tasks differently: they harm reasoning when they disrupt how models combine coarse and fine visual cues, but on the hallucination benchmarks, they can reduce false positives by making models generate more conservative answers.
filter_reasoning: The paper analyzes robustness and hidden stability in VLMs, identifying failure modes related to internal representation drift, which is a core AI safety concern.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: AffectDF: The Most Comprehensive Benchmark for Speech Deepfake Detection against Emotionally Expressive Attacks
abstract: Speech deepfake detection (SDD) systems achieve strong performance on conventional benchmarks; however, existing datasets provide limited coverage of emotionally expressive and recent large audio-language model (LALM)-based attacks. Existing emotional spoofing datasets are also limited in scale and attack diversity, typically covering only voice conversion (VC) or text-to-speech (TTS) attacks. We introduce AffectDF, the most comprehensive benchmark for emotionally expressive speech deepfakes, spanning TTS, VC, emotional VC, and LALM-based spoofing attacks across both acted and spontaneous emotional speech. AffectDF contains approximately 260 hours of speech generated using 21 spoofing attacks across five emotional states. We benchmark state-of-the-art SDD systems under conventional and emotional spoofing conditions. Our experiments reveal severe robustness degradation when models trained on conventional benchmarks are evaluated on AffectDF, with several systems approaching near-random performance. Surprisingly, even large-scale emotional training does not consistently improve cross-domain robustness, indicating that current SDD systems fail to learn generalized spoof representations under emotional and prosodic variability. Robustness further varies substantially across emotional states, attack families, and acted vs spontaneous emotional speech conditions. These findings expose fundamental limitations of current SDD systems and establish AffectDF as a benchmark for developing more robust spoof detection models.
filter_reasoning: The paper addresses the safety and robustness of deepfake detection systems against sophisticated, emotionally expressive attacks.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: HyLaT: Efficient Multi-Agent Communication via Hybrid Latent--Text Protocol
abstract: Communication protocol design is a central challenge in large language model-based multi-agent systems. Existing single-channel approaches face an inherent communication trilemma: text-based methods are interpretable but verbose, while latent-space methods are efficient but opaque and limited to single-round workflows. Inspired by multi-channel communication theory, we propose HyLaT, a hybrid latent-text communication protocol that transmits elaborate cognitive signals through a latent channel for efficiency, while expressing concise critical signals in natural language to preserve interpretability and precision. We introduce a two-stage training framework combining single-agent hybrid generation learning and multi-agent interactive co-training, enabling agents to generate and interpret hybrid messages across multiple rounds of interaction. Experiments demonstrate that HyLaT reduces communication overhead significantly while maintaining competitive task performance, with strong generalization and robustness across diverse settings.
filter_reasoning: The paper focuses on interpretability and precision in multi-agent communication protocols, which is a core technical challenge in AI safety and alignment.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: Scalable Circuit Learning for Interpreting Large Language Models
abstract: A prominent research direction in mechanistic interpretability is learning sparse circuits over LLM components to reveal how they jointly produce model behavior. However, raw neurons are polysemantic, making learned circuits hard to interpret. Sparse autoencoder (SAE) features alleviate this, but their high dimensionality makes existing intervention-based circuit-learning methods computationally prohibitive. We propose CircuitLasso, a scalable circuit-learning approach based on sparse linear regression. CircuitLasso recovers circuits whose structural accuracy matches that of state-of-the-art intervention-based methods on the benchmark data, at a fraction of the computational cost. For interpretability, CircuitLasso efficiently uncovers relationships among SAE features, showing how human-interpretable semantic features propagate through the model and influence its predictions. Finally, we validate the utility of our learned circuits by leveraging their insights to achieve comparable performance at substantially lower cost on a domain-generalization task.
filter_reasoning: This paper focuses on mechanistic interpretability, which is a key technical pillar of AI safety for understanding model internals.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: LogicInception: Discourse-Level Indirect Prompt Injection via Causal Chain Construction
abstract: Existing indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks commonly face a stealth-effectiveness tradeoff: features that make payloads effective can also make them detectable because attack intent is localized in a single payload. LogicInception moves IPI to discourse-level inference: attack logic is decomposed into register-matched declarative fragments distributed across tool outputs and linked by fabricated causal dependencies that the agent reconstructs through reasoning. To our knowledge, it is the first IPI framework to demonstrate successful unauthorized tool execution with no directive instruction anywhere in the injected content. No fragment contains a command or exploits instruction-following; the attack emerges from the agent's own inference. We observe an empirical capability-safety amplification pattern: discourse-level amplification correlates with task capability across the evaluated models. On 1,139 scenarios with 5 defenses, LogicInception achieves 42.9-48.8\% ASR at 88\% per-fragment stealth, while all baselines remain below 8\% composite success. The three prompt-level defenses reduce baseline ASR by up to 72\% but reduce LogicInception by less than 7\%; we trace this asymmetry to three architectural factors that motivate discourse-level rather than content-level countermeasures. This defense asymmetry is larger for higher-utility models in our evaluation, suggesting a tension between reasoning capability and safety.
filter_reasoning: The paper investigates indirect prompt injection attacks and defenses, which is a primary security and safety challenge for agentic LLMs.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: Physiognomy Revisited: How Vision--Language Models Encode Sensitive Attributes Through Image Transformation
abstract: Emergent generative AI technologies, while remarkably beneficial across several tasks and domains, can suffer from unforeseen vulnerabilities and difficult-to-anticipate failure modes. Such failure modes can disparately affect vulnerable communities. This paper investigates two well-known vision language models (VLMs) and inspects how these models encode protected identities while generating images. We show that when VLMs are requested to transform human face images to reflect race identities (e.g., Hispanic, Black, White, or Asian) and sexual orientation (e.g., gay or straight), VLMs often comply with such requests. We demonstrate that compliance (and refusal) is non-deterministic, group-sensitive, and generated images are statistically distinguishable, often accentuating deep-seated stereotypes. We further show that representation biases introduced during image generation can re-emerge in textual reasoning and characterization tasks. Finally, we show that this worrisome finding is not limited to racial identity or sexual orientation, image generation can perpetuate bias around criminality, raising concerning possibilities of AI-assisted profiling.
filter_reasoning: This paper investigates how vision-language models perpetuate social stereotypes and bias, which is a core topic in AI ethics.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: Race in the Record: Measuring Racial Signal and Model Inference in Police Arrest Narratives
abstract: We present RPD-UoF, a corpus of 3,091 police use-of-force narratives obtained via Freedom of Information Law (FOIL) requests from the Rochester Police Department, combining structured demographic metadata with officer-authored free-text accounts. We use this dataset to investigate three related questions: whether officer narratives contain recoverable racial signal after demographic redaction, whether large language models amplify racial framing when conditioned on subject race, and whether that signal survives text redaction to re-emerge in multimodal outputs. Redacted narratives are statistically separable by subject race; LLMs produce structurally longer narratives for White profiles than Black profiles from identical seed texts; and CLIP classifications of GPT-5-generated images differ significantly depending on the racial origin of the source narrative. Together, these analyses provide an initial empirical lens on how race appears in police narratives and how modern language models interact with such sensitive attributes. The dataset and analyses are intended to support future research on fairness, accountability, and transparency in computational studies of policing and criminal justice.
filter_reasoning: This paper investigates racial bias in police narrative processing and LLMs, which is a core topic of algorithmic fairness and AI ethics.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: Do Latent Tokens Think? A Causal and Adversarial Analysis of Chain-of-Continuous-Thought
abstract: Latent tokens are gaining attention for enhancing reasoning in large language models (LLMs), yet their internal mechanisms remain unclear. This paper examines the problem from a reliability perspective, uncovering fundamental weaknesses: latent tokens function as uninterpretable placeholders rather than encoding faithful reasoning. While resistant to perturbation, they promote shortcut usage over genuine reasoning. We focus on Chain-of-Continuous-Thought (COCONUT), which claims better efficiency and stability than explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) while maintaining performance. We investigate this through two complementary approaches. First, steering experiments perturb specific token subsets, namely COCONUT and explicit CoT. Unlike CoT tokens, COCONUT tokens show minimal sensitivity to steering and lack reasoning-critical information. Second, shortcut experiments evaluate models under biased and out-of-distribution settings. Results on MMLU and HotpotQA demonstrate that COCONUT consistently exploits dataset artifacts, inflating benchmark performance without true reasoning. These findings reposition COCONUT as a pseudo-reasoning mechanism: it generates plausible traces that conceal shortcut dependence rather than faithfully representing reasoning processes.
filter_reasoning: The paper analyzes the reliability and faithfulness of reasoning mechanisms in LLMs, specifically addressing the lack of interpretable and faithful reasoning processes.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: Beyond Single-Attribute Auditing: A Configurable Multi-Attribute Benchmark for Intersectional Fairness in LLMs
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly evaluated for fairness, yet most existing benchmarks audit one sensitive attribute at a time. This single-attribute paradigm can miss intersectional harms, where multiple attributes interact non-additively and produce failures that are invisible under marginal evaluation. We introduce ComFair, a configurable benchmark that converts existing fairness data into 479,066 controlled Dual- and Multi-attribute instances and pairs every augmented instance with its task-equivalent source. Across Recognition, Selection, Continuation, and Conversation, this pairing supports a unified audit of performance or bias-score shifts, how often added attributes introduce new errors or mask existing ones, and model-ranking stability. Experiments on ten LLMs show task- and subgroup-dependent sensitivity: discriminative tasks expose both transition directions even when aggregate changes are modest, generative tasks exhibit larger and directionally asymmetric shifts, and rankings vary with attribute composition. ComFair therefore provides a scalable controlled sensitivity audit---rather than a model of the natural joint distribution of identities---for testing the robustness of fairness-benchmark conclusions beyond single-attribute settings.
filter_reasoning: The paper focuses on intersectional fairness in LLMs, which is a core research topic in AI ethics.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: PaSBench-Video: A Streaming Video Benchmark for Proactive Safety Warning
abstract: Between the first visible sign of danger and the moment an accident occurs, there is often a window where intervention remains possible. Video-capable multimodal large language models (MLLMs) could serve as always-on safety monitors that issue warnings during this window. Yet current benchmarks do not test this ability: they rely on static inputs, ignore timing precision, and omit false-positive measurement on safe scenes. We present PaSBench-Video, a 740-video benchmark with 481 risk videos and 259 no-risk videos across four domains: driving, healthcare, daily life, and industrial production. The benchmark is annotated with frame-level risk onset and accident boundaries. A model must observe the video causally and produce a warning that is both temporally calibrated and content-correct. Testing 13 MLLMs, we find that no model exceeds 20.0\% on our strictest metric, and recall is tightly coupled with false-positive rate, with Pearson correlation 0.64: higher detection comes only at the cost of triggering warnings on the majority of safe clips. Performance splits sharply by domain: models achieve moderate recall at low false-positive rates in daily life, where risks are inherently anomalous, yet fire indiscriminately in driving, where routine and hazardous scenes look alike. These results indicate that current models rely on scene-level activity cues rather than reason about emerging harm.
filter_reasoning: This paper addresses the deployment of LLMs as safety monitors for proactive risk warnings, directly touching on the safety and reliability of AI agents in physical environments.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: Safety-Aware Contrastive Decoding for Contextual Safety in Multimodal Large Language Models
abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly deployed in real-world applications, yet their ability to make context-aware safety decisions remains limited. Existing methods often fail to balance oversensitivity (unjustified refusals of benign queries) and undersensitivity (missed detection of visually grounded risks), leaving a persistent gap in safety alignment. To address this issue, we introduce Safety-aware Contrastive Decoding (SafeCoDe), a real-time decoding framework that dynamically adjusts token generation based on multimodal context. SafeCoDe operates in two stages: (1) a contrastive decoding mechanism that highlights tokens sensitive to visual context by contrasting real and Gaussian-noised images, and (2) a global-aware token modulation strategy that integrates scene-level reasoning with token-level adjustment to adapt refusals according to the predicted safety verdict. Extensive experiments across diverse MLLM architectures and safety benchmarks, covering undersensitivity, oversensitivity, and general safety evaluations, show that SafeCoDe consistently improves context-sensitive refusal behaviors while preserving model helpfulness.
filter_reasoning: The paper presents a framework for improving safety alignment in MLLMs by addressing context-aware refusal behaviors and risk detection.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: Countdown-Code: A Testbed for Studying The Emergence and Generalization of Reward Hacking in RLVR
abstract: Reward hacking is a form of misalignment in which models overoptimize proxy rewards without genuinely solving the underlying task. Precisely measuring reward hacking occurrence remains challenging because true task rewards are often expensive or impossible to compute. We introduce Countdown-Code, a minimal environment where models can both solve a mathematical reasoning task and manipulate the test harness. This dual-access design creates a clean separation between proxy rewards (test pass/fail) and true rewards (mathematical correctness), enabling accurate measurement of reward-hacking rates. Using this environment, we study reward hacking in open-weight LLMs and find that such behaviors can be unintentionally learned during supervised fine-tuning (SFT) when even a small fraction of reward-hacking trajectories leak into training data. As little as 1\% contamination in distillation SFT data is sufficient for models to internalize reward hacking which resurfaces during subsequent reinforcement learning (RL). We further show that RL amplifies misalignment and drives its generalization beyond the original domain. We open-source our environment and code to facilitate future research on reward hacking in LLMs. Our results reveal a previously underexplored pathway through which reward hacking can emerge and persist in LLMs, underscoring the need for more rigorous validation of synthetic SFT data.
filter_reasoning: The paper directly addresses 'reward hacking' and 'misalignment' in RL, which are core topics in AI safety.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: CCStories: Improving the Safety and Age-Appropriateness of LLM-Generated Chinese Children's Stories
abstract: Children's stories play a crucial role in early cognitive and language development, yet existing story generation models lack the safety and age-appropriateness required for educational applications, especially in non-English languages. We introduce CCStories, a curated dataset of 22,200 high-quality Chinese children's stories designed specifically to support safe and appropriate AI-generated content for young readers. Unlike general-purpose datasets derived from adult-oriented platforms, CCStories targets three critical dimensions of child-appropriate text: readability, syntactic complexity, and toxicity. We further propose a multi-dimensional evaluation framework that jointly assesses appropriateness and generation quality. As a validation of the dataset's utility, we fine-tune five representative backbones: CPM, PanGu-$\alpha$, GLM-4, Qwen, a Chinese-adapted LLaMA-3 variant (Gigi-Llama-3-8B-zh), and additionally benchmark GPT-5-mini as a zero-shot instruction-tuned reference. Fine-tuning reduces offensive-prompt toxicity by up to 26.7 percentage points and raises readability by up to 14.3 percentage points, narrowing much of the gap to the GPT-5-mini reference. A human evaluation confirms that appropriateness rises from 53\% to 86\% after fine-tuning, and human validation of the toxicity classifier shows that the model ranking it induces matches the human ranking. CCStories provides a publicly available resource for building and benchmarking safer, more age-appropriate Chinese generative models for children's education.
filter_reasoning: This paper focuses on mitigating toxicity and improving age-appropriateness for children, which is a direct contribution to AI ethics.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: EQUAL: Evaluating Pluralistic Alignment of LLMs Across Educational Perspectives
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in education, powering tutoring systems, automated feedback, and curriculum support. Most alignment techniques optimize toward a single aggregated notion of human preference, a mismatch for education, where legitimate disagreement is the norm. Students, parents, teachers, and policymakers often hold deeply conflicting views on assessment, discipline, curriculum, and institutional authority, reflecting genuine value pluralism rather than noise. Pluralistic alignment, which seeks to represent and navigate this diversity, offers a principled path forward. Despite growing interest, no benchmark evaluates how well LLMs handle value-laden disagreement in educational contexts. To address this, we introduce EQUAL (Eliciting QUality sAmples of pLuralistic alignment in education), comprising 14,270 samples---5,824 value-laden scenarios and 8,446 multiple-choice questions, curated from six sources, including over two decades of Phi Delta Kappa polling data, via a lexical filtering pipeline and human validation. EQUAL supports evaluation across Overton, Steerable, and Distributional paradigms. We benchmark nine LLMs under four approaches and additionally evaluate three frontier reasoning-capable models. No single method consistently satisfies pluralistic objectives. These findings provide a foundation for future research on pluralistic alignment in educational AI.
filter_reasoning: The paper addresses the challenge of value alignment in educational contexts, specifically concerning value pluralism and disagreement, which is a core AI ethics research question.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: SkillAttack: Automated Red Teaming of Agent Skills through Attack Path Refinement
abstract: LLM-based agent systems increasingly rely on open-registry skills, which are difficult to vet and expose agents to greater attack risks. These attacks mainly take two forms. Malicious injection attacks embed explicit harmful instructions into skills and are readily caught by auditing. Direct vulnerability attacks target latent flaws in non-malicious skills; however, directly crafted attack prompts often lead to unstable or unverified outcomes. We introduce **SkillAttack**, an automated red-teaming framework that systematically explores executable attack paths from latent vulnerabilities without modifying skill files. Evaluated across 11 target LLMs, SkillAttack substantially outperforms baselines, showing that well-intended skills can pose serious risks in realistic agent interactions. Our evaluation also yields trajectory-level attack traces with verified risk labels, providing a foundation for defense. We also release **SkillRiskBench**, a benchmark for skill risk analysis, and train a lightweight pre-execution risk guard that predicts risky invocations from the user request and skill file. The guard outperforms frontier LLM judges and existing safety guard models, highlighting the value of trajectory-grounded supervision for proactive skill defense. Code is available at https://github.com/Zhow01/SkillAttack.
filter_reasoning: The paper focuses on automated red-teaming and the development of safety guards for AI agents, which are core topics in AI safety.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: DataShield: Uncovering Risky Fine-Tuning Data Across LLMs Through Consensus Subspace Alignment
abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on domain-specific datasets has become a standard paradigm for adapting LLMs to specialized applications. However, recent work has shown that even fine-tuning on benign task-specific data can substantially weaken the safety capabilities of LLMs. While existing efforts have made progress in identifying data responsible for safety degradation, they usually rely on a single mean vector computed over a specific model with its tokenizer to represent the safety direction, which limits both the effectiveness and transferability of their risk assessment measures. To address these limitations, we propose DataShield, a data assessment framework that identifies risky fine-tuning samples and response segments through consensus subspace alignment over joint safety-critical semantic spaces derived from multiple safety-aligned LLMs.Within these spaces, DataShield extracts consensus safe and unsafe subspaces using semantic spectral decomposition over safe and unsafe data representations. The risk of a data sample or segment is then estimated by measuring its relative alignment with the unsafe and safe subspaces, enabling both sample-level filtering and fine-grained segment-level masking. Compared with state-of-the-art filtering and masking baselines, DataShield reduces ASR by 14.6\% with sample filtering and 32.3\% with segment masking, while preserving downstream utility and avoiding target-model-specific risk computation.
filter_reasoning: The paper proposes a framework to assess and filter 'risky' fine-tuning data to prevent safety degradation in LLMs, which is a core AI safety topic.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: ChartAttack: Testing the Vulnerability of LLMs to Malicious Prompting in Chart Generation
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly used to automate chart generation from data tables, improving efficiency but introducing new misuse risks. We present ChartAttack, a framework for evaluating how MLLMs use design misleaders to generate charts that induce incorrect interpretations. We also introduce AttackViz, a chart question-answering (QA) dataset labeled with effective misleaders and their induced incorrect answers. ChartAttack reduces MLLM QA accuracy by 17.2 points in-domain and 11.9 points cross-domain. Conditional deception rates show targeted effects: correct answers shift to attacker-intended answers 11.2\% of the time in-domain and 11.7-14.9\% cross-domain, while originally incorrect answers rarely change. A controlled human study shows that ChartAttack-generated charts also reduce human QA performance. Finally, fine-tuning on AttackViz improves in-domain MLLM robustness to misleading charts. Our findings highlight the need for secure, robust MLLM chart generation. Code and data are publicly available on the project website.
filter_reasoning: This paper investigates vulnerability and adversarial risks in MLLMs and proposes methods to improve robustness against deceptive inputs.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: Why does Weak-OOD Help? A Further Step Towards Understanding Jailbreaking VLMs
abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are susceptible to jailbreak attacks: researchers have developed various attack strategies that bypass the safety mechanisms of VLMs. Among these approaches, jailbreak methods based on the Out-of-Distribution (OOD) strategy have garnered widespread attention due to their simplicity and effectiveness. This paper further advances the understanding of OOD-based VLM jailbreak methods. We show that mild OOD manipulations can achieve stronger jailbreak performance than both clean inputs and overly strong perturbations, a non-monotonic pattern we define as ``weak-OOD''. We explain this phenomenon through a trade-off between two dominant factors: input intent perception and model refusal triggering. Our evidence suggests that these two factors respond differently to OOD manipulations, which is consistent with a discrepancy between broad pre-training robustness and narrower safety alignment. Building on this insight, we draw inspiration from optical character recognition (OCR) capability enhancement, a core task in the pre-training phase of mainstream VLMs. Leveraging this capability, we design JOCR (Jailbreak via OCR-Aware Embedded Text Perturbation), a simple VLM jailbreak method that achieves the best average ASR among evaluated baselines.
filter_reasoning: The paper investigates the mechanisms behind jailbreaking VLMs and proposes a new attack method (red teaming), which is a core topic in AI safety.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: Bargaining with Internal Evidence: Receiver-Constrained Decoding for Factual Reliability in Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models can produce fluent yet factually incorrect responses, limiting their reliability in knowledge-intensive applications. Recent decoding methods seek to mitigate such hallucinations by contrasting or amplifying signals from intermediate layers. However, not every layerwise discrepancy provides a reliable direction for factual decoding. We propose a unified game-theoretic decoding framework for large language models: intermediate-layer signals act as competing evidence, while the final layer retains decision authority under explicit constraints. Rather than applying a fixed layerwise contrast, our framework treats changes in intermediate predictions as evidence of the language model's evolving internal judgment, and uses this evidence to guide decoding under final-layer constraints. Experiments with three backbone language models on multiple truthfulness and hallucination benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework in improving factual reliability.
filter_reasoning: The paper focuses on mitigating hallucinations in LLMs using a game-theoretic framework to improve factual reliability, which is a core safety concern.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: After the Attacker Leaves: Benchmarking Carryover Attacks on LLM Agents
abstract: Modern LLM agents persist state across sessions via two channels: long-lived memory files silently prepended to the system prompt, and scheduled tasks waking the agent without user input. A one-time indirect prompt injection committed to either channel can re-fire across sessions long after the attacker leaves, threats we term carryover attacks. Existing prompt-injection benchmarks evaluate attacks only in the session where malicious content is first observed, leaving the gate governing when and how often a planted payload later re-fires unmeasured. We present CarryoverBench: 12 personal-assistant scenarios and 101 attack tasks across three trigger channels: Instant, same-turn IPI; Autonomous, heartbeat-scheduled; and Latent, memory-resurfaced. A rule-based verifier scores planting and triggering as independent stages. Across five frontier models, planted payloads re-fire without measurable decay over five rounds; conditional on successful planting, the trigger stage often provides little additional protection. Porting the Latent channel to a second runtime, Hermes, attenuates but does not eliminate the effect, suggesting that carryover defense requires runtime-layer controls in addition to prompt-level interventions.
filter_reasoning: The paper investigates 'carryover attacks' on LLM agents, a type of prompt injection vulnerability, which falls under AI security/safety.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: Contrastive Attribution in the Wild: An Interpretability Analysis of LLM Failures on Realistic Benchmarks
abstract: Interpretability methods are increasingly invoked to diagnose Large Language Model (LLM) failures, but most evidence comes from short prompts or toy templates, leaving their utility on practical benchmarks unclear. We cast failure diagnosis as contrastive attribution over target--contrast token pairs, attributing the logit gap between incorrect and correct output tokens to input tokens and internal states, and introduce a batch-packed multi-target backpropagation scheme that scales cross-layer attribution graphs to long-context inputs. Instantiated with LRP-style attribution, the framework is evaluated on IFEval, GAIA2, MATH, and EvalPlus across multiple model sizes and post-training checkpoints. Along the four axes of coverage, visibility, reliability, and dynamics, contrastive attribution surfaces recurring failure modes such as underweighting task-relevant tokens and overweighting distractors, demonstrating its practical value as a scalable diagnostic tool for realistic LLM failures.
filter_reasoning: The paper proposes a method for interpreting LLM failures, which contributes to the interpretability and robustness of AI systems.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: Elias in the Lighthouse, Again? Diagnosing Low Diversity in LLM Stories
abstract: LLM-generated stories are a popular use case, but they show very low variability. We sample 20,000 total stories from four current models using five prompts. We find that 11 words occur in 88.3\% of generated stories, with little difference between models. These words include names (Elias, Mara, Elara), settings (lighthouses), and professions (clockmaker, librarian). These tokens do not often occur in published literature nor pre-training data, but they are found in preference data that is likely to have been used by all current models. Surprisingly, these ``lighthouse'' stories are infrequent when compared with the average post-training story, much of which contains references to copyrighted characters or adult content. This result demonstrates the potentially disproportionate impact of small datasets combined with powerful alignment algorithms.
filter_reasoning: The paper discusses how preference data and alignment algorithms contribute to low diversity in model outputs, a significant topic in AI ethics and social impact.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: Format as Nuisance: Intervention-Inspired Cross-Format Distillation for Knowledge Conflicts
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) encode parametric knowledge but can exhibit format bias when resolving knowledge conflicts. When evidence is rendered as text, tables, or knowledge graphs, LLMs can favor certain formats despite unchanged semantic content. Existing work mainly diagnoses this bias, while existing inference-time mitigation remains tied to a single rendered prompt. We propose FaDe, a cross-format knowledge distillation framework that treats evidence format as a controllable nuisance variable and marginalizes teacher predictions over controlled format assignments. FaDe constructs a format-marginalized soft target from these renderings, then trains the student with an asymmetric two-path objective that combines heterogeneous-format debiasing with all-text anchoring. Experiments on ConflictBank and two QA-derived controlled conflict sets with four model backbones show FaDe reduces format bias while improving dual-source coverage and cross-format stability under single-pass inference. Our code is available at https://github.com/Kaia91/FaDe.
filter_reasoning: The paper addresses 'format bias' in LLMs, which relates to transparency and fairness in how AI systems process and present information.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: Beyond Prompts: Discovering Jailbreak Motifs in Sparse Feature Space
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks that exhibit diverse prompts and rapidly evolving strategies. Existing defenses often operate at the level of prompts or predefined attack methods, limiting their ability to generalize to unseen attacks that share similar underlying structure but differ in wording. In this paper, we investigate whether seemingly different jailbreak attacks exhibit shared SAE feature co-activation patterns, and propose a motif-based framework that models attacks through these recurring patterns. Specifically, we first extract sparse autoencoder (SAE) features from jailbreak queries and discover motifs as recurring co-activation patterns via nonnegative matrix factorization. We show that motifs capture stable relationships across attack methods and generalize to unseen attacks. Building on this structure, we synthesize new jailbreak queries by composing motif-guided attack patterns. We then use the generated queries to construct preference-training data for Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). Experiment results show that SAE motifs serve as a stable and transferable interface for understanding and detecting jailbreak attacks, as well as enabling effective defenses that generalize beyond fixed prompt templates. Training target models with motif-guided synthetic data improves robustness to unseen attacks with modest changes in utility. Our work provides a practical methodology for advancing data-centric LLM safety through structured modeling of jailbreak attacks.
filter_reasoning: The paper focuses on jailbreak attacks and improving the robustness of LLMs against them through sparse feature analysis.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: Will the User Ever Know? Covert Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks on Tool-Using LLM Agents
abstract: As LLM agents take real-world actions through tools, indirect prompt injection (IPI) has emerged as a serious threat. The standard metric, Attack Success Rate (ASR), counts whether an injection succeeds but ignores what the user notices in the agent's final response. Looking at successful injection traces, we find two distinct outcomes: the agent executes the injection while returning an otherwise normal response, or reports the injected action in its final response, giving the user a chance to notice. We call these covert and overt successes. From the user's perspective, we decompose ASR into the ***Covert Success Rate*** **(CSR)**, counting successes leaving no trace in the final response, and the *Overt Success Rate* (OSR), counting successes the user can detect. To understand what drives the gap, we analyze successful trajectories and find that the agent's behavior after the injection separates covert from overt: covert traces hand control back to the user task before ending, while overt traces end at the attack itself. This split follows from the ReAct format, where the final response summarizes the most recent action. Building on this observation, we propose **ICoA** (**I**nduced **Co**vert **A**ttack), an IPI attack designed to induce covert outcomes by steering the agent back to the user task after executing the injection. Across four target models on AgentDojo, ICoA achieves the highest CSR, with gains of 3.79--12.01 percentage points over the strongest baseline.
filter_reasoning: The paper analyzes covert indirect prompt injection attacks, which is a primary AI safety and security research topic.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: Systematic Failure Analysis of Open-Weight LLM Annotators for Classification Tasks: Taxonomy, Uncertainty Signals, and Deployment Boundaries
abstract: Large-scale annotated datasets underpin progress in natural language understanding, yet human annotation remains a persistent bottleneck. Large Language Models promise to bridge this gap, but their reliability as annotators is poorly understood. We evaluate 14 open-weight instruction-tuned models and 5 matched base--instruct pairs across 51,189 instances spanning 10 heterogeneous datasets, revealing that annotation failures are structurally predictable rather than random. We identify three recurring failure modes: Safety Hallucination, Intensity Collapse, and Entailment Bias. Safety hallucination can precede alignment rather than being introduced by it: some base models flag up to 100\% of benign text as hate speech. Alignment benefits scale inversely with base model capability, yielding a +21.6pp gain for the weakest base model yet a negligible +0.5pp shift for the strongest. KL divergence between base and instruct distributions is 2.0x higher on incorrect predictions, providing a lightweight instance-level signal for alignment-associated errors. Inter-prompt unanimity achieves 72--94\% accuracy at 71--90\% coverage on clean tasks, yet can actively degrade performance on tasks dominated by shared systematic bias. We translate these findings into a practical deployment framework with pre-screening diagnostics and tiered quality-routing policies, establishing principled boundaries for when LLM annotation can be trusted and when human intervention remains necessary.
filter_reasoning: The paper performs a failure analysis of LLMs as annotators, focusing on safety hallucinations and biases, contributing to AI reliability and safety.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: Emergent Backdoors in Agentic Recursive Training
abstract: Agentic recursive training systems increasingly reuse model-generated tasks, proxy feedback, and selected trajectories to refine policies over multiple rounds. This creates feedback loops in which small conditional biases can accumulate across training and alter later selection and updates. We study whether trigger-conditional proxy-feedback biases can produce emergent backdoors in a controlled recursive training loop. A Curriculum Agent proposes tasks, an Executor Agent generates rollouts, and environment feedback is selectively biased on rare markers, affecting reward, selection, and curriculum updates. Under matched biased supervision, Reward Hacking + SFT and Reward Hacking + RLHF reach 31.27\% and 53.85\% ASR, while the full loop reaches 97.62\% at comparable clean accuracy. The effect persists across Qwen3-4B, LLaMA-3-8B, BLIP-2-OPT-2.7B, and Qwen2.5-14B, transfers to GSM8K, BBH, and HotpotQA, extends to a tool-augmented setting, and is only partially reduced by post-hoc defenses. These results suggest that feedback and curriculum mechanisms in agentic recursive training should be audited for long-horizon bias amplification.
filter_reasoning: The paper investigates the emergence of 'backdoors' in recursive training loops, a clear AI safety problem related to alignment and reward hacking.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: The Facade of Truth: Uncovering and Mitigating LLM Susceptibility to Deceptive Evidence
abstract: To reliably assist human decision-making, LLMs must maintain factual internal beliefs against misleading injections. While current models resist explicit misinformation, we uncover a fundamental vulnerability to sophisticated, hard-to-falsify evidence. To systematically probe this weakness, we introduce MisBelief, a framework that generates misleading evidence via collaborative, multi-round interactions among multi-role LLMs. This process mimics subtle, defeasible reasoning and progressive refinement to create logically persuasive yet factually deceptive claims. Using MisBelief, we generate 4,800 instances across three difficulty levels to evaluate 7 representative LLMs. Results indicate that while models are robust to direct misinformation, they are highly sensitive to this refined evidence: belief scores in falsehoods increase by an average of 93.0\%, fundamentally compromising downstream recommendations. To address this, we propose Deceptive Intent Shielding (DIS), a governance mechanism that provides an early warning signal by inferring the deceptive intent behind evidence. Empirical results demonstrate that DIS consistently mitigates belief shifts and promotes more cautious evidence evaluation.
filter_reasoning: The paper studies the susceptibility of LLMs to deceptive evidence and proposes a mechanism for intent shielding, which falls under model reliability and robustness.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: Critical or Compliant? The Double-Edged Sword of Reasoning in Chain-of-Thought Explanations
abstract: Explanations are often promoted as tools for transparency, but they can also foster blind trust; users may assume reasoning is correct whenever model outputs appear acceptable. We study this double-edged role of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) explanations in multimodal moral scenarios by systematically perturbing reasoning chains and manipulating delivery tones. Specifically, we perturb reasoning chains generated by vision-language models (VLMs) with three error types (omissions, contradictions, hallucinations) and measure their effects on user trust and error detection through a study with 800 participants, alongside a parallel detection task with models. Our findings reveal two key effects: (1) users often equate trust with outcome agreement regardless of flaws in the model's reasoning, and (2) confident tones suppress scrutiny while leaving agreement and self-reported trust largely unchanged. These results highlight how CoT explanations can simultaneously clarify and mislead in tandem, and point to user-side scrutiny, not just model-side faithfulness, as a critical dimension for calibrated trust in AI reasoning. All code will be released publicly upon acceptance.
filter_reasoning: The paper studies the impact of Chain-of-Thought explanations on user trust and potential for manipulation, which is a core concern for AI transparency and ethics.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
title: AdapTools: Adaptive Tool-based Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks on Agentic LLMs
abstract: As open-source large language models (LLMs) become increasingly powerful, they are rapidly evolving into Agentic LLMs capable of automating complex daily tasks. However, this paradigm shift entails severe security risks, as the agents' necessary integration with external real-time data sources creates a direct pathway for indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks. Existing attack methods are limited by their reliance on static patterns and evaluation on simple language models, failing to address the fast-evolving nature of modern Agentic LLMs. We introduce AdapTools, a novel adaptive IPI attack framework that selects stealthier attack tools and generates adaptive attack prompts to create a rigorous security evaluation environment. Our approach comprises two key components: (1) Adaptive Attack Strategy Construction, which develops transferable adversarial strategies for prompt optimization, and (2) Attack Enhancement, which identifies stealthy tools capable of circumventing task-relevance defenses. Comprehensive experiments on both open-source and commercial agentic LLMs show that AdapTools achieves a per-model average improvement of 2.08\texttimes in attack success rate over the strongest baseline under state-of-the-art defenses (MELON, Pi-Detector), with gains reaching up to 3.06\texttimes on the most resistant reasoning agents.
