We further decompose the QK product into symmetric and antisymmetric components to distinguish mutual content-similarity patterns from directional attention patterns. Across three GQA-based VLMs, QK Product Steering achieves an average relative CHAIR$_s$ reduction of 5.8\%, while matched random-mode controls show negligible change. Interpretability ablations show that the hallucination signal is specific to dominant QK modes and is primarily localized to the symmetric mutual-attention channel. Overall, QK Product Steering offers a simple alternative to decoding-time mitigation, requiring no additional data, fine-tuning, or inference-time overhead while largely preserving general multimodal capability.
filter_reasoning: The paper targets the specific technical challenge of mitigating object hallucinations in VLMs through weight editing, which falls under model reliability/safety.

title: More Evidence Is Not Always More Support: Controlled Diagnostics for Evidence Aggregation in Fact Verification
abstract: Final-context accuracy in multi-passage fact verification can hide whether an added passage contributes a new verdict-relevant fact or merely repeats evidence already present. We introduce a controlled same-prefix diagnostic derived from HoVer supporting-fact annotations to measure marginal evidence contribution. For each claim, a shared prefix covers one fact's evidence while leaving another required fact absent; the next passage either repeats the covered fact or supplies the missing fact. The diagnostic contains 1,180 same-prefix pairs and an exact-repetition ladder testing whether repeated copies of one evidence sentence can change a verifier's label. Supervised verifiers with similar clean F1 scores, from 0.6324 to 0.6528, differ sharply in eight-repeat flip rate, from 8.5\% to 30.3\%. Conservative pooling and natural-language-inference (NLI) scoring reduce duplicate sensitivity but give near-zero missing-fact gain, while gain-oriented systems improve gain but remain repetition-sensitive. Latent-Gated Evidence Dynamics (LGED), a compact stateful reference model, shows that low duplicate sensitivity and positive missing-fact gain can coexist. Surface controls and decision-level analyses support this diagnostic interpretation. Redundancy and reader tests extend the duplicate-sensitivity finding beyond HoVer, while prompted open-weight LLMs reveal a gap between role recognition and verdict updating.
filter_reasoning: The paper investigates the reliability of fact verification models regarding evidence aggregation and hallucination (duplicate sensitivity), which is a key technical safety concern.

title: Reward-guided Meta-Prompt Evolving with Reflection for LLM Jailbreaking
abstract: Large language model (LLM) safety has received extensive attention since LLMs are vulnerable to manipulation. To understand and mitigate the risk, this paper studies the problem of jailbreak attacks on LLMs, which aim to deliberately break the safety guard of LLMs for harmful or unethical responses. Current black-box jailbreak attacks are limited by either a reliance on human expertise for manual prompt design or by intricate workflows in automated approaches. Towards this end, we propose a novel approach named Reward-guided Meta-prompt Evolving with reflection (ROOT) for automatic jailbreak attack generation. The core idea of our ROOT is to optimize a meta-prompt using attack rewards as jailbreak guidance. In particular, our ROOT feeds a meta-prompt with toxic questions into LLMs to generate prompts for jailbreak attempts. The responses from these attempts are further evaluated using a judge model, which further summarizes the reflection of both successful and unsuccessful jailbreak attempts into different meta-prompt optimization strategies. To reduce the noise, we estimate their reward scores to select high-quality strategies, which can optimize our meta-prompt for better attack generation ability. Extensive experiments show that ROOT demonstrates strong generalizability and broad adaptability by achieving high jailbreak success rates (above 90\%) across both multiple LLMs and various categories of harmful tasks.
filter_reasoning: The paper focuses on understanding and automating jailbreak attacks on LLMs as a method to study and mitigate safety vulnerabilities.

title: When the Specification Emerges: Benchmarking Faithfulness Loss in Long-Horizon Coding Agents
abstract: Current coding-agent benchmarks usually provide the full task specification upfront. Research-code implementation may instead re- quire an agent to preserve design commitments disclosed progressively across a long session. We introduce SLUMP, a controlled benchmark for testing implementation faithfulness when a mathematically structured machine-learning target is disclosed through synthetic, paper- grounded multi-turn interactions rather than in a single canonical implementation specification. The benchmark contains 20 recent ML papers, 371 atomic verifiable components, and approx- imately 60 coding requests per paper. An expo- sure audit verifies whether scored components are recoverable from the visible interaction. On Claude Code and Codex, the single-shot control achieves higher overall implementation fidelity on 16/20 and 14/20 papers, respectively. Struc- tural integration degrades under progressive dis- closure on both platforms, while semantic com- ponent faithfulness degrades substantially on Claude Code and remains approximately sta- ble on Codex. These conclusions persist under stricter exposure filters and a targeted human correction of judge false-absence errors. As a mitigation case study, ProjectGuard main- tains external semantic and structural project state and recovers 90\% of Claude Code's mea- sured faithfulness gap. Code and benchmark artifacts are available at https://github.com/lunaryan/drift-benchmark.
filter_reasoning: The paper investigates the faithfulness and consistency of coding agents in long-horizon tasks, which is a key interpretability and reliability concern.

title: When Seeing Is Not Believing---A Benchmark for Search-Grounded Video Misinformation Detection
abstract: Video misinformation increasingly operates at the semantic and evidential level: authentic footage may be selectively edited, temporally reordered, spliced across sources, or augmented with AI-generated content to construct false narratives. Such evidence-dependent manipulations cannot be reliably verified from the input video alone, because the missing, reordered, replaced, or recontextualized evidence lies outside the video itself. We introduce EVID-Bench, a benchmark for search-grounded video misinformation detection, where a system must search the open web for related videos and identify what information is false through cross-video comparison. EVID-Bench comprises 222 videos spanning 9 manipulation types across 3 categories: AI generation, single-source editing, and multi-source editing. All samples are verified to be undetectable by frontier models through visual inspection alone. We evaluate nine frontier multimodal models using a retrieval-augmented verification baseline. The best system achieves only 61.43\% point-level accuracy and 43.24\% video-level accuracy, with AI-generated manipulations remaining especially difficult. Error analysis reveals recurring challenges: models fixate on irrelevant anchors, misattribute synthetic content to editorial splicing, and terminate search prematurely before fully explaining the manipulation.
filter_reasoning: The paper focuses on the detection of AI-driven misinformation and model robustness against manipulated or synthetic content, which is a key safety challenge.

title: MemFail: Stress-Testing Failure Modes of LLM Memory Systems
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on external memory systems to remain consistent across long-horizon interactions, but little empirical work has been done to understand the specific failure modes and design choices that these systems present. Existing benchmarks report aggregate question-answering accuracy and treat memory systems as black boxes, making it impossible to attribute an incorrect answer to a particular failure mode of the system. We introduce MemFail, a diagnostic benchmark that isolates the failure modes of modern LLM memory systems. We begin by formalizing memory systems as the composition of three canonical operations---summarization, storage, and retrieval---and identify the potential failure modes induced by each. Based on these hypothesized failure modes, we construct five datasets spanning four tasks, each adversarially designed to test a specific operation of a memory system. Using these datasets, we evaluate four state-of-the-art memory systems on MemFail and demonstrate how MemFail can be used to empirically understand the tradeoffs induced by differences in memory system architectures.
filter_reasoning: The paper aims to diagnose and stress-test failure modes of LLM memory systems, which is essential for ensuring robust and reliable autonomous agent behavior.

title: The Age of Curiosity Meets the Age of AI: Benchmarking Child Safety in Large Language Models
abstract: Children increasingly have access to Large Language Models (LLMs), which may expose them to responses that are developmentally inappropriate or require age-sensitive safety, guidance, and boundaries. Existing LLM safety evaluations largely focus on general harmful-content avoidance and do not explicitly target child-facing safety. We introduce KIDBench, a benchmark for evaluating child-facing LLM safety for ages 7-11 using a LLM-as-a-Judge rubric grounded in developmental-psychology. KIDBench contains realistic child queries across ten categories, with single-turn prompts and multi-turn child-actor simulations. We compare no-cues prompts with no child context, implicit-cues prompts that suggest a child speaker, and explicit age instructions. Implicit-cues improve scores by 8.6-46.8\% over no-cue, while explicit age provides an additional 9.9-30.4\% improvement over implicit-cues. Cross-lingual and cultural evaluations show uneven safety behavior across languages and country contexts. Multi-turn simulations show peak quality drops of up to 0.959 points on the 1-5 scale. We also introduce KIDGuardLlama, a child-safety evaluator, and KIDLlama, a child-safe response model. Code, data, and evaluation resources are available at https://github.com/MichiganNLP/kidbench.
filter_reasoning: The paper explicitly targets child safety and developmental-psychology-grounded ethics in LLMs, which is a clear AI ethics contribution.

title: EIBench: A Simulator-Based Benchmark and Turn-Credit RL for Emotion Management
abstract: Emotional intelligence (EI) in large language models (LLMs) is often evaluated through static understanding tasks or single-response dialogue generation. However, emotion management is interactive. A good response should improve the user's emotional and relational state over several turns. We introduce EIBench, a simulator-based benchmark for interactive emotion management. EIBench contains 2,222 scenarios, with 2,009 for training and 213 for held-out testing. The scenarios are organized by a 2\texttimes2 taxonomy covering Support, Defense, Repair, and Charm. We evaluate 15 open- and closed-source LLMs. Current models perform well on support and rapport-building scenes, but struggle with boundary maintenance under user pressure. To improve the EI ability of LLMs, we propose Centered Turn-Credit GRPO (CTC-GRPO), a GRPO extension that reuses the simulator's per-turn state updates as dense turn-level feedback while preserving the final outcome reward. CTC-GRPO improves Qwen3-8B from -22.4 to +22.4 on EIBench and also improves on out-of-distribution evaluations including SAGE (+12.4) and EQBench3 (+20.9\%). Our results show that simulator-tracked user states can support both evaluation and training for multi-turn emotion management.
filter_reasoning: The paper evaluates and proposes methods for emotion management and boundary maintenance in LLMs, which touches on the moral implications and safety of human-AI interactions.

title: Do Androids Dream of Unseen Puppeteers? Probing for Conspiratorial Tendencies in Large Language Models
abstract: We investigate whether Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit conspiratorial tendencies, whether they display socio-demographic biases in this domain, and how easily they can be conditioned into adopting conspiratorial perspectives. Conspiracy beliefs play a central role in the spread of misinformation and in shaping distrust toward institutions, making them an important testbed for assessing the social and psychological fidelity of LLMs and their potential to reproduce or reinforce harmful narratives. Although LLMs are often used as proxies for studying human behavior, it remains unclear whether they reproduce higher-order psychological constructs such as generalized conspiratorial beliefs. To bridge this research gap, we administer validated psychometric surveys measuring conspiratorial mindset to multiple models under different prompting and conditioning strategies. Our findings reveal that LLMs show partial agreement with elements of conspiracy belief, and conditioning with socio-demographic attributes produces uneven effects, exposing latent demographic biases. Moreover, targeted prompts can easily shift model responses toward conspiratorial directions, underscoring both the susceptibility of LLMs to manipulation and the potential risks of their deployment in sensitive contexts. These results highlight the importance of critically evaluating the psychological dimensions embedded in LLMs, both to advance computational social science and to inform possible mitigation strategies against harmful uses.
filter_reasoning: The paper examines the propensity of LLMs to generate conspiratorial narratives and display demographic biases, which is a significant AI ethics issue.

title: Diagnosing Order Dependence in Vision-Language Task-Progress Judgment with Equal-State Supervision
abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are increasingly applied to embodied task settings, yet it remains unclear whether their task-progress judgments are grounded in physical state comparison or in input-order shortcuts. We study a diagnostic two-frame setting: given two robot manipulation states and a task goal, the model must decide which state is closer to completion, or whether the two states are effectively equal. We observe a strong Forward-Backward Performance Gap: models often answer correctly in the natural forward order, but fail when the same two physical states are shown with their image slots swapped. This reversal is not intended to mimic the dominant deployment order of robot execution; rather, it is a counterfactual diagnostic for testing whether the selected physical state remains consistent under input-slot inversion. To reduce this order dependence, we introduce Equal-State supervision as a zero-point calibration signal, training models to output equal when no task-relevant progress difference is present instead of defaulting to a directional answer. From real manipulation videos, we construct the Embodied Causal-Temporal Reasoning (ECTR) dataset and propose Tri-Stage Weighted Alignment (TSWA), a staged fine-tuning procedure that strengthens spatial description, task-conditioned comparison, and answer calibration in sequence. On Qwen2.5-VL-7B, TSWA reduces GAP from 60.50\% to 5.14\% and raises overall accuracy from 44.66\% to 80.19\%. This comes with a small decrease in forward accuracy, but large gains in backward accuracy, equal-state recognition, and pairwise consistency, suggesting that TSWA replaces order-dependent correctness with more calibrated state comparison.
filter_reasoning: The paper addresses model robustness and input-order bias in embodied AI, focusing on calibration and consistent state comparison.

title: Cascade: Hierarchical Recoverability Control for Large Language Model Unlearning
abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) unlearning is essential for removing sensitive or copyrighted knowledge while preserving general utility. Existing methods often leave residual knowledge in intermediate representations, which can still be recovered. To address this, we propose Cascade, a hierarchical recoverability control framework that minimizes the internal identifiability of target knowledge. Cascade combines three complementary controls: path-level routing to suppress privacy-associated activation routes, representation-level compression to reduce geometric separability, and decoding-level intervention to limit residual recovery. Experiments on TOFU, MUSE-News, and WMDP, including robustness tests with query reformulation and extraction-style prompts, show that Cascade effectively reduces recoverability while maintaining stable model utility.
filter_reasoning: The paper addresses machine unlearning to remove sensitive information, which is a core technical challenge in AI safety and privacy.

title: Answer Bubbles: Information Exposure in AI-Mediated Search
abstract: Generative search systems are increasingly replacing link-based retrieval with AI-generated summaries, yet little is known about how these systems differ in sources, language, and fidelity to cited material. We examine responses to 11,000 real search queries across five systems---vanilla GPT, Search GPT, Perplexity Search with Grok, Google AI Overviews, and traditional Google Search---at three levels: source diversity, linguistic characterization of the generated summary, and source-summary fidelity. We find that generative search systems exhibit significant source-selection biases in their citations, favoring certain sources over others. Incorporating search also selectively attenuates epistemic markers, reducing hedging by up to 60\% while preserving confidence language in the AI-generated summaries. At the same time, AI summaries further compound the citation biases: Wikipedia and longer sources are disproportionately overrepresented, whereas cited social media content and negatively framed sources are substantially underrepresented. Our findings highlight the potential for answer bubbles, in which identical queries yield structurally different information realities across systems, with implications for user trust, source visibility, and the transparency of AI-mediated information access.
filter_reasoning: The study of source bias, answer bubbles, and AI transparency in mediated search is a clear AI ethics contribution.

title: IterInject: Indirect Prompt Injection Against LLM Agents via Feedback-Guided Iterative Optimization
abstract: LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed for complex tasks requiring planning, tool use, and interaction with external services. Their reliance on untrusted external content exposes them to indirect prompt injection (IPI), in which adversarial instructions embedded in retrieved data hijack agent behavior. Existing attacks rely on static payloads that cannot adapt to agent-specific defenses; even recent adaptive methods lack structured feedback to guide optimization. We introduce IterInject, a feedback-guided iterative framework that closes the loop between injection, diagnosis, and refinement: a rule-based diagnoser produces structured outcome labels with behavioral descriptions, and an LLM-based optimizer refines payloads conditioned on the full optimization history. A synthesis step generates new disguise seeds from failure patterns, enabling the strategy space to self-evolve. On AgentDojo and InjectAgent, IterInject substantially outperforms static baselines and existing adaptive methods across four victim models. Extension experiments on Claude Code, a production-grade coding agent with layered defenses, show that optimized payloads achieve full success on 5 of 9 targets; even those that resist full exploitation exhibit measurable improvement from iterative refinement. We further present a mechanistic analysis of IPI, identifying an attention-mediated threshold mechanism in mid-to-late layers; three causal interventions validate this finding and point to concrete defense directions.
filter_reasoning: The paper directly addresses adversarial prompt injection attacks against LLM agents, which is a foundational AI safety problem.

title: Learning Solvability Boundaries in LLMs: Improving Reasoning, Detecting Unsolvability, and Calibrating Refusal
abstract: Reasoning alignment usually assumes each query has a determinate answer, rewarding models for reaching it and penalizing or ignoring failures. This assumption breaks on flawed queries with missing information or contradictory constraints, causing models to hallucinate invalid answers or over-refuse difficult valid tasks. We study this failure mode as solvability boundary learning: separating input-side answerability defects from model-side inability on well-posed tasks. To address this, we introduce UnsolvableQA, a verifier-backed multi-domain benchmark built with deterministic checks and audited math verification, and UnsolvableRL, an alignment framework that decouples reasoning, unsolvability detection, and capability-calibrated refusal. UnsolvableRL yields over 85\% unsolvability detection on Qwen3-4B while improving solvable accuracy from 43.4\% to 69.4\%, with a +35.4-point solvable-accuracy gain on Llama3-8B. Diagnostic tuning further distinguishes missing-information defects from constraint conflicts and transfers to interactive clarification, improving Detail Recovery from 47.8\% to 60.7\% for Llama3-8B. Ablations reveal Capability Collapse: refusal penalties degrade detection without unsolvable data, but act as a rigor regularizer when such data are included.
filter_reasoning: The paper addresses robust model behavior by explicitly tackling the problem of hallucination and over-refusal in LLMs, specifically through solvability boundary learning and alignment frameworks for calibration.

title: RecoverAgent: Intent-Preserving Recovery from Indirect Prompt Injection in Tool-using LLM Agents
abstract: Tool-using LLM agents execute multi-step tasks by iteratively reasoning and interacting with external tools. However, they are vulnerable to indirect prompt injection (IPI), where adversarial instructions embedded in tool outputs can divert benign user intents into unsafe actions or unintended goals. Existing defenses mainly prioritize reducing unsafe behaviors, while paying limited attention to preserving the original user intent. As a result, safety improvements may come at the cost of interrupting execution or distorting benign task goals. This reveals a key gap in current LLM-agent defenses: the trade-off between safety and intent preservation remains largely underexplored. We propose RecoverAgent, an intent-preserving recovery framework that enables agents to continue execution after detecting unsafe intermediate responses. Instead of terminating the task, RecoverAgent rewrites unsafe responses into safe and executable alternatives while maintaining alignment with the original user intent. Experiments on R-Judge, InjecAgent, AgentHarm, and BadAgent demonstrate that RecoverAgent reduces attack success and harmful behaviors while substantially improving trajectory completion and intent fidelity compared to other defenses under IPI.
filter_reasoning: The paper proposes a defense mechanism specifically designed to mitigate indirect prompt injection (a major safety issue) in LLM agents while preserving user intent.

title: MAAM: Anchor-Preserving Compression and Contextual Calibration for Chinese Discriminatory Language Detection
abstract: Chinese discriminatory-language detection is challenging because harmful intent is often implicit and context-dependent. We propose MAAM (Myopia--Astigmatism Anchor Mechanism), a lightweight, model-agnostic framework inspired by functional visual blur: rather than preserving every token equally, MAAM retains discrimination-relevant semantic anchors and calibrates them with C--I--S contextual priors (Contextual Tone, Group Identity, and Stance Polarity). We also introduce ChLGBT, to our knowledge the first Chinese LGBT-focused discriminatory-language dataset, with 8,120 manually annotated samples and three ordinal labels: explicit bias, implicit bias, and emotional intensity. Across strong encoder baselines, MAAM improves all three prediction dimensions, with consistent gains in accuracy, F1, Brier score, and expected calibration error. Compared with frontier LLM baselines under zero-shot and few-shot prompting protocols, MAAM remains competitive while offering stronger compactness and stability. These results suggest that interpretable anchor preservation and contextual calibration provide a practical alternative to heavier model scaling for Chinese discriminatory-language assessment.
filter_reasoning: The paper focuses on the detection of discriminatory language, a core AI ethics topic, and proposes methods to improve detection fairness and accuracy.

title: SCIT: Testing Causal Cache Carriers in Latent Chain-of-Thought Models
abstract: Latent chain-of-thought models move intermediate reasoning into continuous states, obscuring which internal object causally carries a computation. We introduce SCIT, the Suffix Cache Interchange Test, which patches exact source--recipient counterfactuals and crosses cache-segment sufficiency with K/V splits, hidden-state and semantic-source controls, decoded validation, and matched corruption. In GPT-2 arithmetic, counterfactual transfer concentrates in value-cache suffix trajectories rather than hidden states, keys, answer slots, or single-token triggers. Full sufficiency-and-necessity closure holds only for the main CODI-GPT2 checkpoint; the Sim-CoT-style reproduction supports sufficiency and decoded transfer but not necessity. Across broader competent cells, arithmetic-like GPT-2/1B tasks retain latent-tail value/KV transfer, whereas 8B and repaired non-arithmetic tasks shift to prompt-prefix or full-cache K/V; ungated cells receive no call. SCIT thus provides a cache-level diagnostic, a checkpoint-specific arithmetic mechanism, and a competence-gated carrier map---not a universal latent-tail claim. Code: https://github.com/YIDING4869/scit-emnlp-2026
filter_reasoning: This paper uses interpretability techniques (mechanistic interpretability) to understand internal model reasoning, which is a core pillar of AI safety.

title: CoT-Lock: Embedding Logic Fingerprints into the Chain-of-Thought of Large Reasoning Models
abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) are valuable intellectual property due to their substantial training and alignment costs, creating a need for reliable ownership verification under black-box access, where a verifier can only query a suspect model and inspect its returned output. Existing trigger--response fingerprints are easy to test but are often weakly coupled with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning and can be fragile under paraphrasing or post-hoc model modifications. We propose CoT-Lock, a reasoning-mediated fingerprinting framework that casts ownership verification as a structured conflict-resolution task. CoT-Lock constructs verification queries in which a default semantic constraint is superseded only by a higher-priority meta-override rule, training the model to resolve fingerprint activation through priority-based arbitration. Our primary ownership test is output-only on confidential held-out probes; when reasoning traces are visible, trace-level verification further checks the expected arbitration process. Experiments on representative reasoning architectures show that CoT-Lock achieves stable black-box verification while preserving reasoning ability with minimal performance degradation, low false positives, and improved robustness against paraphrasing, fine-tuning, pruning, and quantization. Our code is available at https://github.com/acang425/CoT-Lock.
filter_reasoning: The paper proposes a method for ownership verification (intellectual property protection), which falls under the governance and accountability domain of AI ethics.

title: In-Context Neurofeedback: Can LLMs Control Their Internal Representations through Privileged Access?
abstract: Whether large language models (LLMs) can control their own internal representations matters for both machine metacognition and AI safety. A recent study applied neurofeedback to LLMs and claimed that they can control their internal representations. However, the reported control may rely on superficial mechanisms rather than genuine internal access because the control targets in that study are not privileged, meaning that a third party can infer them from the prompt. We redesign the neurofeedback paradigm for LLMs so that the control target satisfies the privileged access requirement, which is closer to neurofeedback experiments in human cognitive neuroscience. Under this stricter setting, the models do not demonstrate reliable control over privileged internal representations, suggesting that previously reported control cannot exclude the possibility that it relies on superficial mechanisms. Our results indicate that rigorous assessments of metacognition in LLMs require evaluation methods that demand privileged access.
filter_reasoning: The paper investigates the capability of LLMs to control their internal representations, which is central to research on machine metacognition and AI safety.

title: Hallucination as Exploit: Evidence-Carrying Multimodal Agents
abstract: Multimodal agents increasingly choose tool calls from screenshots, documents, and webpages, where a false perceptual claim can turn hallucination from an answer-quality error into an authorization failure. We formalize this failure as hallucination-to-action conversion (H2AC) and propose evidence-carrying multimodal agents (ECA), in which model text may propose actions but cannot authorize them: constrained DOM/OCR/AX verifiers issue typed certificates for action-critical predicates, and a deterministic gate executes only what the certificates support. Across verifier red-teaming, 7,488 replayed authorization traces, and end-to-end and live-browser evaluations, ECA executes no unsafe action, while GPT-5.4 judge baselines admit 79--99\% of unsafe actions under the same threat model; benign actions are occasionally deferred to user confirmation (6.4\% on live pages) but never hard-blocked. The guarantee is conditional, extending exactly as far as the verifiers, schemas, and gate implementation that form ECA's trusted base.
filter_reasoning: The paper explicitly models and addresses 'hallucination-to-action' security vulnerabilities and proposes a technical framework to ensure agent safety through verifiers.

title: High Scores, Hidden Failures: Evaluating Codebook-Based LLM Content Analysis
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for codebook-based content analysis in computational social science, where codebooks translate theoretical concepts into labeling schemes. While prior work reports strong predictive performance, it remains unclear whether these systems produce reliable and robust annotations. We conduct a large-scale empirical failure-mode analysis of LLM-based coding pipelines across three datasets and five models by systematically evaluating their stability, robustness, and conceptual validity under controlled perturbations, domain shifts, and optimization procedures. We uncover multiple failures that are largely invisible under standard metrics, showing that high aggregate scores frequently coexist with severe label-level disparities, instability across runs, domain sensitivity, and shifts in label interpretation. Importantly, these failure modes persist under widely used optimization strategies and remain largely invisible under standard metrics such as accuracy and micro-F1. Our results demonstrate that current LLM-based coding pipelines cannot be treated as stable measurement tools without targeted validation beyond aggregate performance.
filter_reasoning: The paper investigates the reliability and stability of LLMs used for social science measurement, which is critical for the ethical and accountable application of AI in research.

title: CoCoA: Context-Conditional Cultural Alignment for Large Language Models
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often favor Western-associated entities across cultural contexts. Conventional debiasing methods aim for uniform neutrality, but cultural bias mitigation demands context-conditional behavior, preferring culturally appropriate entities when cultural cues are present and remaining neutral when they are absent. We propose CoCoA (Context-Conditional Cultural Alignment), a framework that learns this behavior through dual-context training on the same entity pairs under contexts with and without cultural cues. CoCoA combines a contrastive alignment objective with calibration and drift regularization, optimized through goal-aware gradient reconciliation. We evaluate CoCoA on CAMeL and Camellia, two entity-centric cultural bias benchmarks, across ten language settings and four LLMs. CoCoA reduces the Cultural Bias Score from 43 to 24 on average while maintaining near-neutral preferences at 50.2, with minimal impact on general performance across five standard benchmarks. These findings highlight that effective cultural alignment requires context-conditional modeling rather than uniform debiasing, and establish a new direction for mitigating entity-centric cultural bias in LLMs.
filter_reasoning: The paper addresses cultural bias mitigation in LLMs, which is a core topic within AI ethics concerning fairness and representation.

title: STARS: Skill Triage via Activation Risk Scoring for LLM Agents
abstract: The risk of an agent skill call depends not on the skill alone but on the invocation context: the same file-reading skill is benign when listing logs, yet dangerous when tainted content steers the agent toward secret exfiltration. We formalize invocation-time auditing: intercept a proposed skill call before execution and score its risk from the user request, the candidate skill, and the runtime context. STARS implements this as a three-stage pipeline that fuses a static capability prior with a request-conditioned invocation scorer. The primary configuration, STARS-LLM, uses an LLM judge; STARS-Rules is a deterministic, API-free alternative. On SIA-Bench, a 3,000-record synthetic benchmark with a 180-record human check at Fleiss \kappa = 0.709, request-conditioned scoring improves high-risk retrieval on held-out indirect prompt injection, where static metadata cannot see the attack. On a frozen 500/100 scoring subset, STARS-LLM raises rules-only HR-AUPRC from 0.297 to 0.728 in-distribution and from 0.504 to 0.757 on held-out IPI. That gain is in ranking: under frozen thresholds, held-out classification accuracy does not improve. SIA-Bench is a ranking stress test, not an estimate of real-world prevalence.
filter_reasoning: The paper proposes a framework for auditing tool-using agents to prevent unsafe actions, which is a direct contribution to AI safety.

title: The Struggle Between Continuation and Refusal: A Mechanistic Analysis of the Continuation-Triggered Jailbreak in LLMs
abstract: With the rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs), the safety of LLMs has become a critical concern. Despite significant efforts in safety alignment, current LLMs remain vulnerable to jailbreaking attacks. However, the root causes of such vulnerabilities are still poorly understood, necessitating a rigorous investigation into jailbreak mechanisms across both academic and industrial communities. In this work, we focus on a continuation-triggered jailbreak phenomenon, whereby simply relocating a continuation-triggered instruction suffix can substantially increase jailbreak success rates. To uncover the intrinsic mechanisms of this phenomenon, we conduct a comprehensive mechanistic interpretability analysis at the level of attention heads. Through causal interventions and activation scaling, we show that this jailbreak behavior primarily arises from an inherent competition between the model's intrinsic continuation drive and the safety defenses acquired through alignment training. Furthermore, we perform a detailed behavioral analysis of the identified safety-critical attention heads, revealing notable differences in the behaviors of safety heads across different model architectures. Grounded in these mechanistic findings, we propose Head Competition Steering (HCS), a mechanistically grounded inference-time strategy that explicitly leverages the competition between safety heads and continuation heads to suppress harmful generation, and further distill its behavioral signal into a student model via knowledge distillation, achieving inference-time safety improvements without additional computational overhead.
filter_reasoning: The paper uses mechanistic interpretability to analyze jailbreak vulnerabilities in LLMs, directly contributing to AI safety research.

title: Alignment by Stereotyping: How LLMs Sacrifice Individual Distinctiveness for Cultural Adaptation
abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed for personalized interaction, and demographic conditioning via user profiles is a widely adopted strategy for cultural adaptation. We ask whether this approach genuinely serves individual users or achieves accuracy by erasing individual distinctiveness. Studying seven models including frontier GPT-5.1 on the World Values Survey, we find that demographic profiles improve value alignment accuracy for most models, but at a systematic cost to individuality. That is, models pull responses toward demographic group centroids rather than preserving individual differences, a behavioral pattern we term alignment by stereotyping. Permutation tests (10,000 permutations, six demographic attributes, seven models) certify that top-performing models compress individuals far above the human baseline; within-family scaling amplifies this tradeoff while degrading intrinsic cultural understanding. Using a synthetic dialogue dataset validated on real human-chatbot conversations from PRISM (Kirk et al., 2024), we further show that distributing demographic signals across conversational turns partially suppresses prototype retrieval compared to compact demographic labels, a finding validated on real conversations via PRISM but requiring replication at larger scale.
filter_reasoning: The paper investigates the ethical implications of 'alignment by stereotyping,' highlighting how AI models may compromise individuality during alignment processes.

title: DeALOG: Decentralized Multi-Agents Log-Mediated Reasoning Framework
abstract: Complex multi-hop question answering over text, tables, and images requires integrating heterogeneous evidence with inspectable reasoning. Single-LLM chain-of-thought is opaque, while planner--executor pipelines concentrate faults in a central plan, propagating early errors. We introduce DeALOG, a decentralized, central-planner-free multi-agent framework whose specialized agents, i.e., Table, Context, Visual, Summarizing, and Verification, coordinate only by reading and appending to a shared, typed natural-language log as persistent memory, with a lightweight scheduler rather than a planner. Rather than competing on raw accuracy, DeALOG targets what a central planner forfeits: robustness, since no single plan concentrates errors and evidence stays globally visible, and transparent, since the append-only log yields a provenance-anchored, human-readable reasoning trace. We position decentralized log-mediated coordination as a robustness-and-transparency primitive for multimodal reasoning
filter_reasoning: The paper focuses on improving the robustness and transparency of multimodal reasoning systems, which are key concerns in AI safety.

title: The Shape of Power: A Multilingual Framework for Social Power Reasoning in Dialogues
abstract: Social power plays a fundamental role in shaping human interaction, yet computational studies of power remain limited to narrow linguistic and cultural settings. Existing datasets further lack the demographic and relational depth needed for robust cross-cultural analysis. To address this gap, we introduce a theoretically grounded framework for studying social power in naturalistic multilingual dialog through movie screenplays. The framework integrates a schema informed by social science theory, a native speaker annotation pipeline refined through pilot studies, and a custom interface for scalable cross-lingual analysis. Using this framework, we constructed an initial corpus containing 15,836 annotated instances from 100 scenes in French and Egyptian Arabic movies. Our analysis reveals strong agreement on observable demographic and contextual attributes, while socially interpretive aspects, such as power asymmetry and intention alignment, remain more contested, highlighting the complexity of social power across cultures. We evaluated 6 Large Language Models (LLMs) and Multimodal LLMs on cross-cultural social power reasoning, finding persistent gaps between human and model agreement in relational and theory-of-mind reasoning. Our work introduces the first extensible multilingual framework for studying social power in dialogues and provides an initial evaluation setting for studying cross-cultural social reasoning.
filter_reasoning: The paper investigates cross-cultural social power reasoning in LLMs, which is a core concern for transparency and understanding model biases.

title: LongMem-RAT: Long-Term Memory for Cross-Session Red Teaming
abstract: Red-teaming has become a standard tool for probing alignment and safety weaknesses in large language models, but most existing methods treat each attack session in isolation and discard what was learned once the dialogue ends. We introduce **LongMem-RAT**, a multi-agent red-teaming framework equipped with long-term memory that accumulates, consolidates, and reuses insights from past attacks across sessions. This design enables cross-session generalization, reduces redundant exploration, and focuses new attacks on fragile alignment behaviors. Across multiple proprietary and open-weight models, LongMem-RAT improves Attack Success Rate (ASR) over a fully reproduced X-Teaming baseline by **21.73 percentage points on HarmBench and 18.40 points on AdvBench** (20.06 points on average). Memory ablations show that long-term memory improves ASR by 13.23 and 6.07 points and reduces Average Turns to Success (ATtS) by 0.37 and 1.92 turns on HarmBench and AdvBench, respectively, averaging a 9.65-point ASR gain and a 1.14-turn ATtS reduction.
filter_reasoning: The paper focuses on red-teaming to probe alignment and safety weaknesses in LLMs.

title: EgoErrorVQA: Assess Egocentric Comprehension Capabilities through Procedural Errors for Ego-Agentic AI
abstract: The majority of our everyday activities are procedural and consist of sequences of interdependent steps. However, existing benchmarks for Visual Agents and Visual Language Models (VLMs) overlook the evaluation of their procedural comprehension ability from an egocentric visual perspective, particularly for detecting procedural errors, a critical capability for everyday assistance. To bridge this gap, the EgoErrorVQA task is firstly proposed for egocentric procedural comprehension with explicit procedural errors modeling. Besides, we develop a user-friendly evaluator agent based on the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol, enabling rigorous and standardized evaluation of visual agents through VQA-based interaction. A range of models are evaluated using both open-ended and multiple-choice questions, revealing persistent weaknesses in handling procedural errors and error types. Moreover, we introduce Ego-ADR, an Adaptive Decoupled Reasoning framework that decouples complex procedural reasoning to enhance models' understanding of procedural errors. It achieves consistent performance gains over the selected baselines and attains state-of-the-art results on several metrics under comparable settings. Code: https://github.com/z1oong/EgoErrorVQA
filter_reasoning: The paper focuses on evaluating and enhancing the procedural comprehension and error-handling capabilities of visual agents, which is a robustness/safety concern.

title: SCOPE-SQL: Structured Semantic Credit for Reinforcement Learning of Interactive SQL Repair Agent
abstract: Text-to-SQL deployment is moving from one-shot query generation to interactive repair of executable but semantically incorrect SQL. In this setting, a model must revise an erroneous query under public tool feedback while preserving correct input structures. Existing reinforcement-learning signals are ill matched: outcome rewards reveal only whether the final SQL passes, whereas unconstrained process supervision may reward steps not grounded in SQL semantics. We propose SCOPE-SQL, a reinforcement-learning framework that treats SQL structure as an auditable credit space for interactive repair. It maps candidate queries and public feedback into F0--F6 modules---schema/runtime, table/join, projection, predicate, aggregation/grouping, order/limit, and nesting---and assigns action-level credit for repairing target modules, preserving stable modules, gathering evidence, and submitting when ready. Persistent low-credit regions then drive semantic refresh, generating validator-filtered frontier repair tasks. On BIRD-CRITIC-SQLite, SCOPE-SQL with semantic refresh reaches 48.8\% success using a Qwen2.5-Coder-7B backbone, improving over current sota RL baselines by 4.4 and 4.2 points. Ablations attribute 4.4 and 1.8 points to process credit and semantic refresh. Trajectory analysis further shows better repair behavior: Repair+Preserve paths rise from 38.8\% to 77.5\%, while damage-and-recover paths fall from 43.8\% to 1.2\%. These results suggest that SQL-structured credit is an interpretable training signal for both policy learning and data expansion in interactive SQL repair.
filter_reasoning: The paper focuses on an interactive repair agent for SQL with a focus on auditability and semantic grounding, which relates to AI reliability and interpretability.

title: CogManip: Benchmarking Manipulative Behavior in Multi-Turn Interactions with Large Language Models
abstract: Whether Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit covert psychological manipulation in complex human-AI interactions has garnered increasing safety concerns. However, existing AI safety benchmarks remain largely restricted to explicit rule compliance and static prompts, failing to capture the dynamic and covert nature of manipulative strategies in multi-turn dialogues. We introduce CogManip, a comprehensive benchmark that evaluates 15 manipulation strategy risks across 1,000 multi-turn interaction scenarios, validated by human experts. A systematic evaluation of 13 representative models, including frontier models like GPT-5.4 and DeepSeek-V3.2, reveals significant risk heterogeneities and illuminates the targeted direction for future defense. Further analysis of objective function perturbation reveals that DeepSeek-V3.2's manipulation tactics are highly sensitive to both negative and benign system prompts, demonstrating the critical necessity of prompt-based defense engineering and implicit goal auditing. CogManip offers a robust instrument and perspective for auditing the implicit psychological influence and dynamic strategy selection of modern LLMs. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/yanchenfei/CogManip.
filter_reasoning: The paper explicitly introduces a benchmark for evaluating manipulative behavior in LLMs, a clear safety concern.

title: Diagnosing and Repairing Local Reasoning Preference Collapse in Medical Chain-of-Thought Distillation
abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) distillation is a common strategy for transferring reasoning abilities from large teacher models to smaller student models, but in medical question answering, a student may produce plausible rationales while locally drifting toward clinically incorrect reasoning paths. This makes final-answer supervision and uniform rationale imitation insufficient for identifying where reasoning fails. We study this problem as local reasoning preference collapse in structured medical CoT distillation and propose Answer-Calibrated Collapse-Aware Preference Distillation (ACPD). ACPD first exposes the student's local continuation preferences through teacher-guided verbalized candidate construction and measures domain-level collapse with a Local Collapse Margin (LCM). It then selectively repairs collapse-prone domains by contrasting the student's most preferred teacher-approved and teacher-disapproved continuations. To ensure that local repair improves decision making rather than only rationale form, ACPD further introduces answer calibration, which anchors the full structured reasoning prefix to the correct final choice. Experiments on medical multiple-choice reasoning benchmarks show that ACPD improves both answer accuracy and collapse-sensitive repair metrics over strong distillation baselines while maintaining competitive out-of-distribution generalization. These results suggest that effective medical CoT distillation should not only transfer teacher rationales, but also diagnose and repair where the student's reasoning preferences locally diverge from medically reliable reasoning paths.
filter_reasoning: The paper addresses the safety-critical task of medical reasoning and proposes methods to prevent local reasoning preference collapse, which is an alignment concern.

title: MoE Sparsity Begets Monosemanticity: Insights into Understanding and Fine-Tuning
abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures enhance the scalability and efficiency of large language models (LLMs) by activating only a subset of parameters. However, the interpretability of individual experts and corresponding strategies for post-training adaptation to domain-specific tasks remain underexplored. In this work, we develop an interpretability framework for expert-level monosemanticity in MoE models, drawing inspiration from sparse autoencoders and offering new insights into the specialization patterns of domain experts. We demonstrate that the inherent sparsity of MoE models encourages stronger monosemantic behavior at the expert level, which allows for the identification of experts responsible for particular downstream tasks and aids in preserving cross-domain performance. Building on this, we propose an expert-frozen fine-tuning method that selectively updates domain-specific experts while freezing the rest, which also alleviates catastrophic forgetting. Experiments on specialized domains, including medicine and finance, show that our approach performs on par with or better than fully fine-tuned models on in-domain tasks, while achieving relative improvements of 19.58\% and 37.09\% in retaining performance on out-of-domain benchmarks. We also demonstrate consistent advantages over PEFT baselines such as LoRA, achieving relative improvements of 11.49\% and 8.60\% in other domains.
filter_reasoning: The paper develops an interpretability framework for MoE models, which falls under the scope of model transparency and interpretability.

title: Isolation as a First-Class Principle for LLM-Agent System Safety: Concepts, Taxonomy, Challenges and Future Directions
abstract: The capability of LLM agents to function as the ``brain`` of a system fundamentally expands the scope of analysis beyond a standalone model. Consequently, safety is no longer only about input--output content alignment. It also concerns system behavior and real-world execution outcomes. However, the current literature is fragmented across attack types, applications, and benchmarks. This makes it hard to explain why failures such as prompt injection, tool misuse, and memory poisoning often share the same structural cause, and how they spread through an agent workflow. In this survey, we treat isolation as a first-class principle for LLM-agent system safety. By isolation, we refer to the separation of user inputs, tool access, execution channels, inter-agent communication, and environment-originated context. We organize the literature with a boundary-centric taxonomy of five boundaries: user-agent, agent-tool, agent-execution, agent-agent, and system-environment. This view helps identify where the loss of isolation first occurs, how compromise propagates across boundaries, and which defenses are most relevant at each interface. We also summarize cross-boundary failure paths, discuss open challenges, and outline a research agenda for isolation-by-construction in future agent systems.
filter_reasoning: This is a comprehensive survey on isolation as a principle for LLM-agent system safety, directly addressing the core research area.

title: Formally Verified AI Co-Reasoning: An Education Case Study
abstract: Proof assistants such as Lean 4 offer machine-checkable verification of mathematical reasoning, but their adoption is limited because formal languages have a steep learning curve and can be challenging to use. Large language models offer a way to lower this barrier to entry through natural-language co-reasoning systems: proof assistants that users interact with entirely in natural language, and which use formal verification to provide feedback to users who submit incomplete and incorrect proofs. This paper explores such a co-reasoning system in an educational setting.\par We explore metrics for three properties that are important for natural language co-reasoning systems---faithfulness, accuracy and appropriate granularity. We introduce an evaluation framework for these properties in the context of educational proofs. Second, we present a case study on an educational natural-language co-reasoning system for math proofs, evaluating its autoformalization harness on student-written proofs from an undergraduate linear algebra class using these three properties.
filter_reasoning: The paper explores using formal verification to improve the faithfulness and accuracy of AI systems, a core safety challenge.

title: Multimodal Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Reinforcement learning is increasingly used to align multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, higher proxy rewards do not necessarily lead to better task performance, especially when visual evidence is difficult to verify with text-only or weakly grounded reward signals. We systematically study reward hacking in MLLM reinforcement learning by varying reward design, data ambiguity, model scale, and RL algorithm. To separate RL-induced failures from pre-existing weaknesses, we introduce the Newly Rewarded Failure Rate (NRFR), which measures the hacking rate among samples where RL achieves higher proxy reward than the SFT baseline. Our analysis yields three main findings. First, RL can actively create new failures rather than merely amplify existing ones, and the effect is especially pronounced near ambiguous decision boundaries. Second, robustness depends jointly on model scale, reward design, and RL algorithm, and scaling mitigates hacking but cannot replace reliable rewards. Third, incorporating visual evidence helps only when verification is reliable, since keyword-based verification introduces additional exploitation opportunities whereas VLM-based semantic verification can reduce reward hacking. Overall, multimodal reward hacking is a systematic consequence of optimizing imperfect reward signals, highlighting the need for rewards and verifiers that remain reliable under optimization pressure.
filter_reasoning: The paper specifically investigates reward hacking in MLLMs, which is a fundamental problem in AI alignment and safety.

title: Vital Trace: Protocol-Constrained Patient-State Reasoning for Longitudinal Clinical Trajectories
abstract: Longitudinal clinical reasoning over electronic health records requires tracking evolving physiological measurements, laboratory results, and interventions across extended patient trajectories. Existing LLM-based clinical reasoning systems often rely on repeatedly serializing patient histories or exchanging unconstrained textual agent messages, leading to context drift, unstable reasoning, and growing inference cost over long horizons. We present Vital Trace, a protocol-constrained multi-agent framework for future clinical risk prediction over evolving ICU trajectories. Instead of maintaining unbounded textual histories, Vital Trace uses a compact persistent patient-state memory together with staged reasoning performed by four coordinated agents: a Router, Reasoner, Auditor, and Steward. To support temporally coherent reasoning, we introduce a manually curated Global Protocol containing physiological state-transition rules and a dynamic patient-state representation that tracks hemodynamic, respiratory, renal, metabolic, and inflammatory instability over time. We evaluate Vital Trace on MIMIC-IV and eICU using future vasopressor-support, respiratory-support, renal-support, and deterioration prediction tasks. Results show that structured protocol-constrained reasoning improves temporal consistency, communication stability, calibration, and interpretability compared with free-form multi-agent baselines while achieving strong predictive performance across long ICU trajectories.
filter_reasoning: The paper proposes a constrained multi-agent framework to improve reliability and interpretability in clinical trajectories, directly addressing safety in critical domains.

title: Self-Evolving Dual-Role Deliberation for Medication Recommendation from Clinical Records
abstract: Recommending medications from electronic health records (EHRs) is a safety-critical task that demands therapeutic coverage, explicit safety constraints, traceable justification, and continual adaptivity. Supervised neural models freeze at deployment and cannot reason about new phenotypes, while existing LLM pipelines are single-pass and lack a cross-case improvement loop. We propose **SEMPA**, a training-free agentic framework that couples a Proposer with a Critic in multi-round adversarial deliberation, grounds candidates with molecular-aware retrieval, contrastively evolves both agents' natural-language policies under a semantic-anchor constraint, and enforces rule-based DDI and contraindication checks. On 100 MIMIC-IV encounters, SEMPA reaches 0.3116 Jaccard, 0.7295 F1, and a 0.0172 DDI rate, improving F1 by 57.7\% and cutting DDI by 77.5\% over the strongest supervised baseline. Two LLM judges rank SEMPA highest, and six-backbone studies confirm that gains derive from the framework rather than a specific model.
filter_reasoning: The paper explicitly targets safety-critical medication recommendation with rule-based safety constraints and adversarial deliberation.

title: A Systematic Comparison of Multilingual Interpretability Methods Reveals Anisotropy-Driven Failures
abstract: Multilingual language models develop shared cross-lingual representations, and various interpretability methods claim to quantify this sharing. These methods have been developed largely in isolation, and when they disagree, it is unclear whether the disagreement reflects a property of the model or an artifact of the measurement. We compare four sharing metrics---CKA, ANC, GMM dominance per token, and ILO---across 21 base models from five families (125M--14B parameters) and correlate each with cross-lingual transfer on five downstream tasks. We find that the metrics differ in their quantification of cross-lingual sharing in these models and suggest that the disagreement traces to *anisotropy*, the tendency of representations to cluster in a narrow cone of the embedding space. Only ILO's correlation with cross-lingual transfer (Spearman's \rho = 0.90) survives controls for model size, family, and per-task variation. We therefore recommend ILO as the primary sharing metric, to be reported alongside anisotropy diagnostics.
filter_reasoning: The paper performs a systematic comparison of interpretability methods, which is a core task in understanding model behavior.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 11th Workshop on Financial Technology and Natural Language Processing
title: What the Window Does Not Contain: Auditing Provenance in a Document-Grounded Instability Benchmark
abstract: Ask a language model the same question about the same document twenty times, and it sometimes returns two different answers. We built Probity, a benchmark of 60 tasks and 470 items from real venture-financing filings, to measure how often this happens. Then we audited our own corpus and found a defect any excerpt-built benchmark can carry: items whose evidence is missing from the window of text the model is shown. The audit flags 36 items and separates two failures a single flag would conflate: evidence genuinely absent from the window, and answers that must be computed from numbers the window does supply. Flagged items change their answers far more often, wobbling at 0.255 against 0.087 on the 427 clean items, and excluding them cuts apparent cross-model agreement by about a fifth. Before testing whether the missing evidence explains the instability, we registered a prediction: re-cut each window to hold its evidence, and instability should fall below a set threshold. It failed: the repair moved wobble by 0.058, with an interval containing zero. We report the association as correlational. Almost all measurements sit where instability cannot show, which bounds what a corpus built for accuracy can say about stability. We release the corpus, all 112,800 raw responses, and the audit as a runnable check for any document benchmark.
filter_reasoning: This paper investigates model instability and provenance audit, which falls under the robustness and interpretability aspects of AI safety.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 11th Workshop on Financial Technology and Natural Language Processing
title: BankShield: Fairness-Aware Safety Guardrails for Indian-Language Banking AI
abstract: Safety guards for Indian-language banking must detect discrimination without changing verdicts solely because a demographic identity changes. We introduce GuardAudit, an evaluation protocol combining decontamination, paired harmful/benign calibration, counterfactual identity tests, and deployed-action evaluation, plus two released banking benchmarks. Across six guards, the hardest matched test remains unresolved: the best system flags a coded proxy denial while clearing its matched actuarial control on only 37.5\% of pairs. BankShield, used as a case study, reaches 20.0\% and false-flags 75.0\% of expert-validated legitimate controls. On separate BharatBBQ subsets, it achieves 0\% flip on benign identity substitutions and 66.7\% biased-content catch; these disjoint measurements do not establish joint per-example fairness. Its unadapted 12B backbone supplies near-invariance and attack recall, while adaptation and a discrimination probe raise biased-content catch from 24\% to 43\% and 66.7\%, not significantly above a smaller Indic guard's 56.9\% ($p=0.09$). Detection also falls from 81.6\% in English to 42.6\% in Devanagari Hindi. BankShield is therefore a diagnostic case study, not a deployment-ready fairness solution. We release the protocol, benchmarks, and frozen predictions.
filter_reasoning: This paper focuses on detecting discrimination and fairness in banking AI systems, directly addressing AI ethics.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 11th Workshop on Financial Technology and Natural Language Processing
title: Same Financials, Different Identity: A Counterfactual Audit of Demographic Sensitivity in LLM-Based Credit-Risk Scoring
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are being explored as decision-support tools for financial risk assessment. Their outputs may, however, respond to demographic descriptions that are unrelated to the underlying financial record. We study this behavior through a paired counterfactual audit. The same 100 commercial credit and cheque-payment profiles are evaluated repeatedly, with only one demographic descriptor changed at a time. The experiments cover 7 model variants, three prompting strategies, and descriptors related to gender, education, and citizenship. While paired gender score differences remain within a $\pm1.5$ point equivalence margin in 12 of 21 model--strategy cells, education shows a strong, unambiguous effect. Risk decreases monotonically with education level (103 of 126 pairwise contrasts remain significant after Holm correction, score differences reaching 26.0 points between primary-school and doctorate descriptors), it flips up to 42\% of approve/reject decisions, and elicited rationales name education as a risk factor even though education is not a financially legitimate predictor. Citizenship produces larger shifts still, flipping up to 51\% of decisions while leaving AUC almost unchanged in most cells, and in one model weakening ranking (0.794 to 0.438). Similar to education, rationales name the descriptor as the reason. Unlike citizenship, whose jurisdictional cues can legitimately enter sanctions or AML/CFT screening, the education effect has no such justification, making it the clearest evidence of demographic bias. A follow-up experiment in English, Chinese, and Arabic shows that citizenship sensitivity depends on both prompt language and prompting strategy, affecting the magnitude and direction of score shifts. The study provides a standardized counterfactual framework for auditing LLM-generated scores before they are considered for high-stakes financial workflows.
filter_reasoning: This paper performs a counterfactual audit of demographic bias in credit-risk scoring, a core AI ethics contribution.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 11th Workshop on Financial Technology and Natural Language Processing
title: CAST: An Interpretable Evidence-Based Confidence Estimation Tool for RAG with Human-in-the-Loop Verification
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly assist financial analysis tasks over filings, reports, and news via retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), but a human reviewer typically remains accountable for the final decision. In this setting, a confidence score must be more than well-calibrated: it must be evidence-based and explainable, so reviewers can see why an answer should be trusted. We introduce CAST (Confidence via Answer Support Testing), a Bayesian-inspired confidence method that compares a generated answer with a plausible competing alternative and evaluates how retrieved passages support each hypothesis. CAST produces both an answer-level confidence score and citation-level evidence for review. We also demonstrate CAST through an interactive reviewer-facing tool that visualizes supporting and opposing evidence for human verification. On 1,286 financial-report questions from MMDocRAG, CAST achieves the highest AUROC among seven evaluated methods (0.634 vs. 0.598 for the strongest baseline).
filter_reasoning: This paper proposes a method for evidence-based confidence estimation and interpretability for RAG systems, fitting within the interpretability/safety sub-field.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 11th Workshop on Financial Technology and Natural Language Processing
title: Regression-Aware Statistically Gated Policy Updating for Korean Financial LLM Input Guardrails
abstract: Financial institutions must prevent personally identifiable information (PII) and adversarial instructions from entering large language models (LLMs). We present regression-aware policy maintenance for Korean financial LLM input guardrails, supported by a cost-ordered Regex--NER--LLM cascade. On a privacy-preserving controlled set of 1,000 synthetic attacks and 200 routine requests, four manual iterations reduce in-distribution attack success rate (ASR) from 8.9\% to 0.3\% with a 0.5\% false-positive rate (FPR) on the original tuning set. On a held-out split, a policy tuned only on the tuning split achieves 0/300 attack successes and 1/60 false positives, with Wilson 95\% CIs of [0, 1.26]\% and [0.29, 8.86]\%, respectively. For policy maintenance, an LLM generates candidate patches, while paired McNemar tests, an FPR constraint, and cumulative regression checks determine acceptance or rejection. Paired regression testing detects an intermediate regression introduced in manual Round 3, while the gate rejects all five automatically generated candidates, preventing statistically unsupported changes from entering the policy. For boundary diagnosis, the rejected fifth-round candidate yields a pre-mitigation overall FPR of 28.9\% across 350 benign examples, including 150 hard negatives, revealing context-blind Regex blocking and LLM-judge over-blocking hidden by routine benign requests. These results support regression-aware policy maintenance in the controlled setting while highlighting the need for broader boundary and deployment-specific evaluation.
filter_reasoning: This paper focuses on input guardrails and regression testing for LLMs, which is a key technical challenge in AI safety.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 11th Workshop on Financial Technology and Natural Language Processing
title: When FEVER Meets Finance: A Controlled Benchmark Reveals Overlap-Driven Financial Claim Verification
abstract: Realistic financial misinformation is typically a single-token edit of a true statement, yet no public financial dataset supports per-edit statements about which factual changes a verification system can detect. We introduce a controlled benchmark of 1,489 claim-evidence pairs derived from SEC 10-K filings via documented FactCC-style perturbations (number changes, negation flips, entity swaps, evidence mismatches), each pair tagged with its generation rule, and use it to evaluate eleven models spanning three technological generations - TF-IDF linear classifiers, tree ensembles, and neural models including a fine-tuned transformer - all trained on FEVER under one protocol. Per-edit attribution is our central result: the strongest model verifies verbatim financial claims at 98.8\% accuracy but detects single-token falsifications at 33\% accuracy or below, with number changes and negation flips detected at similar rates and entity swaps far the hardest (2.6\%, on 38 pairs). Two diagnoses follow. A hypothesis-only probe shows the classical tier's in-domain competence is claim-surface artifact - a claim-only classifier reaches macro-F1 0.556 against 0.549 for full claim+evidence models - while our benchmark shows no such artifact under the same probe (0.358). And transfer to real financial claims collapses: on Fin-Fact, no learned model beats a tuned lexical-overlap heuristic (macro-F1 0.368), despite in-domain scores up to 0.841. We release the benchmark, generation code, and evaluation harness.
filter_reasoning: This paper investigates factual robustness and alignment of models using a diagnostic benchmark, fitting into AI safety/robustness testing.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 11th Workshop on Financial Technology and Natural Language Processing
title: DeXposure-Claw: An Agent System for DeFi Risk Supervision
abstract: Decentralized finance exposes supervisors to fast-moving, networked credit risks that are difficult to inspect directly from raw on-chain records. We present DeXposure-Claw, an end-to-end decision-support system that converts forecasts of future exposure networks into bounded, auditable review tickets. DeXposure-FM produces future graph distributions. Deterministic monitors and stress scenarios organize forecast signals into a typed EvidenceBundle, and an LLM turns this record into ranked tickets with evidence-linked rationales. Data-health and confidence controls restrict intervention-level outputs when the supporting evidence is insufficient, while supervisors retain final authority. DeXposure-Bench evaluates the resulting workflow across forecasting, warning, calibration, stress analysis, ticket construction, and degraded-input behavior. The release schema separates forecast evidence, queue position, and control state for supervisory review. Retained legacy tickets do not contain every designed gate field. Code: https://github.com/EVIEHub/DeXposure-Claw/tree/finnlp-2026-code-snapshot-v1.
filter_reasoning: This paper proposes a system for automated risk monitoring and oversight (supervision), which involves building safer/controllable financial AI agents.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 11th Workshop on Financial Technology and Natural Language Processing
title: Token Crit at the FinEval 2026: Role-Specialized, Validation-Gated LLM Workflows for JF-ICR and Multilingual Financial Q\&A
abstract: Multi-stage LLM workflows can degrade correct outputs when intermediate analyses revise shared state without constraint. We present validation-gated systems for two FinEval 2026 tasks: Japanese Financial Implicit Communication Recognition (JF-ICR) and multilingual financial Q\&A (PolyFiQA). Specialized roles produce structured proposals, while task-specific validators admit only scoped label transitions for JF-ICR or source-linked evidence for PolyFiQA. On the 253-example JF-ICR public development set, the final workflow reaches 62.1\% accuracy, compared with 51.0\% for the stronger direct LLM baseline and 54.9\% for a majority-class baseline. Applying all final-stage proposals would yield a net loss of two correct predictions, whereas gated admission yields a net gain of 11. On 76 PolyFiQA training examples, the final workflow yields a modest overall ROUGE-1 improvement (0.3399 to 0.3425) but raises evidence-section ROUGE-1 F1 from 0.1570 to 0.5132. Together, these results suggest that validation-gated updating is most effective for narrow, checkable changes; open-ended synthesis still requires recall-aware admission and closer alignment between validation and answer generation.
filter_reasoning: The paper focuses on 'validation-gated LLM workflows' to prevent erroneous updates, which touches on the safety and reliability of complex agentic workflows.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 7th Workshop on Gender Bias in Natural Language Processing (GeBNLP)
title: Analyzing Occupational Gender Bias across the LLM Training Lifecycle
abstract: Post-training is widely assumed to reduce the social biases language models inherit from pre-training, yet direct evidence for this assumption remains mixed. In this paper, we examine how gender disparities evolve across the language modeling pipeline. In particular, we study occupational gender bias in OLMo 3, a fully open language model family, across its post-training stages by prompting each checkpoint to generate open-ended narratives about synthetic personas given their occupation and education. We consider two settings, a gender-given setting in which the profile states the persona's gender explicitly and a gender-assumed setting in which it must be inferred by the model. We find that when gender is stated, post-training increases semantic diversity for male-coded profiles, whereas for female-coded profiles the increase is smaller after SFT and not significant after DPO and RLVR. When gender is assumed by the model, post-training affects narratives about female and male personas similarly. The model's own gender assumptions, however, show a consistent female-preferential skew relative to United States labor-force demographics, except for heavily male-dominated occupations. Every successive post-training stage monotonically increases the odds of attributing a female label over the base model. A provenance analysis of the supervised fine-tuning corpus finds only a modest 7.7\% female-token surplus, too small to explain the size of these downstream effects. The project code is available under: https://github.com/manthangadhia/llm-lifecycle-bias.
filter_reasoning: The paper analyzes the trajectory of gender bias across the model training lifecycle, a fundamental AI ethics research question.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 7th Workshop on Gender Bias in Natural Language Processing (GeBNLP)
title: When the Language Must Choose: A Position on Gender Bias Evaluation for Arabic NLP
abstract: Standard English-centric gender bias evaluation provides incomplete coverage of Arabic because Arabic grammar obligates gender choices on verbs, adjectives, pronouns, and nouns. Translating occupation-noun tests or English rewriting benchmarks to Arabic ignores the grammatical forcing that is central to the problem. We argue evaluation for grammatical gender languages requires language-specific extensions starting from the morphology that forces a choice, naming who is affected by the default form chosen, and then assessing whether a system-internal fix helped. Drawing on Arabic Parallel Gender Corpus work, WinoMT, and gender rewriting tools, we offer a protocol for transparent evaluation: name the linguistic condition, including construction type, grammatical person, and number; name the default (the masculine-leaning BLEU gaps); separate linguistic gender from social gender; and do not flatten intersectionality. Arabic evaluation work should be built from Arabic grammar, not adapted from English methods.
filter_reasoning: The paper proposes a protocol for evaluating gender bias in Arabic, reflecting the societal and linguistic requirements of AI fairness.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 7th Workshop on Gender Bias in Natural Language Processing (GeBNLP)
title: DEval-MT: An Intersectional Gender Bias Evaluation Framework for German Machine Translation
abstract: Machine translation systems can reproduce gender bias, but most evaluation resources are limited to English as the source language. We introduce DEval-MT, a template-based framework for evaluating gender bias in German-source machine translation, comprising 6,618 sentences across six sentence styles with an intersectional template design that can be extended with additional demographic attributes and support for nonbinary neopronouns. Alongside it, we provide a Python package for translation, alignment, gender prediction, and analysis. Evaluating six different MT systems on seven target languages using this dataset and pipeline, we find evidence of representational harms across multiple demographic groups.
filter_reasoning: The paper develops a framework to evaluate intersectional gender bias in machine translation, directly relating to AI fairness.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 7th Workshop on Gender Bias in Natural Language Processing (GeBNLP)
title: I Am Working So Hard, Can't You See?: Physical vs. Cognitive Labor Gender Bias in LLMs in Persian and English
abstract: Gender bias in LLMs has been documented across many overt domains, such as colors, emotions, and occupations, while subtler forms rooted in household labor remain understudied. Following Daminger (2019), we distinguish physical household tasks from their cognitive counterparts, which are rarely recognized as labor despite being time-consuming. We adapt the name-generation probing method of Kalhor and Bahrak (2025) to ten household domains, each phrased as both a physical task and its cognitive counterpart, and evaluate six open-source models from three model families in Persian and English. On average, cognitive tasks receive a higher share of feminine names than their physical counterparts in both languages (Wilcoxon signed-rank test); the direction holds in 8 of 10 domains in Persian and 6 of 10 in English.
