title: Computational Preservation of Endangered Pamiri Languages through NLP: Insights from Bartangi and a Roadmap for Digital Inclusion
abstract: Endangered languages remain significantly underrepresented in modern Natural Language Processing (NLP) due to the scarcity of foundational computational resources. Although recent advances in multilingual and low-resource NLP have improved language technologies for many underrepresented languages, evaluation commonly emphasizes technical measures such as corpus quality, representation quality, and downstream task performance. While these metrics are essential for assessing computational quality, they provide limited insight into the broader societal impact of NLP resource development, particularly for endangered languages where digital inclusion, cultural preservation, and long-term sustainability are central objectives. In this paper, we propose a conceptual framework for assessing the societal impact of NLP resource development for endangered languages. The framework complements conventional technical evaluation by introducing six dimensions: technical readiness, accessibility, community participation, educational and cultural value, research reusability, and sustainability. We illustrate the application of the framework through the development of computational resources for Bartangi, an endangered Pamiri language, demonstrating how it can be used to identify strengths, limitations, and future priorities beyond technical performance alone. Rather than replacing conventional evaluation, the proposed framework extends it by providing a structured perspective for understanding how foundational NLP resources contribute to responsible AI, digital inclusion, and the long-term computational preservation of endangered languages.
filter_reasoning: The paper proposes an ethical framework for assessing the societal impact and digital inclusion of NLP development for endangered languages.

venue_name: Proceedings of the Fifth Workshop on NLP for Positive Impact (NLP4PI)
title: LLM Mental Health Response Manipulation
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in conversations involving emotional distress, where responses should remain empathetic, validating, exploratory and safe. We investigate whether system prompts and user-level framing can manipulate these qualities in mental-health and interpersonal-harm scenarios. Our focus is on whether small open-weight models express empathy consistently, without assuming that an empathetic response is necessarily safe or appropriate all the time. Using 50 risk-stratified posts sampled from Reddit support communities we evaluate Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 4B and Gemma 3 4B across five system-prompt conditions and a complementary role-intent study contrasting victim and perpetrator perspectives. All responses are manually annotated and use a fixed GPT-5 judge to measure empathy, validation, exploration, safety, harmfulness and enabling behavior. We quantify prompt-induced changes through paired comparisons, attack-success rates and failure-oriented metrics. This work provides an initial framework for evaluating the robustness of supportive and safe behavior in small LLMs under different forms of prompt manipulation.
filter_reasoning: The paper investigates the robustness and manipulation of LLM supportive behaviors in high-stakes mental health contexts.

venue_name: Proceedings of the Fifth Workshop on NLP for Positive Impact (NLP4PI)
title: Measuring Public Perceptions of the Social Impacts of Artificial Intelligence in YouTube Discourse
abstract: Public discourse can show which consequences people associate with Artificial Intelligence (AI), which groups they expect to be affected, and whether they interpret those consequences as benefits or threats. We analyze public perceptions of AI's social impacts across $n=98,413$ YouTube comments collected from 2022 to 2025 using a two-stage LLM pipeline that filters neutral and off-topic content before annotating target sentiment, fear, sarcasm, and emotion. Target sentiment achieves Quadratic Weighted Kappa (QWK) $=0.738$ against a human-labeled sample. In exploratory keyword-defined subsets, safety and human-control comments exhibit the highest fear (0.659) and most negative sentiment ($-0.521$), while comments mentioning children, families, and workers are more threat-oriented than those mentioning students and teachers. Negative sentiment remains common among the retained evaluative comments, but whether it rises or falls over time depends on how videos are weighted. Interestingly, sentiment changes near product releases are comparable to those at placebo dates. These results can help direct future research and policy attention toward the concerns most visible in public discourse, especially as a starting point for validation with affected groups.
filter_reasoning: The paper analyzes public perceptions of the social impacts and threats associated with AI, which falls under AI ethics as it relates to societal implications of the technology.

venue_name: Proceedings of the Fifth Workshop on NLP for Positive Impact (NLP4PI)
title: On the Neutrality of Model Confidence in German and English Gender-Bias Benchmarks
abstract: Confidence, the probability a model assigns to its prediction, is commonly treated as a signal for correctness, and is central to quality monitoring and selective question answering. We ask whether this signal is neutral with respect to social stereotypes. A model's confidence may reflect correctness well overall and yet be higher where its answers align with a stereotype and detecting this requires comparing confidence across stereotype directions. We investigate this on the gender subset of Bias Benchmark for Question Answering (BBQ) in English and in German (GG-BBQ), evaluating 22 base and instruction-tuned models from five providers. For some models, we find small but directionally consistent effects for both ambiguous and disambiguated questions, suggesting that confidence-based selection can favour stereotype-aligned content and that confidence is worth examining alongside answer-based scores in bias evaluations on multiple-choice questions.
filter_reasoning: The paper investigates gender bias in model confidence levels, which directly relates to the fairness and transparency of AI decisions.

venue_name: Proceedings of the Fifth Workshop on NLP for Positive Impact (NLP4PI)
title: SEAL: SocioEconomic Alignment in LLMs
abstract: According to the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, socioeconomic inequality is one of the defining challenges of the 21st century, as it shapes access to resources and opportunities across societies worldwide. As large language models (LLMs) become widely used for everyday tasks, they have the potential to create positive social impact by expanding access to information, education, writing support, employment guidance, and administrative assistance. However, this potential depends on whether such systems perform equally well for users from different socioeconomic backgrounds. In this paper, we evaluate LLM-generated responses to prompts written by users across socioeconomic groups (lower, middle, and higher), examining disparities in helpfulness, sycophancy, human likeness, emotion, and text complexity. We find differences in quality of service across socioeconomic statuses (SES): lower-SES groups receive responses that are less helpful, less complex, less assertive, more negative in sentiment, less trust-oriented, and more sycophantically validating.
filter_reasoning: The paper evaluates socioeconomic bias (fairness) in LLM-generated responses, which is a core topic in AI ethics.

venue_name: Proceedings of the Fifth Workshop on NLP for Positive Impact (NLP4PI)
title: Uncertainty Quantification to Improve the Reliability of LLM-Based Hate Speech Detection
abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) have been tested for hate speech detection, their reliability in subjective annotation settings remains underexplored. Existing improved prompting approaches for hate speech classification often rely on continuous context retrieval, which can be computationally expensive and unnecessary for confident predictions. To address this, we propose an uncertainty-aware prompting pipeline that integrates Uncertainty Quantification (UQ) into LLM-based hate speech classification. The framework uses uncertainty scores to identify ambiguous and potentially unreliable predictions through threshold-based filtering, enabling selective application of advanced context-enriched prompting only when needed. We evaluate the approach on two benchmark datasets---Measuring Hate Speech (Sachdeva et al., 2022) and CREHate (Lee et al., 2024---across five LLMs using two advanced prompting strategies: Persona-Aware and Annotation-Grounded Few-Shot Prompting. Experimental results show that the proposed pipeline consistently improves classification performance and reduces uncertainty, leading to more reliable model behavior with improved computational efficiency.
filter_reasoning: The paper implements an uncertainty-aware framework to improve the reliability and robustness of hate-speech detection, which is a core AI safety concern.

venue_name: Proceedings of the Fifth Workshop on NLP for Positive Impact (NLP4PI)
title: Whose Good, Whose Place? The Moral Geography of Agentic AI for Social Good
abstract: Agentic AI systems are increasingly proposed for social-good domains, often invoking the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Yet such claims do not necessarily establish accountability to the communities these systems aim to serve. We present a structured survey of 112 papers on agentic AI for social good published between 2015 and 2026. Each paper is coded across eight dimensions using dual-LLM annotation (GPT-4o and Llama-3.3-70B) with stratified human validation on 50 papers.\par We identify a moral-geographic asymmetry: contextual underspecification is concentrated where local context matters most. Overall, 82 of 112 papers (73\%) specify no geographic context. Papers aligned with health or physical/ecological SDGs name a geography 37--40\% of the time, compared with only 13\% for institutional and social-policy SDGs, and 0\% under strict coding that requires a concrete country, city, region, or population ($\chi^2(2)=8.78$, $p=.012$, Cram\'er's $V=.283$; strict: $\chi^2(2)=7.60$, $p=.022$, $V=.263$). The pattern is robust across seven of eight sensitivity analyses. SDG~16 is both the most-covered goal and the least geographically specified.\par We interpret this pattern as consistent with a form of moral abstraction: institutional good is framed more universally despite its dependence on local political, legal, and cultural conditions. Only 28 papers (25\%) report any real-world deployment or small-scale test. We detect no statistically significant differences in deployment rates across architecture, era, or geographic specificity. We conclude with five accountability gaps and a minimal reporting standard for more context-specific, participatory, and accountable research.
filter_reasoning: The paper conducts a meta-analysis of accountability and the 'moral geography' of AI for social good, which is fundamental to AI ethics and governance.

venue_name: Proceedings of the Fifth Workshop on NLP for Positive Impact (NLP4PI)
title: Aligned for Whom? A Brazilian Research Agenda for Culturally Grounded AI Safety Evaluation
abstract: Frontier models were constructed within a few specific cultural and linguistic contexts and validated against a particular set of values. We argue this limitation operates at three levels: technical (safety evaluations fail silently in non-English languages), theoretical (alignment frameworks inherit an implicit universalism about human values that obscures cross-cultural variation), and governance (the power to declare a model safe remains concentrated in private laboratories unaccountable to the populations they affect). Brazilian Portuguese, spoken by over 215 million people, sits at the intersection of these three failures. We propose a Brazilian research agenda structured around three fronts: (i) culturally-grounded dangerous capability benchmarks constructed participatorily in Brazilian Portuguese; (ii) adaptive evaluation methodologies that keep evaluation responsive to evolving models and locally defined risks; and (iii) a distributed safety evaluation infrastructure in which nationally accountable institutions assess frontier models before large-scale deployment.
filter_reasoning: The paper argues for a culturally grounded, participatory approach to AI safety, focusing on the ethical and political implications of current universalist AI alignment frameworks.

venue_name: Proceedings of the Second International Conference on Natural Language Processing and Artificial Intelligence for Cyber Security
title: From Detection to Attribution: Forensic Linguistics and Adversarial Red Teaming as Complementary Responses to LLM Misuse
abstract: The proliferation of Large Language Models (LLMs) has enabled the automation of cyber-attacks (including phishing, social engineering, and impersonation) at unprecedented scale, while existing safeguards remain routinely circumvented. Current detection approaches, predominantly based on stylometric and machine learning methods, face fundamental limitations against adaptive adversaries and struggle with the implicit, contextual, and pragmatic dimensions of language. This article proposes forensic linguistic analysis grounded in the theory of idiolect as a complementary approach to LLM-generated text detection and attribution. We adopt a red teaming methodology to generate synthetic toxic texts that bypass model guardrails to create controlled conditions for testing whether qualitative forensic analysis can succeed where quantitative approaches falter. The findings of our stylometric, character n-gram, and cluster analysis converge to provide moderate evidence that stylometric approaches succeed in discriminating authorship. However, they are not conclusive and hence fall short of current admissibility criteria across diverse jurisdictions. The article thus concludes that idiolect-based forensic analysis can distinguish genuine authorship from LLM-generated impersonation, even when surface features are manipulated. We discuss implications for legal and investigative contexts, where interpretable, theoretically-grounded expert analysis is required over black-box classifier outputs.
filter_reasoning: The paper directly addresses the misuse of LLMs for cyber-attacks and discusses detection and attribution mechanisms, which is a core safety concern.

venue_name: Proceedings of the Second International Conference on Natural Language Processing and Artificial Intelligence for Cyber Security
title: The Human Attack Surface: Detecting Psychological Vulnerabilities to Cyber Threats using AI and Social Media
abstract: Mental health is a crucial factor influencing overall human well-being, and in the digital age, psychological vulnerabilities have increasingly become a critical human attack surface for cyber threats. Individuals experiencing mental health disorders such as depression or anxiety are demonstrably more susceptible to targeted cyber exploitation, including social engineering, phishing, and digital coercion. In response to this intersection of psychological well-being and human-centric cybersecurity, this study explores the use of social media data for the prediction and classification of mental health conditions to identify vulnerable populations, alongside the development of a secure AI-assisted support system. We analyze and combine three datasets to construct a unified dataset of 14 classes, enabling fine-grained risk assessment for conditions including depression, anxiety, and suicidal ideation. For classification, Logistic Regression significantly outperforms Multinomial Naive Bayes, achieving an accuracy of 95\% compared to 74\%. To bridge the gap between detection and intervention, the system integrates a conversational module powered by LLaMA 2 (7B). Activated when severe risk is detected, this module provides context-aware interaction to support individuals and mitigate their vulnerability to both psychological crisis and digital exploitation. Deployed via Streamlit, this research serves as an assistive tool for professionals, highlighting the potential of combining machine learning with conversational AI to secure the human element against multifaceted digital and cognitive threats.
filter_reasoning: The paper deals with detecting vulnerabilities and the potential for AI exploitation in a safety/security context, fitting into the technical challenges of AI safety.

venue_name: Proceedings of the Second International Conference on Natural Language Processing and Artificial Intelligence for Cyber Security
title: A Linguistic Analysis of Prompt Injection in Large Language Models
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed across a wide range of applications, from conversational assistants to decision support systems. However, these systems remain vulnerable to prompt injection attacks, in which carefully crafted inputs manipulate model behavior and circumvent intended safeguards. While existing research has largely approached prompt injection as a technical or security problem, the linguistic mechanisms through which such attacks operate remain insufficiently understood. In this paper, we argue that prompt injection attacks are fundamentally linguistic in nature, exploiting discourse structure, pragmatic framing, and instruction hierarchies encoded in natural language prompts. Drawing on concepts from speech act theory, discourse analysis, and pragmatics, we propose a typology of four linguistic strategies used to manipulate Large Language Models: instruction override, role framing, hypothetical framing, and procedural prompting. Through detailed linguistic analysis of representative examples, we demonstrate how each strategy exploits identifiable properties of natural language interaction to reshape model interpretation and influence output generation. For each strategy, we also discuss implications for detection and mitigation, arguing that effective safeguards must attend to discourse-level patterns in prompts rather than relying solely on surface-level keyword filtering. Our findings contribute to emerging research at the intersection of computational linguistics and AI security and highlight the importance of integrating linguistic expertise into the design of more robust and reliable language-based AI systems.
filter_reasoning: Prompt injection is a classic AI safety and robustness research area focusing on circumventing model safeguards.

venue_name: Proceedings of the Second International Conference on Natural Language Processing and Artificial Intelligence for Cyber Security
title: Grieve-JA: A Psycholinguistic Dictionary for Grievance-Fuelled Language in Japanese
abstract: Since the early 2010s, internet nationalists have been active on Japanese forums, blogs, and social networking services, spreading hate speech and conspiracy. At the same, the involuntary celibate community has gained international notoriety due to acts of mass violence committed by self-identified members. Despite several instances of misogyny motivated violence in Japan, there is little known about Japanese involuntary celibate culture and identity. This paper introduces Grieve-JA, a psycholinguistic dictionary for the analysis of violence, threat, and grievance in Japanese text. The paper outlines the process of developing the dictionary and evaluating it across different corpora representing both neutral and grievance-filled language. As a final measure, the dictionary is used to compare comments from two forums on the Japanese anonymous message board 5channel with comments from Bluesky. Results indicate that Grieve-JA is a useful tool for analyzing extreme language in Japanese as a complement to other psycholinguistic measures.
filter_reasoning: The paper focuses on developing tools to analyze hate speech and violent rhetoric, contributing to the ethics of content monitoring and analysis.

venue_name: Proceedings of the Second International Conference on Natural Language Processing and Artificial Intelligence for Cyber Security
title: Judging the LLM Judges: A Human-Centric Validation of LLM-Generated Training Data for Software Retrieval
abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly generate training data for downstream machine learning systems, the quality of this synthetic data becomes a critical security concern. Low-quality synthetic training data can silently poison retrieval systems deployed in security-sensitive contexts such as software issue triage, user support, and threat intelligence matching. We present a multi-dimensional quality assessment protocol for LLM-generated synthetic training data and apply it to a case study involving 13,579 synthetic user reviews generated from GitHub issues across four open-source Android applications. We evaluate 400 stratified samples using an LLM judge (GPT-4o-mini) along a five-point rubric, find that 10.5\% of generated reviews fail to meaningfully capture their source issues, and identify systematic failure patterns concentrated in developer-internal issues (continuous integration, refactoring) and sarcastic persona framings. To validate the LLM judge against human annotation, we compute Cohen's Kappa between one human rater, a second independent human rater, and the LLM judge on 20 stratified reviews. Our results highlight the need for hybrid human-AI protocols when assessing synthetic data quality for security-critical applications.
filter_reasoning: The paper investigates the security concerns of synthetic data poisoning in security-sensitive systems, which relates to the robustness and reliability of AI training pipelines.

venue_name: Proceedings of the Second International Conference on Natural Language Processing and Artificial Intelligence for Cyber Security
title: Partner Attribution Bias in LLM-Assisted Export Control Screening
abstract: Abstract Automating export control screening with large language models (LLMs) introduces risks of contextual sensitivity to non-technical signals, including partner country identity. This paper presents a reproducible counterfactual framework for diagnosing how partner country information influences LLM compliance decisions across five instruction-tuned models and 249 jurisdictions. Across four controlled experiments, partner identity systematically alters export control classifications even when project content is held constant or removed entirely, with BRICS and GCC partners attracting consistently higher control rates than EU and Five Eyes collaborations. Under causal partner controls, classification deltas become small and statistically non-significant, suggesting that observed disparities reflect contextual cue sensitivity rather than fixed geopolitical bias, though residual associative priors cannot be fully excluded. Model-level analysis reveals qualitatively distinct behavioural patterns, including directionally opposite responses to identical inputs across architectures, indicating that model selection carries consequences beyond accuracy in compliance-sensitive deployments. A structured two-stage prompting protocol reduces decision volatility by 60--80\% while preserving interpretability. The proposed framework provides an auditable diagnostic method for evaluating contextual sensitivity in regulated AI systems and offers practical guidance for accountable compliance automation.
filter_reasoning: The paper explicitly investigates and provides a framework to mitigate algorithmic bias (partner identity sensitivity) in high-stakes automated compliance screening.

venue_name: Proceedings of the Seventh Workshop on Natural Language Processing and Computational Social Science
title: Prompt Perturbations Reveal Human-Like Biases in Large Language Model Survey Responses
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used as proxies for human subjects in social science surveys, but their reliability and susceptibility to known human-like response biases, such as $central tendency, opinion floating$ and $primacy bias$ are poorly understood. This work investigates the response robustness of LLMs in normative survey contexts---we test 18 LLMs on questions taken from the World Values Survey (WVS), applying a comprehensive set of ten perturbations to both question phrasing and answer option structure, resulting in over 334,800 simulated survey interviews. In doing so, we not only reveal LLMs' vulnerabilities to perturbations but also show that almost all tested models exhibit a consistent $recency bias$, disproportionately favoring the last-presented answer option. While larger models are generally more robust, all models remain sensitive to semantic variations like paraphrasing and to combined perturbations. This underscores the critical importance of prompt design and robustness testing when using LLMs to generate synthetic survey data.
filter_reasoning: The paper investigates human-like response biases and robustness in LLMs, directly relevant to the ethical evaluation and reliability of AI systems.

venue_name: Proceedings of the Seventh Workshop on Natural Language Processing and Computational Social Science
title: Towards More Transparent Online Campaigning: Detecting Political Campaign Content in Election-related Social Media Posts
abstract: A large part of political campaigns during elections is now being conducted online, with political actors leveraging their networks on social media platforms. To maintain transparency in political communications, regulations applicable to online campaigning have been put in place in many democracies. While it should be straightforward for voters to determine who produced and funded online advertisements comprising paid political campaigns, it is much more challenging to detect if organic content, i.e., social media posts, pertains to political campaigning, due to possibly subtle yet suggestive language that can be used by certain actors. In this paper, we investigate the feasibility of automatically detecting whether a given tweet posted by a political actor pertains to political campaigning, and if yes, whether it was conveyed in a direct or indirect (subtle) manner. After establishing an annotation scheme for the task of detecting political campaign content in tweets, we fine-tuned three encoder models (BERT, BERTweet and PoliBERTweet) for the same task and evaluated their performance. Our results show that fine-tuning BERTweet leads to the best macro-averaged F1-score (0.776), although all models consistently struggle to detect indirect campaigning.
filter_reasoning: The paper addresses transparency and regulation in online political campaigning, which is a major concern in the ethics of AI governance.

venue_name: Proceedings of the Seventh Workshop on Natural Language Processing and Computational Social Science
title: The Hidden Language of Harm: Examining the Role of Emojis in Harmful Online Communication and Content Moderation
abstract: Social media platforms have become central to modern communication, yet they also harbor offensive content that challenges platform safety and inclusivity. While prior research has primarily focused on textual indicators of offense, the role of emojis, ubiquitous visual elements in online discourse, remains underexplored. Emojis, despite being rarely offensive in isolation, can acquire harmful meanings through symbolic associations, sarcasm, and contextual misuse. In this work, we systematically examine emoji contributions to offensive Twitter messages, analyzing their distribution across offense categories and how users exploit emoji ambiguity. To address this, we propose an LLM-powered, multi-step moderation pipeline that selectively replaces harmful emojis while preserving the tweet's semantic intent. Human evaluations demonstrate that our approach effectively reduces offensiveness while preserving semantic integrity. Our analysis also reveals heterogeneous effects across offense types, offering nuanced insights for online communication and emoji moderation.
filter_reasoning: The paper focuses on AI content moderation and making systems safer by addressing implicit harmful content (emoji-based harm), which falls under AI safety/robustness.

venue_name: Proceedings of the fifth edition of NLPerspectives
title: An Overview of Current Practices and Recommendations for Working with Stereotypes in NLP
abstract: This article presents a discussion on the main challenges and considerations involved in addressing stereotypes within Natural Language Processing (NLP), and proposes a set of guidelines and recommendations for their treatment in research and resource development. On the one hand, the growing interest in fairness, bias mitigation, and inclusivity has led to an increasing number of studies and datasets dealing with stereotypes; on the other hand, their conceptualization and operationalization remain highly heterogeneous across works. The aim of this article is therefore twofold: (1) to provide a concise yet comprehensive overview of existing annotation schemes highlighting their key features and offering a comparative analysis and (2) to propose a set of tentative guidelines and recommendations to foster clarity when working with stereotypes in NLP. Furthermore, as a case study, we conduct an annotation exercise of a subset of texts from the QUEEREOTYPES dataset, containing stereotypes targeting LGBTQIA+ people, using all labels proposed in prior work to assess their clarity, overlap, and practical usefulness.
filter_reasoning: The paper provides guidelines and recommendations for handling stereotypes and bias in NLP research, a core topic in AI ethics.

venue_name: Proceedings of the fifth edition of NLPerspectives
title: GSI:detect - A Perspectivist Approach to Gender Stereotypes Identification in Italian
abstract: The deconstruction of gender stereotypes is essential to prevent discrimination, marginalization and gender-based violence. Despite the increasing attention to this issue, research in this field often focuses on explicitly sexist or hateful communication, leaving out all the cases where stereotypes are produced unconsciously or even with apparently positive intentions. Moreover, the identification and analysis of gender stereotypes is often a very subjective task, heavily influenced by the researcher's background, beliefs and personal sensitivity. In this context GSI:detect, a dataset for gender stereotypes identification in Italian, has been annotated following a perspectivist approach that gives value to the different points of view of four annotators. It has been designed to address (i) the lack of resources focusing on naturally occurring and non-hateful language conveying implicit or ambiguous forms of gender stereotypes, and (ii) the scarcity of datasets that can capture multiple interpretations as well as the inherent variation and disagreement in human perception. Baseline experiments with several LLMs confirm the challenging nature and value of such a linguistic resource, revealing both apparent differences and limitations in performance among the evaluated models, and raising questions about the extent to which current LLMs are suitable for detection and classification tasks in this field. Content warning: Examples taken from the GSI:detect dataset may contain sensitive or potentially distressing content.
filter_reasoning: The paper directly addresses the identification of gender stereotypes and the deconstruction of bias, which falls squarely under AI ethics.

venue_name: Proceedings of the fifth edition of NLPerspectives
title: Quantifying and Predicting Disagreement in Graded Human Ratings
abstract: It is increasingly recognized that humans do not always agree, and disagreement is inherent in many annotation tasks. However, not all items in a given task elicit the same level of opinion divergence. In this paper, we study the extent to which item-level annotation variation and variation structure can be captured from text features, focusing on inappropriate language detection, including offensive language, hate speech, and toxic language detection. We model annotation variation to assess whether the degree of annotation divergence can be predicted from item-level textual features. We also propose the Opposition Index, a metric that quantifies the extent of opposing stances among annotators based on their Likert ratings.
filter_reasoning: The research focuses on annotator disagreement in the context of offensive, hate, and toxic language detection, which is central to AI ethics.

venue_name: Proceedings of the fifth edition of NLPerspectives
title: SubData: Bridging Heterogeneous Datasets to Enable Theory-Driven Evaluation of Political and Demographic Perspectives in LLMs
abstract: As increasingly capable large language models (LLMs) emerge, researchers have begun exploring their potential for subjective tasks. While recent work demonstrates that LLMs can be aligned with diverse human perspectives, evaluating this alignment on downstream tasks (e.g., hate speech detection) remains challenging due to the use of inconsistent datasets across studies. To address this issue, in this resource paper we propose a two-step framework: we (1) introduce SubData, an open-source Python library designed for standardizing heterogeneous datasets to evaluate LLMs perspective alignment; and (2) present a theory-driven approach leveraging this library to test how differently-aligned LLMs (e.g., aligned with different political viewpoints) classify content targeting specific demographics. SubData's flexible mapping and taxonomy enable customization for diverse research needs, distinguishing it from existing resources. We illustrate its usage with an example application and invite contributions to extend our initial release into a multi-construct benchmark suite for evaluating LLMs perspective alignment on natural language processing tasks.
filter_reasoning: The study focuses on evaluating 'perspective alignment' and political/demographic bias in LLMs, which is a key topic in AI ethics.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 3rd Workshop on KNOwledge GRaphs Agentic Systems Interplay (NORA 2026)
title: Failure Modes of Imperfect Relational Context in LLM Document Extraction
abstract: LLM-based extraction pipelines increasingly consume relational context produced upstream, for example by a heuristic linker, a retrieval step, or another model. We study how imperfect relations between document entities affect LLM extraction on FUNSD, a benchmark of scanned forms. Using identical instructions in every condition, four LLMs receive a form's entities with no relations (Flat), relations from a heuristic linker (Heuristic), gold relations (Oracle), or relations that are almost all wrong (Deranged). In a secondary contrast, gold relations raise accuracy for every model (4.0 to 7.9 percentage points, pp). Heuristic and deranged relations lower accuracy by 8 to 25 pp for three models, while GPT-5 shows significantly smaller effects. Comparing the same questions across conditions shows what lies behind the drops. Wrong edges are associated with answers copied from a different field, and missing edges with more blank answers even though the answer text is still present. These patterns appear under two prompt variants, but the prompts were developed on this corpus and every result is a single generation, so we treat the prompt comparison as exploratory.
filter_reasoning: The paper studies the robustness and failure modes of LLMs when dealing with imperfect input context, which is relevant to the reliability of AI systems in safety-critical pipelines.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 3rd Workshop on KNOwledge GRaphs Agentic Systems Interplay (NORA 2026)
title: KG-SFT Contracts: Auditing Evidence Lineage and Loader Retention in Enterprise RAG Adaptation
abstract: KG-assisted supervised fine-tuning depends on evidence selection, context compilation, and data loading. We present KG-SFT Contracts, a provenance-aware interface that audits these stages and links model comparisons to their data and scoring records. In a retrospective Russian enterprise case, a pool of 484 graph candidates contributed no graph-origin distractors to the compiled corpus, and exact loader replay discarded 40 of 946 intended examples before splitting. Removing annotated non-support context restored every row while preserving questions, targets, and verified support. Downstream comparisons remained statistically inconclusive. Controlled checks on a public graph-bearing fixture show how cross-record validation detects unresolved graph references and conflicting source revisions alongside role-aware repair. The installable implementation includes fixture-level CPU measurements, incremental adoption guidance, and an official RuBQ schema-import check. The case illustrates how lineage and retention audits make adaptation pipelines inspectable before model effects are attributed to their configured inputs.
filter_reasoning: The paper focuses on auditing evidence lineage and data retention in RAG pipelines, which is a technical contribution to the interpretability and reliability (safety) of AI systems.

title: Enhancing Factuality and Transparency in Generative Models for Biomedical Question Answering
abstract: Biomedical Question Answering (BQA) systems are vital for providing clinicians and researchers with efficient access to large amount of biomedical scientific studies. Existing automated BQA models, however, often rely on complex hybrid architectures to handle diverse question and answer formats, leading to inefficiency and high complexity. While domain-specific generative language models like BioBART offer a unified and simplified alternative capable of producing fluent human-like responses, they are prone to hallucination and lack interpretability, undermining their trustworthiness in critical healthcare domains. To address these limitations, this work introduces an enhanced model that augments BioBART with a pointer network for accurate token copying and a novel Keyphrase Filter (KPF) to guide attention toward critical information during generation. Experimental results on the BioASQ challenge demonstrate that the proposed Pointer-KPF model significantly outperforms the baseline BioBART, particularly on metrics for ideal answers. Furthermore, our evaluation shows that the model enhances transparency: pointer-guided attention heatmaps reveal improved input-output alignment, while keyphrase scores act as saliency maps to identify the most influential input segments. This approach not only reduces hallucination by strengthening textual grounding but also provides crucial insights into the model's reasoning, thereby increasing confidence and trust in its outputs.
filter_reasoning: The paper explicitly addresses hallucination reduction and interpretability in biomedical QA, focusing on increasing the trustworthiness and grounding of model outputs.

title: Towards Efficient Self-Explainable Climate-Related Claim Verification with Generative Models
abstract: In this work, we present an empirical investigation into two self-explanatory inference paradigms using pre-trained language models with different sizes, based on our participation in the ClimateCheck@NSLP 2026 shared task on climate-related claim verification. This task aims to address the increasing amount of climate misinformation and disinformation on social media, emphasizing the importance of basing claims on reliable scientific evidence. Our study investigates the impact of different explanation strategies on entailment-based verification performance in scientific claim verification, while analyzing the trade-off between reasoning complexity and computational efficiency.
filter_reasoning: The paper explores self-explainable inference paradigms for claim verification, which relates to the safety goal of building more transparent and verifiable AI systems.

venue_name: The Proceedings of the Workshop on Open Reasoning Across Cultures Languages (ORACLE)
title: Does Safety Reasoning Travel? A Multilingual Measurement of Prompt-Injection Attacks and Runtime Monitors in Tool-Using LLM Agents
abstract: It is widely assumed that translating an attack into a lower-resource language makes a language model more vulnerable, and it is natural to expect the same for tool-using agents: an English-built runtime monitor should lose coverage when the same indirect prompt injection is mounted in another language. We test this directly. Using AgentDojo with two models, six languages (English, French, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili), and a fixed, strictly paired 320-scenario sample per cell (3,840 attack trajectories, zero execution errors), we measure attack success, attack-pattern entropy, and cross-lingual transfer of a mined tool-call monitor. Every reported number is re-derived from raw trajectories by an independent verifier (965/965 checks pass). The expected result does not appear. Translating the injection lowers attack success by 3--6\texttimes while task utility rises; attack tool-call structure does not disperse with linguistic distance; and an Englishmined monitor loses no recall across languages once it is evaluated out-of-sample. We further show that the natural in-sample evaluation of a mined monitor manufactures a clean-looking coverage-bound failure that is entirely an artifact of memorization, and that three machinetranslation pipeline defects each independently manufacture a spurious ``safety does not travel'' effect. A pre-registered paraphrase control narrows but does not overturn the finding: a measurable, model-dependent minority (17--33\%) of the drop is surface-form instruction fragility rather than language. We conclude that the multilingual-jailbreak result does not reproduce at the agent layer on this benchmark, and we distill the measurement pitfalls that would have produced the opposite, and wrong, conclusion.
filter_reasoning: This paper directly evaluates prompt-injection attacks, model vulnerability, and the effectiveness of runtime safety monitors, which is core to AI safety research.

venue_name: The Proceedings of the Workshop on Open Reasoning Across Cultures Languages (ORACLE)
title: Mining Motifs in Fairy Tales
abstract: A motif is a pattern that appears across stories, tales, or legends, such as ``a prince falls in love with commoner''. We propose a method based on large language models to extract such motifs automatically from stories. Our approach addresses challenges such as motif synonymy, and achieves high alignment with expert-annotated ground truth. We illustrate the utility of our extraction in downstream applications such as mitigating gender bias in existing motif collections, studying narrative event sequences, quantifying cross-regional story similarity, validating the correlation between linguistically related cultures, and tracing the relatedness of religious traditions.
filter_reasoning: The paper's main contribution involves using AI to mitigate gender bias in narrative collections, which falls under AI ethics.

venue_name: The Proceedings of the Workshop on Open Reasoning Across Cultures Languages (ORACLE)
title: Probing the Think--Say Gap on Sensitive Concepts in Chinese and English Open LLMs
abstract: Open large language models (LLMs) trained under different alignment regimes treat politically sensitive concepts (freedom, democracy, human rights) differently, but outputs alone cannot separate alignment-induced suppression from pretraining culture: a model may withhold what it internally represents, or may simply reproduce the distribution it was trained on. We compare a Chinese-developed model (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) with an Englishdeveloped baseline (Gemma-3-12B-IT) on 360 bilingual, minimally contrastive items with a country-swap control (China vs. a matched democracy, Germany), using Natural Language Autoencoders to verbalize hidden states so that models with incommensurable representation spaces can be compared through text. Both models linearly encode a sensitive-vsneutral direction at the sentence-final state, beyond emotional salience and in both languages. Their behavior, however, diverges sharply: the Chinese model is China-specifically suppressive, justifying restrictions on political grounds far more for China than for a matched democracy, while the English model shows the reverse. The internal side remains inconclusive. Read before the model answers, the state does not support a reliable judgment of whether critical content is present, so we do not claim a think--say gap and identify extraction during generation as the decisive next test.
filter_reasoning: The paper investigates the 'think-say' gap and ideological bias (political suppression) in large language models, which is a core topic in AI ethics.

venue_name: The Proceedings of the Workshop on Open Reasoning Across Cultures Languages (ORACLE)
title: Tokenization Sets the Measurement Scale for Cross-Lingual Diagnostics
abstract: Multilingual evaluation treats translated passages as the same input in different languages, and increasingly reads an internal diagnostic off the model while doing so. Tokenization can make that assumption false before the model answers, because the same passage occupies several times as many token positions in one language as in another, so a fixed window gives the model different amounts of text and gives the attention graph behind the diagnostic a different number of nodes. We derive a comparability criterion from the descriptors' own definitions: on a parallel corpus the tokenizer sets the graph order, so a descriptor whose attainable range grows with graph order can separate languages while measuring segmentation rather than model computation, and because those ranges are analytic the criterion can be checked before any measurement is taken. Replaying a standard analysis against the audited one changes the answer, since most of its significant associations do not survive and about one in five reverse sign. The failures concentrate in the descriptors the criterion flags in advance rather than in spectral descriptors as such, and the same split appears among interpretability descriptors that use no graph at all. Applied to high frequency energy over 60 Belebele languages and three tokenizer matched Llama models, the audit leaves the resource associated profile varying across depth and withdraws the stronger readings the raw profiles invite, among them a stable peak layer, a replicated profile shape, a stable mid-depth effect and a causal mechanism. The practical consequence is that a cross-lingual comparison should establish that its measurements are in comparable units before it reports a difference.
filter_reasoning: The paper audits interpretability descriptors and diagnostic methods used in AI, which is critical for ensuring these tools provide valid insights into model behavior.

venue_name: The Proceedings of the Workshop on Open Reasoning Across Cultures Languages (ORACLE)
title: Recognized but Not Produced: A Generation Benchmark for Culturally Specific Kinship Terms
abstract: Current literature evaluates large language models (LLMs) on multilingual kinship understanding using multiple-choice benchmarks, treating it as a recognition problem. We instead prompt five open-weight LLMs to generate kinship terms in three non-Western languages (Hindi, Tamil, and Korean) across two communicative tasks, and pair this with a matched option-supported selection baseline. On identical relation--language cells, GPT-OSS120B selects the correct term in 90.67\% of 75 valid cells but produces an accepted term in 36.00\% of the corresponding attempts; Llama3.3-70B shows the same pattern (77.92\% versus 24.24\%). Since the four-option condition displays the candidate terms and does not require script production, the difference is interpreted as an evaluation-format gap rather than direct proof that lexical knowledge is intact. On explicitly specified L3 prompts, accuracy varies sharply, from GLM-5.1 at 72.29\% to Llama3.3-70B at 24.24\%. The paternal-lineage advantage is language-specific: it is large in Hindi, but weak or reversed in Korean, while Tamil shared-term pairs provide a control for measurement variation. These results show that culturally specific kinship generation remains difficult even when the relationship is explicitly stated and motivate generation-based evaluation alongside multiple-choice testing.
filter_reasoning: The paper explores how models represent culturally specific knowledge and addresses potential gaps in fairness/representation across different linguistic/cultural groups.

venue_name: The Proceedings of the Workshop on Open Reasoning Across Cultures Languages (ORACLE)
title: Cross Lingual Transfer in Tulu Legal Comprehension: Script-Dependent Improvement and RAG-Induced Knowledge Conflict
abstract: Low-resource languages without an adequate training corpus often use a related, higherresource language as a scaffold for comprehension. Still, there is a need to develop rigorous evaluation methods to identify when models fail in cross lingual low-resource environments. Using the legal domain as a backdrop, three models (Llama3, Hex-1, Sarvam) were tested on the ability to classify legal complaints written in a low resource Dravidian language (Tulu). Transliterating queries across Dravidian scripts allowed models to gain a preliminary understanding of speakers' complaints without the use of wide scale training, though the level of comprehension was heavily script dependent (with Kannada - another relatively low-resource language - producing the strongest positive trend). Retrieving from a corpus of Kannada legal papers across a RAG framework caused mixed results. Some models had a weak positive trend in comprehension under certain conditions, but when models failed, it was often across two axes: fact substitution (fixating on specific passage excerpts that skewed reasoning) and confabulation (hallucination that had no basis in either query or corpus). Within low resource domains, results identify the model's parsing of information and subsequent reasoning as the source of reasoning failure, rather than corpus contents. Script-dependent comprehension and RAG robustness also seem to travel together. This is further supported by the reasoning-trace analysis and a statistical-honesty framework deployed - techniques that are more broadly applicable to low-resource multilingual RAG evaluation.
filter_reasoning: The paper focuses on evaluating robustness and failure modes (fact substitution, confabulation) in RAG systems, which is central to AI safety.

venue_name: The 7th Workshop on Open-Source Arabic Corpora and Processing Tools (OSACT7) with 5 Shared Tasks
title: ARHAHA 2026: The Shared Task on Arabic Humor Automatic Generation
abstract: Humor generation remains one of the most challenging tasks in natural language processing, particularly in Arabic, where cultural context, dialectal variation, and linguistic nuances are central to comedic effect. In this paper, we present the ARHAHA 2026 shared task on constrained Arabic humor generation. The task requires systems to generate jokes that incorporate a given pair of words while adhering to safety and cultural constraints. We describe the task design, dataset construction, and evaluation framework, which combines automatic validation with human evaluation. Nine teams registered for the shared task; among them, three submitted final system outputs and two provided system description papers. Each participating system generated 1,200 Arabic jokes. For each system, a subset of 300 jokes was selected for evaluation by three independent annotators. The evaluation considered humor quality, originality, lexical constraint compliance, and safety. The results show that participating systems can produce safe and original content. However, generating genuinely humorous outputs remains difficult. The top-performing system was judged humorous in only 5.01\% of outputs, highlighting the inherent difficulty of computational humor generation. All three systems maintained very low rates of policy violations and stereotyping, demonstrating the effectiveness of constrained generation for safe content production. However, the very low humor rates indicate a substantial gap between generating fluent, constraint-compliant text and producing genuinely funny content. The top-performing system achieves stronger performance across originality, lexical compliance, and safety, resulting in a final score of 49.25, compared to 44.62 for the second-ranked system and 35.99 for the third-ranked system. These results reveal that humor generation, rather than safety or constraint adherence, is the dominant bottleneck in constrained Arabic humor generation.
filter_reasoning: The paper focuses on constrained generation techniques to ensure humor generation remains safe and avoids stereotyping.

venue_name: Proceedings of the First Workshop on Pluralistic AI NLP
title: LatAm-RT:Toward Culturally Adaptive Red Teaming for AI Safety in Latin America
abstract: Multilingual red-teaming benchmarks often reduce cultural localization to direct translation, overlooking sociotechnical factors shaping AI safety across contexts. By treating culturally distinct contexts as equivalent, this translation-centered approach can flatten regional diversity, obscure diverse perspectives, and reinforce single-ground-truth assumptions in AI safety evaluation. We present LatAm-RT, a context-aware red-teaming benchmark for incorporating Latin American cultural pluralism into AI safety evaluation. Its Layered Localization Taxonomy (LLT) models localization as an explicit experimental variable across three localization levels direct translation (L1), regional adaptation (L2), and national localization (L3) for Mexico, El Salvador, Costa Rica, and Chile while preserving comparable adversarial intent. We evaluate five language models using 284 prompts across three localization layers, four risk domains, and five adversarial framing strategies. Results show that localization is neither uniformly beneficial nor uniformly harmful: country-specific institutional vocabulary is associated with stronger safeguard activation in Privacy and Civic Systems, whereas politically situated narratives retain their adversarial effectiveness in Political and Information Harm. Adversarial framing remains the primary driver of attack success rate (ASR) variation, including a 55-percentage-point gap between GPT-4o and Claude Sonnet 4.6 under defensive framing. LatAm-RT introduces the Localization Effect (LE) to quantify regional robustness differences obscured by translation-based evaluations. These findings motivate pluralistic AI safety evaluation across culturally situated contexts. The dataset and annotation files are available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/Latam26/LatAmRT
filter_reasoning: The paper introduces a context-aware red-teaming benchmark to evaluate the robustness and safety of models across diverse Latin American cultural contexts.

venue_name: Proceedings of the First Workshop on Pluralistic AI NLP
title: BELIEFSIM: Towards Belief-Driven Simulation of Demographic Misinformation Susceptibility
abstract: Misinformation is a growing societal threat, and susceptibility to misinformative claims varies across demographic groups due to differences in underlying beliefs. As Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate human behaviors, we investigate whether they can simulate demographic misinformation susceptibility, treating beliefs as a primary driving factor. We introduce BeliefSim, a simulation framework that constructs survey-derived, demographic-group belief priors organized using a psychology-informed taxonomy. We study prompt-based conditioning and post-training adaptation, and conduct a multi-fold evaluation using: (i) susceptibility alignment and (ii) counterfactual demographic sensitivity. Across datasets PANDORA and MIST, belief priors improve susceptibility alignment, with larger gains on PANDORA. Finally, post-training adaptation reaches 92.4\% accuracy and improves cross-participant generalization.
filter_reasoning: The paper simulates demographic-group belief priors to study misinformation susceptibility, touching upon the social impact and safety of AI in spreading misinformation.

venue_name: Proceedings of the First Workshop on Pluralistic AI NLP
title: What is ``Cultural Representation'' in AI Benchmarks? A Multidimensional Evaluation Framework
abstract: Cultural representation is a prerequisite for the comprehensive evaluation of cultural competence in AI systems. Yet there is no shared, structured way to assess what cultural representation in AI benchmarks involves or how it can be measured. We address this gap by introducing a six-dimensional framework that assesses cultural representation through a structured, dimension-specific scoring instrument, enabling systematic comparison across benchmarks. Applying our framework to 50 benchmarks explicitly targeting culture, we find that none achieves broad coverage across all dimensions. While procedural dimensions such as transparency and bias awareness are comparatively well addressed, benchmarks consistently score lower in linguistic and geographic representation, thematic breadth, and the conceptual grounding of culture. Strikingly, only 32\% of benchmarks explicitly define culture, and annotator demographic information is absent in 82\% of cases. By making these properties measurable and directly comparable, our framework provides a practical foundation for designing and evaluating benchmarks that more validly assess cultural competence in AI systems.
filter_reasoning: The paper proposes a systematic framework for measuring and evaluating cultural representation in AI benchmarks, which is fundamental to AI ethics.

venue_name: Proceedings of the First Workshop on Pluralistic AI NLP
title: Better Reward Models Are Not Always Less Biased: Social Alignment Beyond Standard Reward Benchmarks
abstract: Reward models are central to LLM alignment, yet current benchmarks reveal little about how they represent diverse and sometimes competing social preferences. We extend reward-model evaluation to four socially consequential domains: bias, safety, morality, and ethical reasoning. Our analysis shows that strong benchmark performance can obscure important differences in social behavior. Models may avoid some stereotypes while reinforcing others, and aggregate bias scores can hide these opposing tendencies. We also find that stronger stereotype avoidance can come at the expense of contextual faithfulness, revealing a trade-off between social bias mitigation and sensitivity to context. Across a broad set of reward models, standard benchmark performance is only inconsistently related to socially aligned behavior. These results show that stronger reward models are not uniformly better at navigating pluralistic social expectations and motivate more direct evaluation of the social preferences encoded in reward models.
filter_reasoning: The paper evaluates social bias, morality, and ethical reasoning in reward models, identifying trade-offs between bias mitigation and context sensitivity.

venue_name: Proceedings of the First Workshop on Pluralistic AI NLP
title: Alignment Sharpens Elicited Label Distributions under Logit and Sampled Elicitation
abstract: Alignment may encourage a model to commit to one answer even when human judgments differ. We study this effect by comparing base and aligned checkpoints on ChaosNLI and Measuring Hate Speech using logit, sampled, and verbalized elicitation. Across eight model pairs from 7B to 32B, including a mixture-of-experts model, alignment lowers the entropy of logit-elicited label distributions. Sampled elicitation agrees on the three pairs tested. The effect survives prompt-format, answer-order, word-only, and task-compliance controls. Its implications for human fit are less straightforward: Jensen--Shannon distance worsens on ChaosNLI, but changes in both directions on the native MHS hate-speech task. Six of seven aligned checkpoints in the main sweep fit ChaosNLI annotations worse than a uniform predictor, yet temperature scaling to base mean entropy removes much of the base--aligned gap. Majority-label agreement also changes in both directions. Verbalized probabilities show a different pattern, with entropy increases and decreases across three families and substantial sensitivity to the prompt's numeric example in some base checkpoints. Staged comparisons of two Ai2 lineages further show that the contributions of SFT and DPO depend on task and prompt format. These results support a consistent sharpening effect under logit and sampled elicitation, while showing why entropy alone cannot establish whether alignment reduces a model's ability to represent human disagreement.
filter_reasoning: The paper investigates how alignment training impacts the model's representation of human disagreement and label distributions, relevant to value alignment.

venue_name: Proceedings of the First Workshop on Pluralistic Value Alignment of LLMs
title: StealthRL: Reinforcement Learning Paraphrase Attacks for Multi-Detector Evasion of AI-Text Detectors
abstract: AI-text detectors are increasingly used in high-stakes settings, but their robustness to meaning-preserving adversarial rewriting remains unclear. We introduce StealthRL, a reinforcement learning framework for stress-testing detectors with adaptive paraphrase attacks. StealthRL trains a paraphrase policy against a detector ensemble while enforcing semantic fidelity, then evaluates transfer to held-out detector families on the full filtered MAGE test pool. Across RoBERTa, Fast-DetectGPT, Binoculars, and MAGE, the resulting attack sharply degrades detection performance, driving mean TPR@1\%FPR down to 0.024 while retaining nontrivial semantic overlap and readable prose. The attack also transfers to detectors not used during training, indicating a broader robustness failure rather than overfitting to a single target model. We complement the main results with detector-score analysis, repeated-generation stability checks, and automatic and judge-based quality evaluation. Our findings suggest that current AI-text detectors remain brittle under adaptive paraphrasing pressure and motivate robustness evaluation at deployment-relevant operating points. Our code and the trained model checkpoint are publicly available.
filter_reasoning: The paper focuses on robustness and vulnerability testing of AI-text detection systems against adversarial paraphrasing attacks.

venue_name: Proceedings of the First Workshop on Pluralistic Value Alignment of LLMs
title: C-VoicesCompass: Evaluating Value Alignment of LLMs with Chinese Social Values
abstract: With the widespread deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs), safety evaluation within diverse cultural value contexts has emerged as a critical issue in AI safety research. Existing studies predominantly rely on Western value systems, such as Schwartz's theory of basic values, lacking systematic evaluation frameworks tailored to Chinese cultural values. To address this gap, C-VoicesCompass, a value alignment evaluation framework for LLMs is proposed oriented toward Chinese Social Values (CSV). The framework aims to assess the degree of LLM alignment across 12 CSV dimensions, and constructs the first human-annotated dataset, C-Voices to cover all 12 CSV dimensions, serving as a benchmark to investigate the self-annotation capacities of LLMs. Second, a lightweight value evaluator, C-VoicesEvaluator, is trained by employing an asymmetric loss function to enhance quantitative assessment precision. Finally, a value-oriented evaluation question set is developed to induce value-related responses from LLMs, enabling a systematic alignment evaluation. Experimental results show that the proposed multi-round cross-correction annotation strategy achieves annotation quality close to human annotation. Evaluations on eight mainstream LLMs reveal significant disparities in alignment and distinct value expression tendencies across the 12 dimensions. The evaluation framework has been developed for public testing at https://cvoices.net.
filter_reasoning: The paper establishes a framework for evaluating LLM alignment with Chinese social values, a core topic in the ethics and safety of culturally sensitive AI.

venue_name: Proceedings of the First Workshop on Pluralistic Value Alignment of LLMs
title: Country Name or Cultural Evidence? A Causal Audit of Population-Grounded Steering in Large Language Models
abstract: When a country name and an observed population distribution point in different directions, which does a large language model follow? We introduce a four-condition counterfactual audit comprising a no-cue baseline, a country label, matched population evidence, and a conflict condition in which the label and evidence refer to different populations. On a quality-controlled diagnostic subset of GlobalOpinionQA, we select 100 population pairs and evaluate both reciprocal directions, yielding 200 directed contrasts and 3,200 likelihood-based predictions from four instruction-tuned models in the 7B-9B range. Country labels yield modest mean gains in fit to the named population (Country Influence: 0.028-0.071), whereas direct population evidence yields substantially larger gains (Evidence Influence: 0.184-0.284). The paired evidence advantage is positive for every model. Under conflict, normalized Evidence Override ranges from 0.543 to 0.728, 85.5-97.5\% of predictions are closer to the evidence population, and all four models agree on the evidence side for 161 of 200 contrasts. These results establish a clear hierarchy of steering signals: country names influence model behavior, but explicit population distributions exert far greater influence and usually prevail when the two disagree. The pattern is consistent with evidence-weighted updating from a weaker, defeasible country cue. Our audit provides an evaluation protocol for pluralistic alignment, connecting steerable and distributional pluralism by testing not merely whether a model can be steered toward different populations, but whether its behavior tracks the observed plurality within those populations.
filter_reasoning: The paper performs a causal audit of how population-grounded steering impacts model behavior, which is central to pluralistic value alignment.

venue_name: Proceedings of the First Workshop on Pluralistic Value Alignment of LLMs
title: PlurVA-LLM-2026 Shared Task Track-1: Curriculum Fine-Tuning with Soft Labels and Positional Consistency for Cross-Cultural Value Alignment
abstract: Pluralistic value alignment asks whether a language model can adapt its judgements to distinct, locally grounded value systems rather than reflecting a single aggregated notion of human preference. The PlurVA-LLM shared task evaluates this setting by unifying three independently constructed, culturally grounded multiple-choice value dilemmas across Chinese, Indonesian, and Sri Lankan datasets. We present a single-model submission based on Qwen3.5-4B with LoRA fine-tuning, trained only on the 1,359 labelled development instances provided by the task. Our method combines three ideas motivated directly by the task structure: soft-label supervision for Indonesian annotator-vote distributions, consistency regularisation across option permutations to reduce answer-position bias, and a staged multilingual curriculum with cross-validation-based iteration selection. On the hidden test set, our system achieves a macro-average accuracy of 0.8062, with 0.7788 on Chinese, 0.7139 on Indonesian, and 0.9260 on Sri Lankan, outperforming a manually tuned reference curriculum from our internal development. These results show that a single parameter-efficient model can unify culturally and structurally distinct value-alignment benchmarks under a low-resource training budget.
filter_reasoning: The paper addresses the challenge of pluralistic value alignment, specifically aiming to adapt LLMs to multiple diverse cultural value systems.

venue_name: Proceedings of the First Workshop on Pluralistic Value Alignment of LLMs
title: Concepts at Work: Testing Rival Conceptions of Liberty in Large Language Models
abstract: Work on pluralistic alignment asks whether language models can represent the range of things people value. That work often treats plurality as disagreement between values, preferences, or cultural positions. We study a different kind of disagreement: two people can share a value and still disagree about its meaning. Liberty is an example. On one view, you are unfree when someone blocks actions. On another, you are unfree when actions depend on unchecked power. We ask whether models prompted to hold one of these conceptual views are able to make it legible, transferable, and operative. We test this with five instruction-tuned models and one frontier reasoning model on 20 vignettes across five domains. Results show prompted views are usually legible and transferable, and these positions can coexist with reduced operativeness. Additionally, when we impose no view at all, models more often default to a non-domination conception of freedom.
filter_reasoning: The paper explores pluralistic value alignment in LLMs, specifically examining how models represent and operationalize complex philosophical concepts like liberty.

venue_name: Proceedings of the First Workshop on Pluralistic Value Alignment of LLMs
title: PlurVA-LLM-2026 Shared Task Track-2: PluriGuide---Principle Distillation and Identifier-Bound Demonstrations for Pluralistic Value Alignment
abstract: We present PluriGuide, a parameter-free system for the PlurVA-LLM 2026 shared task on pluralistic value alignment across China, Indonesia, and Sri Lanka. The central challenge is not factual recall but selecting among competing, culturally situated values from limited labeled data. Our system converts the development sets into compact decision guidance through a rationale-map-reduce pipeline. A reasoning model first produces gold-conditioned, structured rationales; it then abstracts these rationales within answer groups and reduces the group summaries into a small set of principles, failure modes, and, for Indonesia, plurality instructions. After a light human review, stable principle identifiers connect this guidance to deliberately selected few-shot demonstrations. Chinese demonstrations contrast procedural accountability with common avoidance patterns, while Indonesian demonstrations span unanimous, majority, and tied-plurality cases. Sinhala items use a task-specific four-label instruction without distilled principles. A single GPT-5.6-sol model performs all test-time inference without parameter updates or per-instance human intervention. On the official Track-2 leaderboard, PluriGuide obtains 0.764, 0.696, and 0.949 accuracy on the three datasets, respectively, for a macro-average of 0.803, placing second overall in the track. These results show that compact, culturally grounded decision rules can provide an effective interface between labeled examples and inference-time reasoning.
filter_reasoning: The paper addresses pluralistic value alignment across culturally distinct populations, focusing on the ethical challenge of aligning models to diverse social norms.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 3rd Workshop on Natural Language Processing for Political Sciences (PoliticalNLP 2026)
title: Reproducibility under Threat: Proposing a Framework for Reliable LLM-Research in Psychology and Computational Social Science
abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI), particularly large language models (LLMs), into research across the social sciences has accelerated innovation but also introduced significant challenges to reproducibility - a cornerstone of scientific integrity. In this review of scientific practices, we examine the reproducibility crisis in AI-driven research with a focus on psychology, identifying common pitfalls, reviewing proposed solutions, and advocating for best practices. Common pitfalls in current practices in the social sciences are identified and highlighted through synthesized research scenarios, such as: (1) using inaccessible datasets or language models with restricted access, (2) treating black-box API outputs as stable observations ignoring updates and hidden changes, (3) producing single runs for measurements instead of stochastic draws for aggregated performances, (4) failing to report full LLM version, prompting, and sampling parameters, and (5) opaque training and fine-tuning of LLMs. Our recommended practices include precisely documenting the model used, fixing all inference parameters, using automation and scripts to control prompts, context, and outputs, and standardizing the environment and API conditions. By embracing transparency and methodological rigour, we can transform the challenges of AI-driven research into opportunities for more robust and impactful science, ensuring that innovation never comes at the cost of credibility.
filter_reasoning: The paper advocates for methodological rigor and reproducibility in AI research, which is a critical aspect of AI safety/reliability.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 3rd Workshop on Natural Language Processing for Political Sciences (PoliticalNLP 2026)
title: Do LLMs Transfer Political Framing across Languages? A Cross-Lingual Analysis of LLM-Generated Discourse
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) increasingly mediate political information across linguistic contexts, concerns emerge regarding cross-lingual consistency in political framing. We investigate whether multilingual LLMs generate systematically different rhetorical and semantic frames when prompted in English versus Arabic on the politically salient issue of migration. Focusing on two widely used models, i.e., GPT-4o and Jais-13B, we implement a controlled prompt design (N = 800 generations; 400 per language), to isolate language as the primary experimental variable. We introduce a mixed method evaluation framework that combines lexical frame analysis, statistical association testing, and qualitative discourse analysis. Our results show a significant association between language and framing distribution (\chi2 = 43.32, p = 2.11 \texttimes 10-9). While security-oriented framing is prominent in both languages, English generations exhibit substantially higher rates of institutional and legislative framing, whereas Arabic generations show greater concentration in security and communitarian discourse. These findings indicate that input language acts as a conditioning signal that systematically modulates political framing within multilingual LLMs, even under controlled semantic prompts. We conceptualize this phenomenon as cross-lingual framing drift and discuss its implications for multilingual alignment, political bias evaluation, and global information ecosystems. We conclude by outlining an evaluative protocol for detecting language-conditioned asymmetries in generative models. We make all data, code, and experimental settings publicly available at: https://github.com/NRAwwad/-A-Cross-Lingual-Analysis-of-Political-Framing-in-English-and-Arabic.git.
filter_reasoning: The paper investigates cross-lingual political bias and framing drift in LLMs, which is a core concern in AI ethics.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 3rd Workshop on Natural Language Processing for Political Sciences (PoliticalNLP 2026)
title: When Neutral Turns Negative: Cross-Domain Failure Modes in Hinglish Political Sentiment Analysis
abstract: Sentiment analysis models are increasingly deployed to analyze political discourse, yet strong in-domain performance does not guarantee robustness under domain shift. We study cross-domain generalization in Hinglish (Hindi--English code-mixed) sentiment analysis by evaluating a fine-tuned XLM-RoBERTa classifier, trained on 29,000 general-domain Hinglish sentences, on a curated benchmark of politically oriented Hinglish text. While the model achieves 92.02\% accuracy in-domain, performance drops to 71.83\% under political domain shift. Error analysis reveals a pronounced directional bias with 48.9\% of neutral political statements misclassified as negative, indicating a systematic neutrality-to-negative shift. In addition, 87.5\% of incorrect predictions are assigned confidence scores above 95\%, pointing to severe miscalibration under distribution shift. We further compare these results against an instruction-tuned large language model (Llama 3.3), which achieves 90.85\% zero-shot accuracy and 94.37\% accuracy with contextual prompting, while substantially reducing neutrality bias. Our findings indicate the need for domain-aware evaluation, calibration diagnostics, and explicit reporting of failure modes when deploying sentiment models in politically sensitive settings.
filter_reasoning: The paper investigates miscalibration, domain shift, and neutrality bias in models used for sentiment analysis, which relates to AI safety and robustness.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 3rd Workshop on Natural Language Processing for Political Sciences (PoliticalNLP 2026)
title: PReSS: An Automated Black-Box Framework for Evaluating Political Stance Stability in LLMs
abstract: Existing evaluations of political bias in large language models (LLMs) typically classify outputs as left- or right-leaning. We extend this perspective by examining how ideological tendencies vary across topics and how consistently models maintain their positions, a property we refer to as stability. To capture this dimension, we propose PReSS (Political Response Stability under Stress), an automated black-box framework that evaluates LLMs by jointly considering model and topic context, categorizing responses into four stance types: stable-left, unstable-left, stable-right, and unstable-right. Applying PReSS to 9 widely used LLMs across 19 political topics reveals substantial variation in stance stability; for instance, a model that is left-leaning overall can exhibit stable-right behavior on certain topics. This highlights the importance of topic-aware and fine-grained evaluation of political ideologies of LLMs. Moreover, stability has practical implications for controlled generation and model alignment: interventions such as debiasing or ideology reversal should explicitly account for stance stability. Our empirical analyses reveal that when models are prompted or fine-tuned to adopt the opposite ideology, unstable topic stances are more likely to change, whereas stable ones resist modification. Thus, treating stability as a moderating factor provides a principled foundation for understanding, evaluating, and guiding interventions in politically sensitive model behavior.
filter_reasoning: The paper focuses on evaluating and controlling political bias and stance stability in LLMs, which is a fundamental AI ethics topic.

venue_name: Proceedings of the 3rd Workshop on Natural Language Processing for Political Sciences (PoliticalNLP 2026)
title: Cultural Adaptation in Large Language Models for Political Discourse
